# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ7 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ7 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; with page | SQ2 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; with page | SQ3 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated; with page | SQ4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased, and whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used, counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ7 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ7 |

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

# SQ16

## Question
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

Its stated goal "is not to provide an exhaustive overview of every actor system in existence" (p. 1). Does not cover kernels or hardware. |
| de Boer et al. (2017). *A Survey of Active Object Languages*. ACM Computing Surveys 50(5). | Compares four major actor and active-object languages along chosen dimensions (abstract). | Language level only; no operating system or hardware (abstract). |
| Tong (2025). *Descriptor-Based Object-Aware Memory Systems: A Comprehensive Review*. arXiv 2510.27070v2. | Survey of descriptor-based, object-aware memory systems as a way to bridge the semantic gap at the hardware/software interface (p. 1). | Covers memory objects and descriptors, not messages between objects or actors, and not the operating system (p. 1, Fig. 1 p. 2). |

No systematic (Kitchenham-style) review on message semantics below the language level was found. The agent lists the 12 web searches it ran on 2026-10-06; the last four returned primary papers, project pages or forum posts, not reviews.

## `criteria.md`: Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no date limit. "Message-based" means "meets I1".

| ID | Inclusion |
|---|---|
| I1 | The paper describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or OS kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level. That means one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate. Examples of (c) are microkernels, multikernels, and operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without a conventional kernel underneath. The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, IPC, method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | The paper is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one architecture its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven. It must report measured performance or a stated reason for that performance, adoption, abandonment, or the architecture becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | The paper is an empirical study of concurrency defects in real programs or systems, not only the authors' own examples. It must report counts or proportions split by communication mechanism (shared memory vs message passing), or for message-passing-only systems. (SQ7) |

| ID | Exclusion |
|---|---|
| X1 | Meets none of I1–I3. |
| X2 | Applies to papers included only through I1. Excluded if messages appear only at the application, library, runtime, VM or network-protocol level, on a processor with no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c). Examples: an actor library, the Erlang VM, MPI, a Smalltalk VM hosted on Unix or Windows. Does not apply under I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A cluster or network of separate conventional computers, where the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | Hardware stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (neural-network inference, DSP, packet switching, graphics) and not stated to run general programs. |
| X5 | Not one of these types: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or chapter; PhD or master's thesis; technical report from a university, research lab or standards body; ACM, IEEE or USENIX magazine article; manufacturer's reference manual. Patents, slides, posters, abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blogs, forums, encyclopaedias and brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | Full text not in English. |
| X7 | Full text not obtainable from the publisher, an author or institution page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive or the university library. The sources tried are recorded. |
| X8 | Same system and same results as another included paper. The longer one is kept; the other is kept too only if it adds a measurement, design element or stated reason. |
| X9 | Presented as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy, with no measurement of its own and no I2 reason of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

## `quality.md`: Quality checklist (yes / partly / no)

| ID | Question |
|---|---|
| Q1 | Is the aim or contribution stated explicitly? yes: in one place; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. |
| Q2 | Is the communication mechanism described well enough to reimplement it? The four points are message format, naming or addressing, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy. yes: all four; partly: 1–3; no: none. For I3 studies, the studied programs' mechanisms count instead. |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel running real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3: yes: real bug trackers or commits; partly: benchmark suites; no: examples only. |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim; partly: some; no: none. |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported (workloads and why they were chosen, configuration, number of runs or sample size)? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none. |
| Q6 | Is every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions backed by a table, figure or passage in the body? yes / partly / no. |
| Q7 | Are attributed causes supported by a measurement that isolates them, such as an ablation or breakdown? yes: every cause; partly: some; no: none, or only asserted. |
| Q8 | Are limitations or threats to validity discussed? yes: in a dedicated section or paragraph; partly: in passing; no: not at all. |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is a designer; partly: some are; no: all are, or nothing is evaluated. |

## `extraction-form.md`: Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field. Every field also records the page it comes from.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; the criteria that included it | SQ1–7 |
| Paper type | Design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, or empirical defect study | SQ1–7 |
| System | Name, year, builder; status (design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / commercial) | SQ1, 5, 6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, ISA, kernel, runtime/VM, language): is a send the primitive? yes / no / not stated | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages; whether its state can be read or written by anything else, and how | SQ1, 2, 7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; behaviour when busy; dispatch | SQ1, 3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every non-send mechanism kept (shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, DMA, I/O ports…), and at which level | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are written in the system's own objects and messages and which are outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change them | SQ2 |
| Interposition | Can a third component sit between sender and receiver without changing either? Mechanism and level | SQ3 |
| OS functions | Protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming, failure handling: how each is provided, and whether a central component is involved | SQ4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch, and on what hardware | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Core or node counts, metric, result at each count, baseline | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give, quoted or paraphrased closely, and whether a measurement isolates it | SQ5, 6 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system and every reason given for it; who states it (designers or a third party) | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Population, number of defects, categories, counts per mechanism, defects a design claims to prevent by construction | SQ7 |
| Quality | Q1–Q9, each with a page | SQ1–7 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures | SQ1–7 |

## SQ1–SQ7

Each file holds the question, *Why it matters to the observation*, and *Origin*.

**SQ1** (origin: observation): Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware? At which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold?
*Why:* the observation claims message abstractions stop above the OS and the hardware. This tests that claim against the systems that tried to go lower, and maps how far down each one got.

**SQ2** (observation): In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers)? Which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages?
*Why:* the observation says systems below the language rest on primitives that break their own rules, so they can't define themselves. This finds where each attempt kept such escape routes and how far its self-definition reached.

**SQ3** (observation): Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, and by what mechanism?
*Why:* networks allow layers in between because their parts talk only through messages, while low-level machines expose shared state where no layer can be put in between. Did earlier attempts below the language keep that property?

**SQ4** (notes): How do operating systems and machines built from message-passing parts that share no state provide protection, scheduling, resource allocation and naming? Which of these functions still rely on a central coordinator?
*Why:* the notes aim for no central coordinator and leave open how the usual OS functions would be provided.

**SQ5** (notes): What performance have message-based or object-based processors, instruction sets and kernels reported against conventional baselines? This includes the cost of one message send and the scaling with core count, and the causes the authors give for the differences.
*Why:* gathers the measured evidence H2 and H3 rest on, and the baselines and metrics later steps can reuse.

**SQ6** (notes): According to their designers and to later evaluations, why were language-directed, object-based and message-based machines abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary?
*Why:* H1 must be checked against the stated reasons for their decline.

**SQ7** (notes): What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?
*Why:* the notes motivate the thesis with shared-state bugs and already name the Go counter-evidence. This collects both sides.

# 1b, by `skeptic`

## SQ8–SQ19 (origin: counter-evidence, added by skeptic)

**SQ8:** What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?
*Why:* the premise "the machine model shapes how programs are written" rests only on two Turing Award lectures, which are essays, not measurements. If the language or runtime decides, changing the hardware doesn't change the programs, and the motivation needs another basis.

**SQ9:** What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap, by raising the hardware interface toward the language, harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation? Do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?
*Why:* the RISC argument (Patterson & Ditzel 1980) was made against exactly this goal. If it carries over, the observation describes a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.

**SQ10:** What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures? Can either be built on the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?
*Why:* Lauer & Needham (1978/79) argue the two are duals. If so, the gap may only be about which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing a layer above can't give.

**SQ11:** Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages? What do they report that the pure message model can't express or makes too costly?
*Why:* Tasharofi, Dinges & Johnson (2013, ECOOP) report that most large actor programs they studied mix models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers build escape routes whenever they can, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

**SQ12:** Where do measured costs and scaling limits come from in actor and message-passing runtimes on conventional hardware? Do their authors name the hardware's shared-memory model as the limiting factor, or report software techniques that remove the limit?
*Why:* compiler techniques already made language-specific processors unnecessary for Smalltalk and Self. If actor runtimes (e.g. on the Savina benchmarks, Imam & Sarkar 2014) hit limits a message machine wouldn't change, the "improve execution" half of the design problem is lost.

**SQ13:** Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels? How were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?
*Why:* H3's target has been built before: the Transputer with occam channels, and Intel's 48-core SCC (Howard et al. 2010, ISSCC). If those were dropped for reasons that still apply, H3 doesn't separate this work from earlier failures.

**SQ14:** What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory OS kernels scale to many cores? What limits do studies report on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?
*Why:* three sources each weaken a premise of H3 or of the parallel-hardware motivation:
- Martin, Hill & Sorin (2012, CACM): coherence can scale.
- Boyd-Wickizer et al. (2010, OSDI): no scalability reason to give up traditional kernels on 48 cores.
- Esmaeilzadeh et al. (2011, ISCA): dark silicon limits multicore scaling.

**SQ15:** Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement, or to work better with central or logically central coordination? What do decentralised versions cost or give up?
*Why:* agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (FLP 1985), and networking, the notes' own model, moved toward logically central control with SDN (Kreutz et al. 2015). If key OS functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

**SQ16:** What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms? What must remain outside it as a base, and what does that base cost or prevent?
*Why:* Smith's reflective tower (1984, POPL) is an infinite stack of levels, at least virtually, and Squeak's VM is written in Smalltalk but translated to C to run (Ingalls et al. 1997). If every self-defining system needs an outside base, the goal becomes moving the base, not removing it.

**SQ17:** Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, IOMMU)? How do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?
*Why:* the observation says low-level layers "cannot be put in between the way the network allows", yet virtualisation does exactly that (Popek & Goldberg 1974). SQ3 only looks at message-based systems, so it can't find this.

**SQ18:** What costs of object-based and capability-based hardware do independent evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves, rather than to compilers or implementation? How large are those costs?
*Why:* H2 rests on one paper by the 432's own evaluators, and that paper still names a 1–4× residual slowdown as inherent (Colwell et al. 1988, pp. 336–337, via the notes). Hansen et al. 1982 (citation not fully verified) and CHERI (Woodruff et al. 2014, ISCA) measure the cost from other angles.

**SQ19:** Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed? What factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?
*Why:* the specialisation that succeeded may be narrow and data-parallel (the TPU, Jouppi et al. 2018), far from general-purpose actor machines. The barriers that sank earlier machines may not have changed.

The review could only report how far down messages went, never that going down is unnecessary or impossible. | Reasoning: only SQ7 names a comparison. | Add SQ8–SQ19. Make `criteria.md` include papers that answer a counter-evidence SQ even if they never mention messages or objects. |
| SQ1 | Can't be answered as written: "message semantics hold" has no test. It also only samples systems that succeeded. | Reasoning. | Define a test for "holds at level L" in the extraction form (e.g. every state change at L is caused by a send). Record systems that started message-based and later added shared-memory paths. |

# Gate

How a skill runs a gate row. The decision is mine; the skill prepares it, records it, and checks it.

1. **Present.** For each file waiting at this gate: its path, one line on what it holds, and every flag raised by its reviews (`.skeptic.md`, `.citations.md`, `.examiner.md` next to it). Give the paths so I can open the files myself.
2. **Wait** for my decision on each file: accept, change, or reject. My decision is the only input to the next step; a file I have not decided on stays `proposed`.
3. **Apply.**
   - Accept: `status: accepted`.
   - Change: apply exactly the edits I give, then `status: changed`.
   - Reject: `status: rejected`.
   - Gates that assign values in a table (P IDs in 2b and 2d) write those values too.
4. **Record.** One decision file per decided file, from `ai/template/ai-log/decision.md`, saved as `research/ai-log/decisions/{date}-{row}-{id}.md`. *What I changed and why* holds my words. *Raw log entries* holds the session ID given at session start and the time span from the row's first dispatch to this gate (`ai/ai-log.md`).
5. **Check.** Run `just check`.

The gate is done when every file waiting at it has a status other than `proposed` and a decision file.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.

-What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?

+What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects, in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?
## Why it matters to the observation

The notes motivate the thesis by the share of concurrency bugs caused by shared state, and already name counter-evidence that message passing causes most blocking bugs in Go. This question collects both sides as published evidence.

The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |

| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |

| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. |

| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
-| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is not in English. |
+| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |

| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |

| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |

| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Selection criteria

| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |

| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |

| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only. (SQ7) |
+| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |
| ID | Exclusion criterion |
-| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3. |
+| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |

| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |

| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |

-| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. |

+| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |

| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |

| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |

# SLS 2 — Search

Runs one round of rows 2a–2d of `ai/flow-sls.md`, following `ai/running.md`. Requires the protocol frozen (1c done).

## Which round
- No `sls/2-search/R0.md` yet → the start set: rows 2a, 2b.
- Otherwise → round `k` = last round + 1: rows 2c, 2d, built from the papers included in round `k-1`.
- Round `k-1` included no new papers → the stop rule is already met: tell me and stop.

2. **2b / 2d** — gate. I decide each candidate; included papers get the next free P IDs, in order, written in the round file's *P ID* column and *Newly included* section.

Done when the round's gate is done.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).
----
# Flow: SLS

Rows run by the `sls` skill (`skills.md`), after step 0 (`kickstart.md`). Paths are relative to `research/`. `{n}` is an ID number, `{k}` a round number. Every gate also writes one decision file (`ai-log.md`). `↺` rows are loop decisions.

| # | Who | Input | Output | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SLS 1 Protocol** · `sls-1-protocol` | | | | |
| 1a | `protocol-critic` | `0-start/*.md` | `sls/1-protocol/`: `need.md`, `SQ{n}.md`, `criteria.md`, `quality.md`, `extraction-form.md` | — |
| 1b | `skeptic` | `0-start/*.md`, `sls/1-protocol/SQ*.md` | `sls/1-protocol/SQ{n}.md` (counter-evidence SQs), `protocol.skeptic.md` | — |
| 1c | Me | 1a + 1b files | Status of each set | **Protocol frozen.** Later changes: `sls/1-protocol/changes/{date}-{slug}.md` |
| **SLS 2 Search** · `sls-2-search` | | | | |
| 2a | `snowballer` | `sls/1-protocol/criteria.md`, `0-start/seeds.md` | `sls/2-search/search-string.md`, `R0.md` (candidates, each with its I/X criterion) | — |
| 2b | Me | `sls/2-search/R0.md` | P IDs assigned in `R0.md` | **Include/exclude** |
| 2c | `snowballer` | `sls/2-search/R{k-1}*.md`, `sls/1-protocol/criteria.md` | `sls/2-search/R{k}-backward.md`, `R{k}-forward.md` | — |
| 2d | Me | 2c files | P IDs assigned | **Include/exclude** |

| 3a | `reader` | `papers/P{n}.pdf` (else the paper online), `sls/1-protocol/quality.md`, `extraction-form.md` | `sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`, `papers/P{n}.pdf` if downloaded | — |
| 3b | `citation-checker` | `sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`, the paper | `sls/3-reading/P{n}.citations.md` | — |
| 3c | Me | 3a + 3b files | Status set; key papers read in full; PDFs published with `just papers-push` | **Record accepted** |
| **SLS 4 Synthesis** · `sls-4-synthesis` | | | | |
| 4a | `synthesizer` | Accepted `sls/3-reading/P*.md`, `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` | `sls/4-synthesis/C{n}.md` (definition, papers, comparison), new or updated | — |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## W2035362408 1985 article | Impossibility of distributed consensus with one faulty process | Michael J. Fischer, Nancy Ann Lynch, Michael S. Paterson | Journal of the ACM | pp 374-382
   The consensus problem involves an asynchronous system of processes, some of which may be unreliable. The problem is for the reliable processes to agree on a binary value. In this paper, it is shown that every protocol for this problem has the possibility of nontermination, even with only one faulty process. By way of contrast, solutions are known for the synchronous case, the “Byzantine Generals” problem.

   Conventional programming languages are growing ever more enormous, but not stronger. Inherent defects at the most basic level cause them to be both fat and weak: their primitive word-at-a-time style of programming inherited from their common ancestor—the von Neumann computer, their close coupling of semantics to state transitions, their division of programming into a world of expressions and a world of statements, their inability to effectively use powerful combining forms for building new programs from existing ones, and their lack of useful mathematical properties for reasoning about programs.    Since 2005, processor designers have increased core counts to exploit Moore’s Law scaling, rather than focusing on single-core performance. The failure of Dennard scaling, to which the shift to multicore parts is partially a response, may soon limit multicore scaling just as single-core scaling has been curtailed. This paper models multicore scaling limits by combining device scaling, single-core scaling, and multicore scaling to measure the speedup potential for a set of parallel workloads for the next five technology generations. For device scaling, we use both the ITRS projections and a set of more conservative device scaling parameters. To model singlecore scaling, we combine measurement

   The design challenge for large-scale multiprocessors is (1) to minimize communication overhead, (2) allow communication to overlap computation, and (3) coordinate the two without sacrificing processor cost/performance. We show that existing message passing multiprocessors have unnecessarily high communication costs. Research prototypes of message driven machines demonstrate low communication overhead, but poor processor cost/performance. We introduce a simple communication mechanism, Active Messages, show that it is intrinsic to both architectures, allows cost effective use of the hardware, and offers tremendous flexibility.    Virtual machine systems have been implemented on a limited number of third generation computer systems, e.g. CP-67 on the IBM 360/67. From previous empirical studies, it is known that certain third generation computer systems, e.g. the DEC PDP-10, cannot support a virtual machine system. In this paper, model of a third-generation-like computer system is developed. Formal techniques are used to derive precise sufficient conditions to test whether such an architecture can support virtual machines.

   Commodity computer systems contain more and more processor cores and exhibit increasingly diverse architectural tradeoffs, including memory hierarchies, interconnects, instruction sets and variants, and IO configurations. Previous high-performance computing systems have scaled in specific cases, but the dynamic nature of modern client and server workloads, coupled with the impossibility of statically optimizing an OS for all workloads and hardware variants pose serious challenges for operating system structures.

   Many operating system designs can be placed into one of two very rough categories, depending upon how they implement and use the notions of process and synchronization. One category, the "Message-oriented System," is characterized by a relatively small, static number of processes with an explicit message system for communicating among them.    This paper analyzes the scalability of seven system applications (Exim, memcached, Apache, PostgreSQL, gmake, Psearchy, and MapReduce) running on Linux on a 48core computer. Except for gmake, all applications trigger scalability bottlenecks inside a recent Linux kernel. Using mostly standard parallel programming techniques— this paper introduces one new technique, sloppy counters—these bottlenecks can be removed from the kernel or avoided by changing the applications slightly. Modifying the kernel required in total 3002 lines of code changes. A speculative conclusion from this analysis is that there is no scalability reason to give up on traditional operating system organizations just yet. 1

   Go is a statically-typed programming language that aims to provide a simple, efficient, and safe way to build multi-threaded software. # Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

# Quality assessment checklist

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. # Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |

| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

| Field | What to record | Serves |

| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

# Quality assessment checklist

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. | yes / partly / no |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. | yes / partly / no |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. | yes / partly / no |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. | yes / partly / no |

# Quality assessment checklist

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. | yes / partly / no |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. | yes / partly / no |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. | yes / partly / no |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. | yes / partly / no |
