# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).

# Quality assessment checklist

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. | yes / partly / no |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. | yes / partly / no |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. | yes / partly / no |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. | yes / partly / no |

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Quality assessment checklist

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. | yes / partly / no |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. | yes / partly / no |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. | yes / partly / no |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. | yes / partly / no |

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Quality assessment checklist

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. | yes / partly / no |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. | yes / partly / no |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. | yes / partly / no |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. | yes / partly / no |

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1/I2/I3) | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Paper type | One of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

[p1] Introduction
[p1] 
[p1] Go [20] is a statically typed language originally developed
[p1] by Google in 2009. Over the past few years, it has quickly
[p1] gained attraction and is now adopted by many types of software in real production. These Go applications range from
[p1] libraries [19] and high-level software [26] to cloud infrastructure software like container systems [13, 36] and key-value
[p1] databases [10, 15].
[p1] A major design goal of Go is to improve traditional multithreaded programming languages and make concurrent programming easier and less error-prone. For this purpose, Go
[p1] centers its multi-threading design around two principles:
[p1] 1) making threads (called goroutines) lightweight and easy
[p1] to create and 2) using explicit messaging (called channel)
[p1] to communicate across threads. With these design principles, Go proposes not only a set of new primitives and new
[p1] libraries but also new implementation of existing semantics.
[p1] It is crucial to understand how Go’s new concurrency primitives and mechanisms impact concurrency bugs, the type of
[p1] bugs that is the most difficult to debug and the most widely
[p1] studied [40, 43, 45, 57, 61] in traditional multi-threaded programming languages. Unfortunately, there has been no prior
[p1] work in studying Go concurrency bugs. As a result, to date,
[p1] it is still unclear if these concurrency mechanisms actually
[p1] make Go easier to program and less error-prone to concurrency bugs than traditional languages.
[p1] In this paper, we conduct the first empirical study on
[p1] Go concurrency bugs using six open-source, productiongrade Go applications: Docker [13] and Kubernetes [36],
[p1] two datacenter container systems, etcd [15], a distributed
[p1] key-value store system, gRPC [19], an RPC library, and CockroachDB [10] and BoltDB [6], two database systems.
[p1] In total, we have studied 171 concurrency bugs in these applications. We analyzed the root causes of them, performed
[p1] experiments to reproduce them, and examined their fixing
[p1] 
[p1]  patches. Finally, we tested them with two existing Go concurrency bug detectors (the only publicly available ones).
[p2] Our study focuses on a long-standing and fundamental
[p2] question in concurrent programming: between message passing [27, 37] and shared memory, which of these inter-thread
[p2] communication mechanisms is less error-prone [2, 11, 48].
[p2] Go is a perfect language to study this question, since it provides frameworks for both shared memory and message
[p2] passing. However, it encourages the use of channels over
[p2] shared memory with the belief that explicit message passing
[p2] is less error-prone [1, 2, 21].
[p2] To understand Go concurrency bugs and the comparison
[p2] between message passing and shared memory, we propose
[p2] to categorize concurrency bugs along two orthogonal dimensions: the cause of bugs and their behavior. Along the cause
[p2] dimension, we categorize bugs into those that are caused
[p2] by misuse of shared memory and those caused by misuse of
[p2] message passing. Along the second dimension, we separate
[p2] bugs into those that involve (any number of) goroutines that
[p2] cannot proceed (we call them blocking bugs) and those that
[p2] do not involve any blocking (non-blocking bugs).
[p2] Surprisingly, our study shows that it is as easy to make concurrency bugs with message passing as with shared memory,
[p2] sometimes even more. For example, around 58% of blocking
[p2] bugs are caused by message passing. In addition to the violation of Go’s channel usage rules (e.g., waiting on a channel
[p2] that no one sends data to or close), many concurrency bugs
[p2] are caused by the mixed usage of message passing and other
[p2] new semantics and new libraries in Go, which can easily be
[p2] overlooked but hard to detect.
[p2] To demonstrate errors in message passing, we use a blocking bug from Kubernetes in Figure 1. The finishReq function creates a child goroutine using an anonymous function at line 4 to handle a request—a common practice in
[p2] Go server programs. The child goroutine executes fn() and
[p2] sends result back to the parent goroutine through channel
[p2] ch at line 6. The child will block at line 6 until the parent
[p2] pulls result from ch at line 9. Meanwhile, the parent will
[p2] block at select until either when the child sends result to ch
[p2] (line 9) or when a timeout happens (line 11). If timeout happens earlier or if Go runtime (non-deterministically) chooses

[p2] return from requestReq() at line 12, and no one else can

[p2] blocked forever. The fix is to change ch from an unbuffered
[p2] channel to a buffered one, so that the child goroutine can

[p2] Background and Applications
[p2] 
[p2] Go is a statically-typed programming language that is designed for concurrent programming from day one [60]. Almost all major Go revisions include improvements in its concurrency packages [23]. This section gives a brief background
[p2] on Go’s concurrency mechanisms, including its thread model,
[p2] inter-thread communication methods, and thread synchronization mechanisms. We also introduce the six Go applications we chose for this study.
[p2] 2.1
[p2] 
[p2] Goroutine
[p2] 
[p2] Go uses a concept called goroutine as its concurrency unit.
[p2] Goroutines are lightweight user-level threads that the Go
[p2] 
[p2]  runtime library manages and maps to kernel-level threads
[p3] in an M-to-N way. A goroutine can be created by simply
[p3] adding the keyword go before a function call.
[p3] To make goroutines easy to create, Go also supports creating a new goroutine using an anonymous function, a function
[p3] definition that has no identifier, or “name”. All local variables
[p3] declared before an anonymous function are accessible to the
[p3] anonymous function, and are potentially shared between
[p3] a parent goroutine and a child goroutine created using the
[p3] anonymous function, causing data race (Section 6).
[p3] 2.2
[p3] 
[p3] Synchronization with Shared Memory
[p3] 
[p3] Go supports traditional shared memory accesses across
[p3] goroutines. It supports various traditional synchronization primitives like lock/unlock (Mutex), read/write lock
[p3] (RWMutex), condition variable (Cond), and atomic read/write
[p3] (atomic). Go’s implementation of RWMutex is different from
[p3] pthread_rwlock_t in C. Write lock requests in Go have a
[p3] higher privilege than read lock requests.
[p3] As a new primitive introduced by Go, Once is designed
[p3] to guarantee a function is only executed once. It has a Do
[p3] method, with a function f as argument. When Once.Do(f)
[p3] is invoked many times, only for the first time, f is executed.
[p3] Once is widely used to ensure a shared variable only be
[p3] initialized once by multiple goroutines.
[p3] Similar to pthread_join in C, Go uses WaitGroup to allow multiple goroutines to finish their shared variable accesses before a waiting goroutine. Goroutines are added to
[p3] a WaitGroup by calling Add. Goroutines in a WaitGroup use
[p3] Done to notify their completion, and a goroutine calls Wait
[p3] to wait for the completion notification of all goroutines in
[p3] a WaitGroup. Misusing WaitGroup can cause both blocking
[p3] bugs (Section 5) and non-blocking bugs (Section 6).
[p3] 2.3
[p3] 
[p3] Synchronization with Message Passing
[p3] 
[p3] Channel (chan) is a new concurrency primitive introduced
[p3] by Go to send data and states across goroutines and to build
[p3] more complex functionalities [3, 50]. Go supports two types
[p3] of channels: buffered and unbuffered. Sending data to (or
[p3] receiving data from) an unbuffered channel will block a goroutine, until another goroutine receives data from (or sends
[p3] data to) the channel. Sending to a buffered channel will only
[p3] block, when the buffer is full. There are several underlying
[p3] rules in using channels and the violation of them can create
[p3] concurrency bugs. For example, channel can only be used
[p3] after initialization, and sending data to (or receiving data
[p3] from) a nil channel will block a goroutine forever. Sending
[p3] data to a closed channel or close an already closed channel
[p3] can trigger a runtime panic.
[p3] The select statement allows a goroutine to wait on multiple channel operations. A select will block until one of its
[p3] cases can make progress or when it can execute a default
[p3] branch. When more than one cases in a select are valid, Go
[p3] 
[p3] will randomly choose one to execute. This randomness can
[p3] cause concurrency bugs as will be discussed in Section 6.
[p3] Go introduces several new semantics to ease the interaction across multiple goroutines. For example, to assist the
[p3] programming model of serving a user request by spawning a set of goroutines that work together, Go introduces
[p3] context to carry request-specific data or metadata across
[p3] goroutines. As another example, Pipe is designed to stream
[p3] data between a Reader and a Writer. Both context and
[p3] Pipe are new forms of passing messages and misusing them
[p3] can create new types of concurrency bugs (Section 5).

[p3] Go Applications
[p3] 
[p3] Recent years have seen a quick increase in popularity and
[p3] adoption of the Go language. Go was the 9th most popular
[p3] language on GitHub in 2017 [18]. As of the time of writing,
[p3] there are 187K GitHub repositories written in Go.
[p3] In this study, we selected six representative, real-world
[p3] software written in Go, including two container systems
[p3] (Docker and Kubernetes), one key-value store system (etcd),
[p3] two databases (CockroachDB and BoltDB), and one RPC
[p3] library (gRPC-go1 ) (Table 1). These applications are opensource projects that have gained wide usages in datacenter
[p3] environments. For example, Docker and Kubernetes are the
[p3] top 2 most popular applications written in Go on GitHub,
[p3] with 48.9K and 36.5K stars (etcd is the 10th, and the rest are
[p3] ranked in top 100). Our selected applications all have at least
[p3] three years of development history and are actively maintained by developers currently. All our selected applications
[p3] are of middle to large sizes, with lines of code ranging from 9
[p3] thousand to more than 2 million. Among the six applications,
[p3] Kubernetes and gRPC are projects originally developed by
[p3] Google.

[p3] Go Concurrency Usage Patterns
[p3] 
[p3] Before studying Go concurrency bugs, it is important to first
[p3] understand how real-world Go concurrent programs are like.
[p3] This section presents our static and dynamic analysis results

p1: Commodity computer systems contain more and more
p1: processor cores and exhibit increasingly diverse architectural tradeoffs, including memory hierarchies, interconnects, instruction sets and variants, and IO configurations. Previous high-performance computing systems
p1: have scaled in specific cases, but the dynamic nature of
p1: modern client and server workloads, coupled with the
p1: impossibility of statically optimizing an OS for all workloads and hardware variants pose serious challenges for
p1: operating system structures.
p1: We argue that the challenge of future multicore hardware is best met by embracing the networked nature of
p1: the machine, rethinking OS architecture using ideas from
p1: distributed systems. We investigate a new OS structure,
p1: the multikernel, that treats the machine as a network of
p1: independent cores, assumes no inter-core sharing at the
p1: lowest level, and moves traditional OS functionality to
p1: a distributed system of processes that communicate via
p1: message-passing.
p1: We have implemented a multikernel OS to show that
p1: the approach is promising, and we describe how traditional scalability problems for operating systems (such
p1: as memory management) can be effectively recast using
p1: messages and can exploit insights from distributed systems and networking. An evaluation of our prototype on
p1: multicore systems shows that, even on present-day machines, the performance of a multikernel is comparable
p1: with a conventional OS, and can scale better to support
p1: future hardware.

p2: The model we develop, called a multikernel (Figure 1),
p2: is not only a better match to the underlying hardware
p2: (which is networked, heterogeneous, and dynamic), but
p2: allows us to apply insights from distributed systems to
p2: the problems of scale, adaptivity, and diversity in operating systems for future hardware.
p2: Even on present systems with efficient cache-coherent
p2: shared memory, building an OS using message-based
p2: rather than shared-data communication offers tangible
p2: benefits: instead of sequentially manipulating shared
p2: data structures, which is limited by the latency of remote data access, the ability to pipeline and batch messages encoding remote operations allows a single core
p2: to achieve greater throughput and reduces interconnect
p2: utilization. Furthermore, the concept naturally accommodates heterogeneous hardware.
p2: The contributions of this work are as follows:
p2: 
p2: In this section, we argue that the challenges facing a
p2: general-purpose operating system on future commodity
p2: hardware are different from those associated with traditional ccNUMA and SMP machines used for highperformance computing. In a previous paper [8] we argued that single computers increasingly resemble networked systems, and should be programmed as such.
p2: We rehearse that argument here, but also lay out additional scalability challenges for general-purpose system
p2: software.

p2: 2.1
p2: 
p2: A general-purpose OS today must perform well on an
p2: increasingly diverse range of system designs, each with
p2: different performance characteristics [60]. This means
p2: that, unlike large systems for high-performance computing, such an OS cannot be optimized at design or implementation time for any particular hardware configuration.
p2: To take one specific example: Dice and Shavit show
p2: how a reader-writer lock can be built to exploit the
p2: shared, banked L2 cache on the Sun Niagara processor [40], using concurrent writes to the same cache line
p2: to track the presence of readers [20]. On Niagara this is
p2: highly efficient: the line remains in the L2 cache. On a
p2: traditional multiprocessor, it is highly inefficient: the line
p2: ping-pongs between the readers’ caches.
p2: This illustrates a general problem: any OS design tied
p2: to a particular synchronization scheme (and data layout policy) cannot exploit features of different hardware.
p2: Current OS designs optimize for the common hardware
p2: case; this becomes less and less efficient as hardware becomes more diverse. Worse, when hardware vendors introduce a design that offers a new opportunity for optimization, or creates a new bottleneck for existing designs, adapting the OS to the new environment can be
p2: prohibitively difficult.
p2: Even so, operating systems are forced to adopt increasingly complex optimizations [27, 46, 51, 52, 57] in
p2: order to make efficient use of modern hardware. The recent scalability improvements to Windows7 to remove
p2: the dispatcher lock touched 6000 lines of code in 58
p2: files and have been described as “heroic” [58]. The
p2: Linux read-copy update implementation required numerous iterations due to feature interaction [50]. Backporting receive-side-scaling support to Windows Server 2003
p2: caused serious problems with multiple other network
p2: subsystems including firewalls, connection-sharing and
p2: even Exchange servers1 .

p2: In the next section, we survey trends in hardware which

[p5] bugs in other languages [40, 42, 45]. Some of them are related to new concurrency primitives or libraries introduced

[p5] Bug taxonomy. We propose a new method to categorize Go
[p5] concurrency bugs according to two orthogonal dimensions.
[p5] The first dimension is based on the behavior of bugs. If one or
[p5] more goroutines are unintentionally stuck in their execution
[p5] and cannot move forward, we call such concurrency issues
[p5] blocking bugs. If instead all goroutines can finish their tasks
[p5] but their behaviors are not desired, we call them non-blocking
[p5] ones. Most previous concurrency bug studies [24, 43, 45]
[p5] categorize bugs into deadlock bugs and non-deadlock bugs,
[p5] where deadlocks include situations where there is a circular
[p5] wait across multiple threads. Our definition of blocking is
[p5] broader than deadlocks and include situations where there
[p5] is no circular wait but one (or more) goroutines wait for
[p5] resources that no other goroutines supply. As we will show
[p5] in Section 5, quite a few Go concurrency bugs are of this
[p5] kind. We believe that with new programming habits and
[p5] semantics with new languages like Go, we should pay more
[p5] attention to these non-deadlock blocking bugs and extend
[p5] the traditional concurrency bug categorization mechanism.
[p5] The second dimension is along the cause of concurrency
[p5] bugs. Concurrency bugs happen when multiple threads try to
[p5] communicate and errors happen during such communication.
[p5] Our idea is thus to categorize causes of concurrency bugs by
[p5] how different goroutines communicate: by accessing shared
[p5] memory or by passing messages. This categorization can
[p5] help programmers and researchers choose better ways to
[p5] perform inter-thread communication and to detect and avoid
[p5] potential errors when performing such communication.

[p5] of 85 blocking bugs and 86 non-blocking bugs, and there
[p5] are a total of 105 bugs caused by wrong shared memory

[p6] Blocking Bugs
[p6] This section presents our study results on blocking bugs,
[p6] including their root causes, fixes, and the effectiveness of the
[p6] built-in runtime Go deadlock detector on detecting blocking

[p6] Root Causes of Blocking Bugs
[p6] Blocking bugs manifest when one or more goroutines conduct operations that wait for resources, and these resources
[p6] are never available. To detect and avoid blocking bugs, it is
[p6] important to understand their root causes. We study blocking bugs’ root causes by examining which operation blocks
[p6] a goroutine and why the operation is not unblocked by other
[p6] goroutines. Using our second dimension of bug categorization, we separate blocking bugs into those that are caused by
[p6] stuck operations that are intended to protect shared memory accesses and those that are caused by message passing
[p6] operations. Table 6 summarizes the root causes of all the
[p6] blocking bugs.
[p6] Overall, we found that there are around 42% blocking bugs
[p6] caused by errors in protecting shared memory, and 58% are
[p6] caused by errors in message passing. Considering that shared
[p6] memory primitives are used more frequently than message
[p6] passing ones (Section 3.2), message passing operations are
[p6] even more likely to cause blocking bugs.
[p6] Observation 3: Contrary to the common belief that message
[p6] passing is less error-prone, more blocking bugs in our studied
[p6] Go applications are caused by wrong message passing than by
[p6] wrong shared memory protection.
[p6] (mis)Protection of Shared Memory
[p6] Shared memory accesses are notoriously hard to program
[p6] correctly and have always been one of the major focuses
[p6] on deadlock research [35, 51, 54]. They continue to cause
[p6] blocking bugs in Go, both with traditional patterns and new,
[p6] Go-specific reasons.
[p6] Mutex 28 blocking bugs are caused by misusing locks
[p6] (Mutex), including double locking, acquiring locks in conflicting orders, and forgetting to unlock. All bugs in this category
