[p6] RWMutex As explained in Section 2.2, Go’s write lock requests have a higher privilege than read lock requests. This
[p6] unique lock implementation can lead to a blocking bug when
[p6] a goroutine (th-A) acquires one RWMutex twice with read
[p6] locking, and these two read lock operations are interleaved
[p6] by a write lock operation from another goroutine (th-B).
[p6] When th-A’s first read lock operation succeeds, it will block
[p6] th-B’s write lock operation, since write locking is exclusive.
[p6] However, th-B’s write lock operation will also block th-A’s
[p6] second read lock operation, since the write lock request has
[p6] a higher privilege in Go’s implementation. Neither th-A nor
[p6] th-B will be able to proceed.
[p6] Five blocking bugs are caused by this reason. Note that the
[p6] same interleaving locking pattern will not cause blocking
[p6] bugs for pthread_rwlock_t in C, since pthread_rwlock_t
[p6] prioritize read lock requests under the default setting. The
[p6] RWMutex blocking bug type implies that even when Go uses
[p6] the same concurrency semantics as traditional languages,
[p6] there can still be new types of bugs because of Go’s new
[p6] implementation of the semantics.

p5: The multikernel model
p5: In this section we present our OS architecture for heterogeneous multicore machines, which we call the multikernel model. In a nutshell, we structure the OS as a
p5: distributed system of cores that communicate using messages and share no memory (Figure 1). The multikernel
p5: model is guided by three design principles:
p5: 1. Make all inter-core communication explicit.
p5: 2. Make OS structure hardware-neutral.
p5: 3. View state as replicated instead of shared.
p5: These principles allow the OS to benefit from the
p5: distributed systems approach to gain improved performance, natural support for hardware heterogeneity,
p5: greater modularity, and the ability to reuse algorithms
p5: developed for distributed systems.
p5: After discussing the principles in detail below, in Section 4 we explore the implications of these principles by
p5: describing the implementation of Barrelfish, a new operating system based on the multikernel model.
p5: 3.1
p5: Make inter-core communication explicit
p5: Within a multikernel OS, all inter-core communication
p5: is performed using explicit messages. A corollary is that
p5: no memory is shared between the code running on each
p5: core, except for that used for messaging channels. As
p5: we have seen, using messages to access or update state
p5: rapidly becomes more efficient than shared-memory access as the number of cache-lines involved increases. We
p5: can expect such effects to become more pronounced in
p5: the future. Note that this does not preclude applications
p5: sharing memory between cores (see Section 4.8), only
p5: that the OS design itself does not rely on it.
p5: Explicit communication patterns facilitate reasoning
p5: about the use of the system interconnect. In contrast

p6: A multikernel separates the OS structure as much as possible from the hardware. This means that there are just
p6: two aspects of the OS as a whole that are targeted at
p6: specific machine architectures – the messaging transport
p6: mechanisms, and the interface to hardware (CPUs and

p6: cross-cutting changes to the code base (as was the case
p6: with recent scalability enhancements to Linux and Windows). This will become increasingly important as deployed systems become more diverse.

p6: crucially dependent on hardware-specific optimizations

p6: Hardware-independence in a multikernel means that we

1: 1. Introduction
1: 
1: The reality of multi-core hardware has made concurrent programs
1: pervasive. Unfortunately, writing correct concurrent programs is
1: difficult. Addressing this challenge requires advances in multiple
1: directions, including concurrency bug detection, concurrent program testing, concurrent programming model design, etc. Designing effective techniques in all these directions will significantly
1: benefit from a deep understanding of real world concurrency bug

1: This paper provides the first (to the best of our knowledge) comprehensive real world concurrency bug characteristic study. Specifically, we have carefully examined concurrency bug patterns, manifestation, and fix strategies of 105 randomly selected real world
1: concurrency bugs from 4 representative server and client opensource applications (MySQL, Apache, Mozilla and OpenOffice).
1: Our study reveals several interesting findings and provides useful guidance for concurrency bug detection, testing, and concurrent
1: programming language design.
1: Some of our findings are as follows: (1) Around one third of
1: the examined non-deadlock concurrency bugs are caused by violation to programmers’ order intentions, which may not be easily
1: expressed via synchronization primitives like locks and transactional memories; (2) Around 34% of the examined non-deadlock

1: non-deadlock concurrency bugs were not fixed by simply adding
1: or changing locks, and many of the fixes were not correct at the
1: first try, indicating the difficulty of reasoning concurrent execution
1: by programmers.

1: Motivation
1: 
1: Concurrent programs are becoming prevalent due to the reality
1: of multi-core hardware. Nowadays, not only high-end servers but
1: also desktop machines need concurrent programs to make the best
1: use of their multi-core hardware. As a result, the difficulty of
1: concurrent programming is hitting the entire software development
1: community, rather than just the elite few. Writing good quality
1: concurrent programs has become critically important.
1: Unfortunately, writing correct concurrent programs is difficult.
1: Most programmers think sequentially and therefore they make mistakes easily when writing concurrent programs. Even worse, the
1: notorious non-determinism of concurrent programs makes concurrency bugs difficult to repeat during interactive diagnosis.
1: Addressing the above challenges will require efforts from multiple related directions including those listed as follows, all of which
1: have made some progress over the past years but still have many
1: open, unsolved issues:
1: (1) Concurrency bug detection Most previous concurrency bug
1: detection research has focused on detecting data race bugs [7, 10,
1: 31, 33, 37, 42] and deadlock bugs [3, 10, 37]. Data race occurs when
1: two conflicting accesses to one shared variable are executed without proper synchronization, e.g., not protected by a common lock.
1: Deadlock occurs when two or more operations circularly wait for
1: each other to release the acquired resource (e.g., locks). Recently,
1: several approaches have also been proposed to detect atomicityviolation bugs [12, 23, 41], which are caused by concurrent execution unexpectedly violating the atomicity of a certain code region.
1: Although previous work has proposed effective methods to detect certain types of concurrency bugs, it is still far from providing a complete solution. In particular, several open questions about
1: concurrency bug detection still remain: (i) Can existing bug detection tools detect all real world concurrency bugs? Specifically, what
1: types of concurrency bugs exist in real world? Is there any type that
1: has not been addressed yet by existing work? In addition, are the
1: assumptions of existing tools about concurrency bugs valid? For example, most previous race detection and many atomicity bug detection techniques focus on synchronization among accesses to a single variable. How many concurrency bugs are missed by this single
1: variable assumption? (ii) How helpful are existing tools in diagnosing and fixing the real world concurrency bugs detected by them?
1: For example, many concurrency bug detection tools remind programmers that some conflicting accesses are not protected by the
1: same lock. Such information can help programmers add or change
1: lock operations. However, how often are real world bugs fixed by
1: adding or changing lock operations? More generally, how do pro-

2:  grammers fix real world concurrency bugs and what information do
2: they need?
2: (2) Concurrent program testing and model checking Testing is
2: a common practice in software development. It is a critical step for
2: exposing software bugs before release.
2: Existing testing techniques mainly focus on the sequential aspects of programs, such as statements, branches, etc. and can not effectively address concurrent programs’ concurrency aspects, such
2: as multi-thread (or multi-process) interleavings [28].
2: The major challenge of concurrency testing is the exponential interleaving space of concurrent programs. Exposing concurrency bugs requires not only a bug-exposing input, but also a bugtriggering execution interleaving. Therefore, to achieve a complete
2: testing coverage of concurrent programs, testing needs to cover every possible interleaving for each input test case [39], which is infeasible in practice.
2: To address the above challenge, an open question in concurrency testing is as follows: can we selectively test a small number of representative interleavings and still expose most of the concurrency bugs? Motivated by this problem, previous work such as
2: the ConTest project [4, 9] has proposed some methods to perturb
2: program execution and force certain interleavings by injecting artificial delays after every synchronization point. While an inspiring attempt, it is unclear, both quantitatively and qualitatively, what
2: portion of concurrency bugs can be exposed by such heuristics.
2: Ultimately, designing practical and effective test cases for concurrent programs requires a good understanding of the manifestation conditions of real world concurrency bugs. That is, we need
2: to know what conditions are needed, besides program inputs, to reliably trigger a concurrency bug. Specifically, how many threads,
2: how many variables, and how many accesses are usually involved
2: in a real world concurrency bug’s manifestation?
2: Similar questions are also encountered in software verification
2: and model checking [13, 28, 34] for concurrent programs. Better
2: understanding of the manifestation of real world concurrency bugs
2: can help model checking prioritize the program states and alleviate
2: its state explosion problem.
2: (3) Concurrent programming language design Good concurrent programming languages can help programmers correctly express their intentions and therefore avoid certain types of concurrency bugs. Along this direction, transactional memory (TM)
2: [1,2,15,16,25,26,27,36] is one of the popular trends. TM provides
2: programmers an easier way to specify which code regions should
2: be atomic. Further, it automatically protects the atomicity of the
2: specified region against other specified regions through underlying
2: hardware and software support.
2: Although TM shows great potential, there are many open questions, including (i) What portion of bugs can be avoided by using
2: TM? (ii) What are the real world concerns that TM design needs
2: to pay attention to? (iii) Besides TM, what other programming language supports will be useful for programmers to write correct concurrent programs?
2: Addressing the open questions in all of the above directions
2: will significantly benefit from a better understanding of real world
2: concurrency bug characteristics—basically, we can learn from the
2: common mistakes programmers are making in writing concurrent
2: programs. For example, if many real world concurrency bugs involve multiple shared variables, we need to extend concurrency bug
2: detection techniques to address multi-variable concurrency bugs; if

2: testing only needs to cover pairwise interleavings for every pair of
2: program threads; if there are some concerns in avoiding real world
2: concurrency bugs with existing synchronization primitives, we can

2: extend transactional memory model or design new language support to further ease writing concurrent programs; if a certain type of
2: information is frequently used by programmers in fixing real world
2: concurrency bugs, bug detection tools can be extended to provide
2: such information and thus become more useful in practice.
2: In the past, many empirical studies on general program bug
2: characteristics (not specific to concurrency bugs) have been done.
2: Their findings have provided useful guidelines and motivations for
2: bug detection, testing and programming language design. For example, the study of bug types in IBM software systems [38] in

2: (2) Concurrency bugs are not easy to understand. Their patterns and manifestations usually involve complicated interactions

3: Concurrency bug detection can focus on these two bug

p5: Discussion
p5: The architecture of future computers is far from clear but
p5: two trends are evident: rising core counts and increasing
p5: hardware diversity, both between cores within a machine,
p5: and between systems with varying interconnect topologies and performance tradeoffs.
p5: This upheaval in hardware has important consequences for a monolithic OS that shares data structures
p5: across cores. These systems perform a delicate balancing
p5: act between processor cache size, the likely contention
p5: and latency to access main memory, and the complexity and overheads of the cache-coherence protocol. The
p5: irony is that hardware is now changing faster than software, and the effort required to evolve such operating
p5: systems to perform well on new hardware is becoming
p5: prohibitive.
p5: Increasing system and interconnect diversity, as well
p5: as core heterogeneity, will prevent developers from optimizing shared memory structures at a source-code level.
p5: Sun Niagara and Intel Nehalem or AMD Opteron systems, for example, already require completely different optimizations, and future system software will have
p5: to adapt its communication patterns and mechanisms at
p5: runtime to the collection of hardware at hand. It seems
p5: likely that future general-purpose systems will have limited support for hardware cache coherence, or drop it entirely in favor of a message-passing model. An OS that
p5: can exploit native message-passing would be the natural
p5: fit for such a design.
p5: We believe that now is the time to reconsider how the
p5: OS should be restructured to not merely cope with the
p5: next generation of hardware, but efficiently exploit it.
p5: Furthermore, rather than evolving an inherently sharedmemory model of OS structure to deal with complex
p5: tradeoffs and limited sharing, we take the opposite approach: design and reason about the OS as a distributed,
p5: non-shared system, and then employ sharing to optimize
p5: the model where appropriate.

p5: The multikernel model
p5: In this section we present our OS architecture for heterogeneous multicore machines, which we call the multikernel model. In a nutshell, we structure the OS as a
p5: distributed system of cores that communicate using messages and share no memory (Figure 1). The multikernel
p5: model is guided by three design principles:
p5: 1. Make all inter-core communication explicit.
p5: 2. Make OS structure hardware-neutral.
p5: 3. View state as replicated instead of shared.
p5: These principles allow the OS to benefit from the
p5: distributed systems approach to gain improved performance, natural support for hardware heterogeneity,
p5: greater modularity, and the ability to reuse algorithms
p5: developed for distributed systems.
p5: After discussing the principles in detail below, in Section 4 we explore the implications of these principles by
p5: describing the implementation of Barrelfish, a new operating system based on the multikernel model.
p5: 3.1
p5: Make inter-core communication explicit
p5: Within a multikernel OS, all inter-core communication
p5: is performed using explicit messages. A corollary is that
p5: no memory is shared between the code running on each
p5: core, except for that used for messaging channels. As
p5: we have seen, using messages to access or update state
p5: rapidly becomes more efficient than shared-memory access as the number of cache-lines involved increases. We
p5: can expect such effects to become more pronounced in
p5: the future. Note that this does not preclude applications
p5: sharing memory between cores (see Section 4.8), only
p5: that the OS design itself does not rely on it.
p5: Explicit communication patterns facilitate reasoning
p5: about the use of the system interconnect. In contrast
p5: 5

p6: memory, or the messages used for cache coherence), the
p6: knowledge of what parts of shared state are accessed
p6: when and by who is exposed. It is, of course, established
p6: practice in OS kernels to design point-solution data structures that can be updated using only one or two cache
p6: misses on particular architectures, but it is hard to evolve
p6: such operations as hardware changes, and such optimizations ignore the wider picture of larger state updates in
p6: the OS involving multiple structures.

p6: 3.2
p6: Make OS structure hardware-neutral
p6: A multikernel separates the OS structure as much as possible from the hardware. This means that there are just
p6: two aspects of the OS as a whole that are targeted at
p6: specific machine architectures – the messaging transport
p6: mechanisms, and the interface to hardware (CPUs and
p6: devices). This has several important potential benefits.
p6: Firstly, adapting the OS to run on hardware with new
p6: performance characteristics will not require extensive,
p6: cross-cutting changes to the code base (as was the case
p6: with recent scalability enhancements to Linux and Windows). This will become increasingly important as deployed systems become more diverse.
p6: In particular, experience has shown that the performance of an inter-process communication mechanism is
p6: crucially dependent on hardware-specific optimizations
p6: (we describe those used in Barrelfish in Section 4.6).
p6: Hardware-independence in a multikernel means that we
p6: can isolate the distributed communication algorithms
p6: from hardware implementation details.
p6: We envision a number of different messaging implementations (for example, a user-level RPC protocol using
p6: shared memory, or a hardware-based channel to a programmable peripheral). As we saw in Section 2.5, hardware platforms exist today without cache coherence, and
p6: even without shared memory, and are likely to become
p6: more widespread. Once the message transport is optimized, we can implement efficient message-based algorithms independently of the hardware details or memory
p6: layout.
p6: A final advantage is to enable late binding of both the
p6: protocol implementation and message transport. For example, different transports may be used to cores on IO
p6: links, or the implementation may be fitted to the observed workload by adjusting queue lengths or polling
p6: frequency. In Section 5.1 we show how a topology-aware
p6: multicast message protocol can outperform highly optimized TLB shootdown mechanisms on commodity operating systems.
p6: We have previously argued that as the machine increasingly resembles a network, the OS will inevitably
p6: behave as a distributed system [8]. Explicit communication allows the OS to deploy well-known networking
p6: optimizations to make more efficient use of the interconnect, such as pipelining (having a number of requests in
p6: flight at once), and batching (sending a number of requests in one message, or processing a number of messages together). In Section 5.2 we show the benefit of
p6: such techniques in the case of distributed capability management.
p6: This approach also enables the OS to provide isolation
p6: and resource management on heterogeneous cores, or to
p6: schedule jobs effectively on arbitrary inter-core topologies by placing tasks with reference to communication
p6: patterns and network effects. Furthermore, the message
p6: abstraction is a basic requirement for spanning cores
p6: which are not cache-coherent, or do not even share memory.
p6: Message passing allows operations that might require
p6: communication to be split-phase, by which we mean that
p6: the operation sends a request and immediately continues,
p6: with the expectation that a reply will arrive at some time
p6: in the future. When requests and responses are decoupled, the core issuing the request can do useful work, or
p6: sleep to save power, while waiting for the reply. A common, concrete example is remote cache invalidations. In
p6: a highly concurrent scenario, provided that completing
p6: the invalidation is not required for correctness, it can be
p6: more important not to waste time waiting for the operation to finish than to perform it with the smallest possible
p6: latency.
p6: Finally, a system based on explicit communication is
p6: amenable to human or automated analysis. The structure of a message-passing system is naturally modular,
p6: because components communicate only through welldefined interfaces. Consequently it can be evolved and
p6: refined more easily [23] and made robust to faults [30].
p6: Indeed, a substantial theoretical foundation exists for reasoning about the high-level structure and performance of
p6: a system with explicit communication between concurrent tasks, ranging from process calculi such as Hoare’s
p6: communicating sequential processes and the π-calculus,
p6: 3.3
p6: View state as replicated
p6: Operating systems maintain state, some of which, such
p6: as the Windows dispatcher database or Linux scheduler
p6: queues, must be accessible on multiple processors. Traditionally that state exists as shared data structures protected by locks, however, in a multikernel, explicit communication between cores that share no memory leads
p6: naturally to a model of global OS state replicated across
p6: cores.

p7:  Replication is a well-known technique for OS scalability [4, 24], but is generally employed as an optimization to an otherwise shared-memory kernel design. In
p7: contrast, any potentially shared state in a multikernel is
p7: accessed and updated as if it were a local replica. In
p7: general, the state is replicated as much as is useful, and
p7: consistency is maintained by exchanging messages. Depending on the consistency semantics required, updates
p7: can therefore be long-running operations to coordinate
p7: replicas, and so are exposed in the API as non-blocking
p7: and split-phase. We provide examples of different update
p7: semantics in Section 4.
p7: Replicating data structures can improve system scalability by reducing load on the system interconnect, contention for memory, and overhead for synchronization.
p7: Bringing data nearer to the cores that process it will result in lowered access latencies.
p7: Replication is required to support domains that do not
p7: share memory, whether future general-purpose designs
p7: or present-day programmable peripherals, and is inherent in the idea of specializing data structures for particular core designs. Making replication of state intrinsic
p7: to the multikernel design makes it easier to preserve OS
p7: structure and algorithms as underlying hardware evolves.
p7: Furthermore, replication is a useful framework within
p7: which to support changes to the set of running cores in an
p7: OS, either when hotplugging processors, or when shutting down hardware subsystems to save power. We can
p7: apply standard results from the distributed systems literature to maintaining the consistency of OS state across
p7: such changes.
p7: Finally, a potentially important optimization of the
p7: multikernel model (which we do not pursue in this paper)
p7: is to privately share a replica of system state between a
p7: group of closely-coupled cores or hardware threads, protected by a shared-memory synchronization technique
p7: like spinlocks. In this way we can introduce (limited)
p7: sharing behind the interface as an optimization of replication.

p7: cores.
p7: The performance and availability benefits of replication are achieved at the cost of ensuring replica consistency. Some operations will inevitably experience longer
p7: latencies than others, and the extent of this penalty will
p7: depend on the workload, the data volumes and the consistency model being applied. Not only that, the model
p7: supports multiple implementations of the agreement protocols used to maintain consistency. This increases the
p7: burden on the developer who must understand the consistency requirements for the data, but on the other hand,
p7: can also precisely control the degree of consistency. For
p7: example, a global flush of the TLB on each CPU is orderinsensitive and can be achieved by issuing a single multicast request, whereas other operations may require more
p7: elaborate agreement protocols.
p7: From an OS research perspective, a legitimate question is to what extent a real implementation can adhere
p7: to the model, and the consequent effect on system performance and scalability. To address this, we have implemented Barrelfish, a substantial prototype operating
p7: system structured according to the multikernel model.
p7: Specifically, the goals for Barrelfish are that it:
p7: • gives comparable performance to existing commodity operating systems on current multicore hardware;
p7: • demonstrates evidence of scalability to large numbers of cores, particularly under workloads that
p7: stress global OS data structures;
p7: • can be re-targeted to different hardware, or make
p7: use of a different mechanism for sharing, without
p7: refactoring;
p7: • can exploit the message-passing abstraction to
p7: achieve good performance by pipelining and batching messages;
p7: • can exploit the modularity of the OS to place OS
p7: functionality according to the hardware topology or
p7: load.
p7: Applying the model
p7: Like all models, the multikernel, while theoretically elegant, is an idealist position: no state is shared and the
p7: OS acts like a fully distributed system. This has several
p7: implications for a real OS.
p7: We discussed previously (in Section 2.6) the software engineering concerns of message-passing systems
p7: in general. Within the operating system kernel, which
p7: typically consists of a smaller amount of code written by
p7: expert programmers, software development challenges
p7: are more easily managed. However, the drawback of a
p7: idealist message-passing abstraction here is that certain
p7: platform-specific performance optimizations may be sac-
p7: In the next section we describe Barrelfish, and in Section
p7: 5 we explore the extent to which it achieves these goals.

p7: Implementation
p7: While Barrelfish is a point in the multikernel design
p7: space, it is not the only way to build a multikernel. In
p7: this section we describe our implementation, and note
p7: which choices in the design are derived from the model
p7: and which are motivated for other reasons, such as local
p7: performance, ease of engineering, policy freedom, etc. –

p8: The CPU driver enforces protection, performs authorization, time-slices processes, and mediates access to the
p8: core and its associated hardware (MMU, APIC, etc.).
p8: Since it shares no state with other cores, the CPU driver
p8: can be completely event-driven, single-threaded, and
p8: nonpreemptable. It serially processes events in the form
p8: of traps from user processes or interrupts from devices or
p8: other cores. This means in turn that it is easier to write
p8: and debug than a conventional kernel, and is small2 enabling its text and data to be located in core-local memory.
p8: As with an exokernel [22], a CPU driver abstracts very
p8: little but performs dispatch and fast local messaging between processes on the core. It also delivers hardware
p8: interrupts to user-space drivers, and locally time-slices

p8: standard system call instructions with a cost comparable
p8: to Linux on the same hardware.

p8: expect CPU drivers for other processors to be similarly architecture-specific, including data structure layout, whereas the monitor source code is almost entirely
p8: processor-agnostic.

p9: In a multikernel, all inter-core communication occurs
p9: with messages. We expect to use different transport implementations for different hardware scenarios. However, the only inter-core communication mechanism
p9: available on our current hardware platforms is cachecoherent memory. Barrelfish at present therefore uses a
p9: variant of user-level RPC (URPC) [10] between cores: a
p9: region of shared memory is used as a channel to transfer
p9: cache-line-sized messages point-to-point between single
p9: writer and reader cores.
p9: Inter-core messaging performance is critical for a multikernel, and our implementation is carefully tailored to
p9: the cache-coherence protocol to minimize the number of
p9: interconnect messages used to send a message. For example, on the fast path for a HyperTransport-based system, the sender writes the message sequentially into the
p9: cache line, while the receiver polls on the last word of the
p9: line, thus ensuring that in the (unlikely) case that it polls
p9: the line during the sender’s write, it does not see a partial message. In the common case, this causes two round
p9: trips across the interconnect: one when the sender starts
p9: writing to invalidate the line in the receiver’s cache, and
p9: one for the receiver to fetch the line from the sender’s
p9: cache. The technique also performs well between cores
p9: with a shared cache.
p9: As an optimization, pipelined URPC message
p9: throughput can be improved at the expense of singlemessage latency through the use of cache prefetching instructions. This can be selected at channel setup time for
p9: workloads likely to benefit from it.
p9: Receiving URPC messages is done by polling memory. Polling is cheap because the line is in the cache
p9: until invalidated; in addition, keeping the endpoints in
p9: an array can allow a hardware stride prefetcher to further improve performance. However, it is unreasonable
p9: to spin forever; instead, a dispatcher awaiting messages
p9: on URPC channels will poll those channels for a short
p9: period before blocking and sending a request to its local
p9: monitor to be notified when messages arrive. At present,

p9: Monitors
p9: Monitors collectively coordinate system-wide state, and
p9: encapsulate much of the mechanism and policy that
p9: would be found in the kernel of a traditional OS. The
p9: monitors are single-core, user-space processes and therefore schedulable. Hence they are well suited to the
p9: split-phase, message-oriented inter-core communication
p9: of the multikernel model, in particular handling queues
p9: of messages, and long-running remote operations.
p9: On each core, replicated data structures, such as memory allocation tables and address space mappings, are
p9: kept globally consistent by means of an agreement protocol run by the monitors. Application requests that access
p9: global state are handled by the monitors, which mediate

p10: memory used to store a hardware page table or other OS

p10: Any OS faces the same problem of tracking ownership
p10: and type of in-memory objects. Most systems use some
p10: kind of unique identifiers together with accounting information, such as file descriptors in Unix or object handles in Windows, managed by data structures in shared
p10: memory. For Barrelfish, we decided to use a capability system modeled on that of seL4 [39]. In this model,
p10: all memory management is performed explicitly through
p10: system calls that manipulate capabilities, which are userlevel references to kernel objects or regions of physical
p10: memory. The model has the useful property of removing
p10: dynamic memory allocation from the CPU driver, which
p10: is only responsible for checking the correctness of operations that manipulate capabilities to memory regions
p10: through retype and revoke operations.
p10: All virtual memory management, including allocation
p10: and manipulation of page tables, is performed entirely by
p10: user-level code [28]. For instance, to allocate and map in
p10: a region of memory, a user process must first acquire capabilities to sufficient RAM to store the required page tables. It then retypes these RAM capabilities to page table
p10: capabilities, allowing it to insert the new page tables into
p10: its root page table; although the CPU driver performs the
p10: actual page table and capability manipulations, its sole
p10: task is checking their correctness. The user process may
p10: then allocate more RAM capabilities, which it retypes to
p10: mappable frame capabilities, and finally inserts into its
p10: page tables to map the memory.
p10: We chose capabilities so as to cleanly decentralize resource allocation in the interests of scalability. In hindsight, this was a mistake: the capability code is unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient than scalable perprocessor memory managers used in conventional OSes
p10: like Windows and Linux. All cores must still keep their
p10: local capability lists consistent, to avoid situations such
p10: as user-level acquiring a mapping to a hardware page table.
p10: However, one benefit has been uniformity: most operations requiring global coordination in Barrelfish can
p10: be cast as instances of capability copying or retyping, allowing the use of generic consistency mechanisms in the
p10: monitors. These operations are not specific to capabilities, and we would have to support them with any other

5: Finding (1): Most (72 out of 74) of the examined non-deadlock
5: concurrency bugs are covered by two simple patterns: atomicityviolation and order-violation.
5: Implications: Concurrent program bug detection, testing and
5: language design should first focus on these two major bug patterns.
5: The Finding (1) can be explained by the fact that programmers
5: generally put their intentions on atomic regions and execution orders, but it is not easy to enforce all these intentions correctly and
5: completely in implementation.
5: Since programmers think sequentially, they tend to assume that
5: small code regions will be executed atomically. For example, in
5: Figure 1, programmers assume that if S1 reads a non-NULL value
5: from thd->proc info, S2 will also read the same value. However, such an atomicity assumption can be violated by S3 during
5: concurrent execution, and it leads to a program crash.
5: It is also common for programmers to assume an order between
5: two operations from different threads, but programmers may forget
5: to enforce such an order. As a result, one of the two operations may
5: be executed faster (or slower) than the programmers’ assumption,
5: and it makes the order bug manifest. In the Mozilla bug shown in
5: Figure 2, it is easy for programmers to assume wrongly that thread
5: 2 would dereference mThread after thread 1 initializes it, because
5: thread 2 is created by thread 1. However, in real execution, thread
5: 2 may be very quick and dereference mThread before mThread is
5: initialized. This unexpected order leads to program crash. Note that
5: even though the bug can be fixed with locks, the root cause of the
5: bug is not an atomicity violation, but an order violation.

p12: TLB shootdown – the process of maintaining TLB consistency by invalidating entries when pages are unmapped – is one of the simplest operations in a multiprocessor OS that requires global coordination. It is also

p12: In Linux and Windows, inter-processor interrupts

p12: In Barrelfish, we use messages for shootdown. In the
p12: naive algorithm, the local monitor broadcasts invalidate
p12: messages to the others and waits for all the replies. We
p12: would expect this to show higher latency than the IPI
p12: approach, since the remote monitors handle the messages only when “convenient”. However, fortunately, the
p12: message-passing paradigm allows us to improve on this
p12: approach without significantly restructuring the code. In
p12: particular, we can exploit knowledge about the specific
p12: hardware platform, extracted from the system knowledge
p12: base at runtime, to achieve very good TLB shootdown
p12: performance.
p12: Figure 6 shows the costs of the raw inter-core messaging mechanisms (without TLB invalidation) for four
p12: URPC-based TLB shootdown protocols on the 8×4-core
p12: AMD system.
p12: In the Broadcast protocol, the master monitor uses a
p12: single URPC channel to broadcast a shootdown request
p12: to every other core. Each slave core polls the same shared
p12: cache, waiting for the master to modify it, and then acknowledges with individual URPCs to the master. This
p12: performs badly due to the cache-coherence protocol used
p12: by AMD64 processors [1, section 7.3]. When the master updates the line, it is invalidated in all other caches.
p12: Each slave core then pulls the new copy from the master’s cache. With N cores, the data crosses the interconnect N times, and latency grows linearly with the number
p12: of cores.
p12: The Unicast protocol sends individual requests to each
p12: slave over unicast URPC so that the cache lines are only
p12: shared by two cores. While this performs much better

p12: much a placeholder. We are interested in appropriate network stack design for multikernels, and in particular we
p12: feel many ideas from RouteBricks [21] are applicable to
p12: a scalable end-system multikernel.
p12: The principal difference between current OS designs
p12: and the multikernel model is not the location of protection or trust boundaries between system components, but
p12: rather the reliance on shared data as the default communication mechanism. Examples from monolithic systems include process, thread, and virtual machine control
p12: blocks, page tables, VFS objects, scheduler queues,5 network sockets and inter-process communication buffers.
p12: Some of this state can be naturally partitioned, but (as
p12: we saw in Section 1) the engineering effort to do this
p12: piecemeal in the process of evolving an OS for scalability can be prohibitive. Furthermore, state which is inherently shared in current systems requires more effort
p12: to convert to a replication model. Finally, the sharedmemory single-kernel model cannot deal with cores that
p12: are heterogeneous at the ISA level.
p12: In contrast, starting with a multikernel model, as in
p12: Barrelfish, allows these issues to be addressed from the
p12: outset. From a research perspective, Barrelfish can be
p12: seen as a useful “proving ground” for experimenting with
p12: such ideas in an environment freed from the constraints
p12: of an existing complex monolithic system.

p13: The HyperTransport interconnect is effectively a
p13: broadcast network, where each read or write operation
p13: results in probes being sent to all other nodes. However, newer 4-core Opteron processors have a shared onchip L3 cache and appear as a single HyperTransport
p13: node, and so cache lines shared only by these cores will
p13: not result in interconnect traffic. This motivates using
p13: an explicit two-level multicast tree for shootdown messages. Hence in the Multicast protocol, the master sends
p13: a URPC message to the first core of each processor,
p13: which forwards it to the other three cores in the package.
p13: Since they all share an L3 cache, this second message is
p13: much cheaper, but more importantly all eight processors
p13: can send in parallel without interconnect contention. As
p13: shown in Figure 6, the multicast protocol scales significantly better than unicast or broadcast.
p13: Finally, we devised a protocol that takes advantage of
p13: the NUMA nature of the machine by allocating URPC
p13: buffers from memory local to the multicast aggregation
p13: nodes, and having the master send requests to the highest latency nodes first. Once again, there are many analogies to networked systems which motivate these changes.
p13: The resulting protocol, labeled NUMA-Aware Multicast
p13: on Figure 6 scales extremely well across the 32-way system, showing steps only when the number of levels in the
p13: tree increases.
p13: This communication protocol has good performance
p13: for the 8×4-core AMD system, but relies on hardware knowledge (including the interconnect topology
p13: and memory locality) that differs widely between systems, and only works when initiated from the first core.
p13: In Barrelfish, we use a query on the system knowledge
p13: base to construct a suitable multicast tree at runtime:
p13: for every source core in the system, the SKB computes
p13: an optimal route consisting of one multicast aggregation
p13: node per processor socket, ordered by decreasing message latency, and its children. These routes are calculated
p13: online at startup, and used to configure inter-monitor
p13: communication.

p13: to the local monitor, the per-message cost of marshaling
p13: and event demultiplexing, scheduling effects in the monitors, and variable overhead when a core’s monitor is not
p13: currently its polling channels.

7: for programmers to specify correct transactions or atomic regions

7: Implications: Concurrent program testing can focus on the partial order among every small groups of accesses. This simplifies
7: the interleaving testing space from exponential to polynomial regarding to the total number of accesses, with little loss of bug
7: exposing capability.
8:  The Finding (8.1) can be easily understood, considering that
8: most of the examined concurrency bugs have simple patterns and
8: involve a small number of variables. Most of the exceptions come
8: from those bugs that involve more than two threads and/or more
8: than two variables.
8: The Finding (8.2) is also natural, considering that most of our
8: examined deadlock bugs involve only two resources.
8: The above findings have significant implication for concurrent
8: program testing. The challenge in concurrent program testing is
8: that the number of all possible interleavings is exponential to the
8: number of dynamic memory accesses, which is too big to thoroughly explore. Our finding provides support to a more effective
8: design of interleaving testing [21]: exploring all possible orders
8: within every small groups of memory accesses, e.g. groups of 4
8: memory accesses. The complexity of this design is only polynomial
8: to the number of dynamic memory accesses, which is a huge reduction from the exponential-sized all-interleaving testing scheme.
8: Furthermore, the bug exposing capability of this design is almost
8: as good as exploring all interleavings. It would miss only few bugs
8: in our examination.
8: A recent model checking work [28] uses the heuristic to start
8: the checking from interleavings with small numbers of context
8: switches. Our study provides support for this heuristic.
8: Of course, enforcing a specific partial order among a set of accesses is not trivial. The program input and many accesses need to
8: be controlled to achieve that. How to leverage our finding to enable practical and powerful concurrent program testing and model
8: checking remains as future work.

p16: Related work
p16: Although a new point in the OS design space, the multikernel model is related to much previous work on both
p16: operating systems and distributed systems.
p16: In 1993 Chaves et al. [17] examined the tradeoffs between message passing and shared data structures for
p16: an early multiprocessor, finding a performance tradeoff
p16: biased towards message passing for many kernel operations.
p16: Machines with heterogeneous cores that communicate
p16: using messages have long existed. The Auspex [11] and
p16: IBM System/360 hardware consisted of heterogeneous
p16: cores with partially shared memory, and unsurprisingly
p16: their OSes resembled distributed systems in some respects. We take inspiration from this; what is new is
p16: the scale of parallelism and the diversity of different machines on which a general-purpose OS must run. Similarly, explicit communication has been used on largescale multiprocessors such as the Cray T3 or IBM Blue
p16: Summary
p16: It would be wrong to draw any quantitative conclusions from our large-scale benchmarks; the systems in16
p17:  Gene, to enable scalability beyond the limits of cachecoherence.
p17: The problem of scheduling computations on multiple
p17: cores that have the same ISA but different performance
p17: tradeoffs is being addressed by the Cypress project [62];
p17: we see this work as largely complementary to our own.
p17: Also related is the fos system [69] which targets scalability through space-sharing of resources.
p17: Most work on OS scalability for multiprocessors to
p17: date has focused on performance optimizations that reduce sharing. Tornado and K42 [4, 24] introduced clustered objects, which optimize shared data through the use
p17: of partitioning and replication. However, the base case,
p17: and the means by which replicas communicate, remains
p17: shared data. Similarly, Corey [13] advocates reducing
p17: sharing within the OS by allowing applications to specify sharing requirements for OS data, effectively relaxing
p17: the consistency of specific objects. As in K42, however,
p17: the base case for communication is shared memory. In a
p17: multikernel, we make no specific assumptions about the
p17: application interface, and construct the OS as a sharednothing distributed system, which may locally share data
p17: (transparently to applications) as an optimization.
p17: We see a multikernel as distinct from a microkernel,
p17: which also uses message-based communication between
p17: processes to achieve protection and isolation but remains
p17: a shared-memory, multithreaded system in the kernel.
p17: For instance, Barrelfish has some structural similarity to
p17: a microkernel, in that it consists of a distributed system
p17: of communicating user-space processes which provide
p17: services to applications. However, unlike multiprocessor microkernels, each core in the machine is managed
p17: completely independently – the CPU driver and monitor
p17: share no data structures with other cores except for message channels.
p17: That said, some work in scaling microkernels is related: Uhlig’s distributed TLB shootdown algorithm is
p17: similar to our two-phase commit [67]. The microkernel
p17: comparison is also informative: as we have shown, the
p17: cost of a URPC message is comparable to that of the best
p17: microkernel IPC mechanisms in the literature [44], without the cache and TLB context switch penalties.
p17: Disco and Cellular Disco [14, 25] were based on the
p17: premise that large multiprocessors can be better programmed as distributed systems, an argument complementary to our own. We see this as further evidence that
p17: the shared-memory model is not a complete solution for
p17: large-scale multiprocessors, even at the OS level.
p17: Prior work on “distributed operating systems” [66]
p17: aimed to build a uniform OS from a collection of independent computers linked by a network. There are obvious parallels with the multikernel approach, which seeks
p17: to build an OS from a collection of cores communicating
p17: over links within a machine, but also important differ-
p17: ences: firstly, a multikernel may exploit reliable in-order
p17: message delivery to substantially simplify its communication. Secondly, the latencies of intra-machine links are
p17: lower (and less variable) than between machines. Finally, much prior work sought to handle partial failures
p17: (i.e. of individual machines) in a fault-tolerant manner,
p17: whereas in Barrelfish the complete system is a failure
p17: unit. That said, extending a multikernel beyond a single machine to handle partial failures is a possibility for
p17: the future that we discussion briefly below.
p17: Despite much work on distributed shared virtual memory systems [2, 56], performance and scalability problems have limited their widespread use in favor of
p17: explicit message-passing models. There are parallels
p17: with our argument that the single-machine programming
p17: model should now also move to message passing. Our
p17: model can be more closely compared with that of distributed shared objects [6, 32], in which remote method
p17: invocations on objects are encoded as messages in the
p17: interests of communication efficiency.
p17: Experience and future work
p17: The multikernel model has been strongly influenced
p17: by the process of building a concrete implementation.
p17: Though not by any means yet a mature system, we have
p17: learned much from the process.
p17: Perhaps unsurprisingly, queuing effects become very
p17: important in a purely message-oriented system, and we
p17: encountered a number of performance anomalies due to
p17: extreme sensitivity to message queue lengths. Understanding such effects has been essential to performance
p17: debugging. Scheduling based on queue lengths, as in
p17: Scout [53], may be a useful technique to apply here.
p17: When implementing transports based on cachecoherent shared memory, we found it important to understand exactly the cache-coherence protocol. We experimented with many URPC implementations, with often unexpected results that were explained by a careful
p17: analysis of cache line states and interconnect messages.
p17: Related future work includes efficient multicast, incast
p17: and anycast URPC transports. As we found in the case of
p17: unmap, there are cases where a multicast tree is more efficient for performing global operations than many pointto-point links, and we expect such transports will be important for scalability to many cores.
p17: Our current implementation is based on homogeneous
p17: Intel and AMD multiprocessors, and so does not represent a truly heterogeneous environment. A port is in
p17: progress to the ARM processor architecture, which will
p17: allow us to run a Barrelfish CPU driver and monitor on
p17: programmable network cards. This will also allow us to
p17: experiment with specializing data structures and code for
p17: different processors within the same operating system.
p18:  Acknowledgments
p18: There are many ideas for future work that we hope to
p18: explore. Structuring the OS as a distributed system more
p18: closely matches the structure of some increasingly popular programming models for datacenter applications,
p18: such as MapReduce [19] and Dryad [35], where applications are written for aggregates of machines. A distributed system inside the machine may help to reduce
p18: the “impedance mismatch” caused by the network interface – the same programming framework could then run
p18: as efficiently inside one machine as between many.
p18: Another area of interest is file systems. Barrelfish currently uses a conventional VFS-style file-oriented API
p18: backed by NFS. It may be fruitful to draw on techniques
p18: from high-performance cluster file systems and the parallel IO models of cloud computing providers to construct
p18: a scalable, replicated file system inside the computer.
p18: Barrelfish is at present a rather uncompromising implementation of a multikernel, in that it never shares
p18: data. As we noted in Section 2.1, some machines are
p18: highly optimized for fine-grained sharing among a subset of processing elements. A next step for Barrelfish is
p18: to exploit such opportunities by limited sharing behind
p18: the existing replica-oriented interfaces. This also raises
p18: the issue of how to decide when to share, and whether
p18: such a decision can be automated.

p18: Concluding Remarks
p18: Computer hardware is changing faster than system software, and in particular operating systems. Current OS
p18: structure is tuned for a coherent shared memory with
p18: a limited number of homogeneous processors, and is
p18: poorly suited to efficiently manage the diversity and scale
p18: of future hardware architectures.
p18: Since multicore machines increasingly resemble complex networked systems, we have proposed the multikernel architecture as a way forward. We view the OS
p18: as, first and foremost, a distributed system which may be
p18: amenable to local optimizations, rather than centralized
p18: system which must somehow be scaled to the networklike environment of a modern or future machine. By
p18: basing the OS design on replicated data, message-based
p18: communication between cores, and split-phase operations, we can apply a wealth of experience and knowledge from distributed systems and networking to the
p18: challenges posed by hardware trends.
p18: Barrelfish, an initial, relatively unoptimized implementation of the multikernel, already demonstrates many
p18: of the benefits, while delivering performance on today’s hardware competitive with existing, mature, monolithic kernels. Its source code is available at http://www.
p18: barrelfish.org/.

9: Table 10. Can TM help avoid concurrency bugs?
9: Finding (11): TM can help avoid many concurrency bugs (41
9: out of the 105 concurrency bugs we examined).
9: Implication: Although TM is not a panacea, it can ease programmers correctly expressing their synchronization intentions
9: in many cases, and help avoid a big portion of concurrency bugs.
9: Atomicity violation bugs and deadlock bugs with relatively
9: small and simple critical code regions can benefit the most from
9: TM, which can help programmers clearly specify this type of atomicity intention. Figure 8 shows an example, where programmers use
9: a consistency check with re-execution to fix the bug. Here, a transaction (with abort, rollback and replay) is exactly what programmers want.
10:  Finding (12): TM can potentially help avoid many concurrency bugs (44 out of the 105 concurrency bugs we examined),
10: if some concerns can be addressed, as shown in Table 10.
10: Implication: TM design can combine system supports and
10: other techniques to solve some of these concerns, and further
10: ease the concurrent programming.
10: One concern, not a surprise, is I/O operations. As operations
10: like I/O are hard to roll back, it is hard to use TM to protect the
10: atomicity of code regions which include such operations. Take the
10: concurrency bug in Figure 1 as an example. Since S2 involves a file
10: operation, TM might need non-trivial undo techniques to protect
10: the S1–S2 atomic region.
10: Other concerns, such as atomic region size and special code
10: nature, also exist. For example, the atomic code regions of several
10: Mozilla bugs include the whole garbage collection process. These
10: regions could have too large memory footprint to be effectively
10: handled by hardware-TM.
10: Many of the above concerns are addressable in TM, but with
10: higher overhead and complexity. For example, some of the rollback concerns can be addressed using system supports. Very long
10: transactions can be addressed by combining software and hardware
10: TMs.
10: Finding (13): 20 out of the 105 concurrency bugs that we
10: examined cannot benefit from the basic TM designs, because
10: the violated programmer intentions, such as order intentions,
10: cannot be guaranteed by the basic TM.
10: Implications: Apart from atomicity intentions, there is also a
10: significant need for concurrent programming language features
10: to help programmers express order intentions easily.
10: Programmers’ order intention is the major type of intention that
10: cannot be easily enforced by the basic TM design or locks. In
10: general, the basic TM designs cannot help enforce the intention that
10: A has to be executed before B. Therefore, they cannot help avoid
10: many related order-violation bugs 2 . Among all order-violation
10: bugs, we find a sub-type of order intentions that are extremely hard
10: to be enforced by basic TM designs: A must be either executed
10: before B or not executed at all. In other words, programmers do
10: not want B to wait for A. They simply skip A if B is already
10: executed. For example, in one Mozilla bug, thread 1 keeps inserting
10: entities to a cache and thread 2 would destroy the cache at some
10: moment. Based on the description in the bug report, programmers
10: do not want thread 2 to wait for thread 1 to finish all insertions.
10: The program simply skips any insertion attempt after the cache is
10: destroyed. This happens for 7 bugs.
10: In order to help avoid above 20 bugs, the semantic design,
10: instead of implementation schemes, of the basic TM needs to be
10: enhanced. Recently, some TM designs [5, 17] are equipped with
10: rich semantics (such as watch/retry, retry/orElse) and can help
10: enforce some of the above synchronization intentions. We hope our
10: bug characteristic study can help future research to decide the best
10: TM design.
10: 6. Other characteristics
10: Bug impacts: Among our examined concurrency bugs, 34 of them
10: can cause program crashes and 37 of them cause program hangs.
10: This validates that concurrency bug is a severe reliability problem.
10: 2 Some order-violation bugs can be avoided by TM. In those cases, order
10: intentions can be enforced as side effects while TM enforces the atomicity
10: of related code regions (an example is shown in Figure 2).
10: Some concurrency bugs are very difficult to repeat. In one bug
10: report (Mozilla#52111), the reporter complained that “I develop
10: Mozilla full time all day, and I get this bug only once a day”. In
10: another bug report (Mozilla#72599), the reporter said that “I saw
10: it only once ever on g (never on other machines). Perhaps the dual
10: processor of g makes it occur.”
10: Test cases are critical to bug diagnosis. Programmers’ discussions show that a good test case to repeat a concurrency bug is very
10: important for diagnosis. In Mozilla bug report #73291, the programmers once gave up on this bug and closed the bug report, because they could not repeat the bug. Fortunately, somebody worked
10: out a way to reliably repeat the bug, and the bug was fixed subsequently. In another Mozilla bug report (Mozilla#72599), the programmers finally gave up repeating the bug and simply submit a
10: patch based on their “guessing”, and this led to a wrong fix.
10: Programmers lack diagnosis tools. From the bug reports, we
10: notice that many concurrency bugs are diagnosed simply by programmers reading the source code. For example, for 29 out of the
10: 57 Mozilla bugs, the bug reports did not mention that the programmers ever leveraged any information from any tools, core dumps,
10: or stack traces, etc. Sometimes programmers tried gdb, but could
10: not get useful information. We have never seen programmers mentioned that they used any automatic diagnosis tools. In contrast,
10: in many bug reports about memory bugs, programmers mentioned
10: that they got help from Valgrind, Purify, etc [20].
10: 7. Related work
10: Bug characteristic studies A lot of work has been done to study
10: the bug characteristics in large software systems. Many of them
10: provide precious information to help improve software reliability
10: from different aspects, such as bug detection [8, 38], fault tolerance [14], failure recovery [6], fault prediction and testing [32],
10: etc. In a recent work [43], people also studied how the recent trends
10: (availability of commercial tools, open-source, etc) affect the general bug characteristics (bug distribution, fixing time) for all bugs.
10: Unfortunately, few previous work have studied concurrency
10: bugs, probably because real world concurrency bugs are hard to
10: collect and analyze. For example, in a previous study [6], only 12
10: concurrency bugs were collected from three applications: MySQL,
10: GNOME and Apache. Under this situation, a previous concurrency
10: bug pattern study [11] had to ask students to purposely write concurrent programs containing bugs, which cannot well represent
10: the real world bug characteristics. Unlike previous work, we study
10: the bug pattern, manifestation, and fix of 105 real world concurrency bugs from 4 large open source applications. Our study provides many findings and implications for addressing the correctness
10: problems in concurrent programming.
10: Improving concurrent program reliability Techniques to improve concurrent program quality is related to our work. Due to
10: space limit, here we briefly discuss the work that have not been
10: discussed in previous sections.
10: In software testing, people proposed different coverage criteria
10: in order to selectively test concurrent program interleavings. Unfortunately, these proposals are either too complicated [39] or based
10: on heuristics [4, 9]. Our study of concurrency bug manifestation
10: can help understand the trade-off between testing complexity and
10: bug exposing capability and help design better coverage criteria.
10: In programming language area, designs other than transactional
10: memory are also studied. AtomicSet [40] associates synchronization constraints with data instead of code region. This design can
10: help avoid some multiple variable related concurrency bugs. Autolocker [24] eases programmers specifying atomic regions by
10: automatically assigning locks. Our characteristics study provides
10: more motivation for these new language features.
11:  8. Conclusions and future work
11: This paper provides a comprehensive study of the real world concurrency bugs, examining their pattern, manifestation, fix strategy
11: and other characteristics. Our study is based on 105 real world
11: concurrency bugs, randomly collected from 4 representative opensource programs: MySQL, Apache, Mozilla, and OpenOffice. The
11: result of our study includes many interesting findings and implications for concurrency bug detection, testing and concurrent programming language design. Future research can benefit from our
11: study in various aspects. For example, future work can design new
11: bug detection tools to address multiple-variable bugs and orderviolation bugs; can pairwisely test concurrent program threads and
11: focus on partial orders of small groups of memory accesses to make
11: the best use of testing effort; can have better language features to
11: support “order” semantics to further ease concurrent programming.
11: In the future, we will extend our study with other types of real world
11: applications.

                     William J. Dally, Roy Davison? , J.A. Stuart Fiske, Greg Fyler? ,

                                               Abstract
         The Message-Driven Processor (MDP) is an integrated multicomputer node that provides
      ecient mechanisms for parallel computing. It incorporates a 36-bit integer processor, a mem-
      ory management unit, a router for a 3-D mesh network, a network interface, a 4K-word 2 36-bit
      SRAM, and an ECC DRAM controller in a single 1.1M transistor VLSI chip. Rather than being
      specialized for a single model of computation, the MDP incorporates ecient primitive mecha-
      nisms for communication, synchronization and naming. These mechanisms eciently support
      most proposed parallel programming models. Each processing node of the MIT J-Machine
      consists of an MDP with 1 MByte of DRAM. MDPs have been operational since June 1991
      and J-Machines built from them have been on-line since July 1991.


1     Introduction
The Message-Driven Processor (MDP) is a 36-bit single-chip microcomputer specialized to operate
eciently in a multicomputer. The MDP chip includes the processor, a 4K-word by 36-bit memory,
and a network port. An on-chip memory controller with ECC permits local memory to be expanded
to 1M-words by adding external DRAM chips.
    The processor is message driven in the sense that processing is performed in response to messages
(via the dispatch mechanism). There is no receive instruction. A task is created to handle each
arriving message. A computation is advanced (driven) by the messages carrying tasks about the
network.
    The design of the MDP was driven by two primary goals:

    1. To implement a general-purpose multicomputer processing node that provides the communica-
       tion, synchronization, and naming mechanisms required to eciently support several di erent
       parallel programming models.
    2. To create an inexpensive jellybean VLSI component that can be used to build cost-ecient
       parallel computers. The nodes should be inexpensive and plentiful VLSI commodity parts
       (like real jellybean candies) that can be networked together to form a Jellybean Machine
       (J-Machine) multicomputer.

Ecient Parallel Mechanisms Support Many Programming Models: Mechanisms are
the primitive operations provided by a computer's hardware. The abstractions that make up a
programming system are built from these mechanisms [15]. For example, most sequential machines
provide some mechanism for a push-down stack to support the last-in- rst-out (LIFO) storage

                                                    1
 allocation required by many sequential programming models. Most machines also provide some
form of memory relocation and protection to allow several processes to coexist in memory at a single
time without interference. The proper set of mechanisms can provide a signi cant improvement in
performance over a brute-force interpretation of a programming model.
    Over the past 40 years, sequential von Neumann processors have evolved a set of mechanisms
appropriate for supporting most sequential programming models. It is clear, however, from e orts to
build concurrent machines by wiring together many sequential processors, that these highly-evolved
sequential mechanisms are not adequate to support most parallel models of computation. These
mechanisms do not eciently support synchronization of events, communication of data, or global
naming of objects. As a result, these functions, inherent to any parallel model of computation, must
be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead. For example, sequential machines
require hundreds of instructions to create a new process. This cost prohibits the use of ne-grain
programming models where processes typically last only a few tens of instructions.
    The MDP supports a broad range of parallel programming models (including shared-memory [16],
data parallel [17], data ow [26], actors [1], and explicit message-passing [5]) by providing low-
overhead primitive mechanisms for communication, synchronization, and naming. Communication
mechanisms are provided that permit a user-level task on one node to send a message to any other
node in a 4K-node machine in < 2s. No processing resources on intermediate nodes are consumed
and bu er memory is automatically allocated on the receiving node. On message arrival, a task is
created and dispatched in < 1s. Synchronization is provided by presence tags on all storage loca-
tions. Three separate register sets allow fast task switching. The translation mechanism maintains
bindings between arbitrary names and values; it may be used to support a global virtual address
space. These mechanisms have been selected to be both general and amenable to ecient hard-
ware implementation. To support ne-grain concurrent programming systems, the mechanisms are
designed to eciently handle small objects (8 words) and small tasks (20 instructions).

Sidebar: The Problem of Incoherence
Incoherence. To illustrate the incoherence problem, consider the multiple cores and corresponding private caches in the upper-right of the
diagram below. If core 1 writes the block labeled B by updating its private cache only, subsequent reads by core 2 would see the old value
indefinitely. This incoherence can lead to incorrect behavior. For example, if the block holds a synchronization variable for implementing
mutual exclusion using a lock, such incoherent behavior could allow multiple cores into a critical section or prevent cores waiting for the
release of the lock from making forward progress.

The coherence invariant. The mainstream solution to preventing incoherence is a hardware cache coherence protocol. Although there are
many possible coherence protocols, they all maintain coherence by ensuring the single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant. That is,
for a given block, at any given moment in time, there is either:
    • only a single core with write (and read) permission to the block (in state M for modified) or
    • zero or more cores with read permission to the block (in state S for shared).

A 3-D Array of Fine-Grain Processing Nodes is Physically Ecient: The MDP is an ex-
ample of an inexpensive ne-grain multicomputer building block. Being ne-grain does not mean a
node has a slow processor; a competent processor can be built in a fraction of a modern VLSI chip's
area. A ne-grain node implies an inexpensive node with a small amount of memory. The result is
greater arithmetic performance and local memory bandwidth per unit cost. The fast communica-
tion and global address space prevent the small local memories from limiting programmability or
performance.
    In a multicomputer, system cost is very sensitive to processor cost. A less expensive node results
in a comparably priced system with more processors and, to rst order, higher performance. In
these systems, costly features that give a small incremental return in processor performance (such
as large caches) are avoided in favor of building systems with more nodes, an option not available
to the designer of a sequential computer.
   The 3-D network that connects MDPs gives the highest throughput and lowest latency for a
given wire density [10]. This network makes use of all three dimensions of physical space. It allows
the processing nodes to be packed densely and results in uniformly short wires. No communication
bandwidth is wasted by embedding an esoteric topology into physical space. Messages traveling
through the network follow a Manhattan shortest path in physical space; they never backtrack.

Background: The MDP builds on previous work in multicomputer design. Like the Caltech
Cosmic Cube [4], the Intel iPSC [3], the N-CUBE [24], and the Ametek [2], each MDP in the J-
Machine has a local memory and communicates with other nodes by passing messages. Because of
its low overhead, the MDP can exploit concurrency at a much ner grain than these early message-
passing multicomputers. Delivering a message and dispatching a task in response to the message's
arrival takes < 2s on the J-Machine, as opposed to 5ms on an iPSC-1 or 300s on an iPSC-2.
Like the BBN Butter y [19] and the IBM RP3 [8], the MDP supports a global virtual address

space. The same IDs (virtual addresses) are used to reference local (on the same node) and remote
(on a di erent node) objects. Like the InMOS transputer [6], the Caltech MOSAIC [20], and the
Intel iWARP [7], the MDP is a single chip processing element integrating a processor, memory, and
a communication unit. The MDP is unique in that it extends these previous e orts with ecient
primitive mechanisms for communication, synchronization and naming [15]. The MDP uses a direct
communication network based on the work reported in [12, 10, 14].
   The MDP was built as part of a collaborative project between MIT and Intel Corporation. The
project was funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

Outline: The next section describes the system architecture of the MDP from hardware and
software points of view. Section 3 describes the MDP instruction set with emphasis on instructions
that support parallelism. The network architecture is discussed in Section 4. Section 5 brie y
describes the implementation of the MDP with attention given to the subsystems that implement
the MDP's mechanisms. MDP software is addressed in Section 6.


2     System Architecture
Hardware View: To the hardware designer, the MDP appears as a component with a memory
port, six bidirectional network ports, and a diagnostic port as shown in Figure 1.
   The memory port provides a direct (no glue) interface to up to 1M-word of ECC DRAM memory
consisting of 11 multiplexed address lines, a 12-bit data bus, and 3 control signals. Static-column or
page mode DRAMs are cycled three times to access a 36-bit data word and a fourth time to check
or update the ECC check bits. Current J-Machines use 3 1Mx4 memory parts to form a 4-chip
processing node with 260KW of memory that measures 2x2.75 inches as shown in Figure 2.
    The network ports are used to connect MDPs together into a 3-dimensional mesh network. Each
of the six network ports corresponds to one of the six cardinal directions (+X; 0X; +Y; 0Y; +Z; 0Z )
and consists of nine data and six control lines. Each port connects directly to the opposite port on
an adjacent MDP. Details of the 3-D network are given in Section 4.
    The diagnostic port is used to issue supervisory commands and to read and write MDP memory

from a console processor. The port consists of two control lines, a serial input, and a serial output.
Using this port, a console processor can read or write any location in the MDP's address space, as
well as reset, interrupt, halt, or single-step the processor.

Software View: To a systems programmer, a bare J-Machine appears as a collection of node
memories and register les that can be operated on by an instruction set that includes communica-
tion, synchronization, and naming mechanisms. The systems programmer uses these mechanisms
to implement a programming model. For example, one can build a shared memory model that gives
the application programmer a single, shared address space.
    The implementation of a combining tree [27] illustrates the use of the MDP mechanisms. The
combining tree (Figure 3) consists of a number of nodes each containing a value, a count, and a
pointer to a parent node. The value is initialized to zero and count is initialized to the number of
inputs expected. Summing a set of values computed by a number of processes distributed across
the nodes of the machine is accomplished by each process sending a combine message containing its
result to a combining node. When the message arrives at the processor containing the combining
node, a task is created that executes a combine routine. The routine adds the message value to the
node's value and decrements the count. When the count reaches zero, a combine message is sent
to the node's parent.
    The MDP supports communication using a SEND instruction for message formatting, a fast
network for delivery, automatic message bu ering, and task creation upon message arrival. A series
of SEND instructions is used to send a message of arbitrary length to any node in the machine.
Upon arrival, the message is bu ered in a hardware queue. When the message arrives at the head
of the queue, a task is dispatched to handle the message. In the combining tree example, a pair of
SEND instructions is used to send the combine message to a node. Upon message arrival, the MDP
bu ers the message and creates a task to execute the combine routine.
   Synchronization in the MDP is performed using message dispatch and presence tags on all state.

The dispatch of a process on each message arrival allows messages to be used to signal events on
remote nodes. For example, in the combining tree example above, each combine message signals
its own arrival and causes the combine routine to be executed.
   Presence tags are used to synchronize on the arrival of data. For example, access to the value
produced by the combining tree may be synchronized by initially tagging as empty the location
that will hold this value. An attempt to read this location before the combining tree had written it
would raise an exception and cause the reading task to be suspended until the value is written by
the root of the tree. Synchronization on data availability in this manner is quite common in many
parallel programs.
    The MDP supports naming with segmented memory management and with translation instruc-
tions. In the combining tree example, a memory segment would be allocated to hold the state
of each combining node. Accesses to the node would be relocated and protected using a segment
descriptor. To make combining nodes relocatable across processing nodes, a node's virtual address
would be translated to nd the processing node on which it resides. Upon reaching this node, a
second translation would locate the segment descriptor for the combining node.


3      Instruction Set Architecture
The MDP extends a conventional microprocessor instruction-set architecture (ISA) with instruc-
tions to support parallel processing. Speci cally, the MDP provides ecient hardware mechanisms
for communication, synchronization and naming. This section describes the MDP ISA with partic-
ular emphasis on these mechanisms. Further details of the MDP ISA are described in [11].

Register Set: The MDP provides separate register sets to support rapid switching between three
execution levels: background, priority 0 (P0 ), and priority 1 (P1). The MDP executes at the
background level when there are no pending messages. Each arriving message creates a task and
initiates execution at P0 or P1 depending on the priority of the message. The MDP executes the
highest priority task at any point in time. Thus, the arrival of a P1 message while the MDP is
executing a P0 task will cause the MDP to switch execution levels (and thus register sets). When
the P1 task completes, execution at P0 is resumed by switching to the P0 register set which holds
the register state of the suspended task.
     The register set at each priority level includes:
      4 general-purpose data registers: R0-R3
      4 address registers:                  A0-A3
      4 ID registers:1                      ID0-ID3
      1 instruction pointer:                IP

    Most instructions operate on the general registers R0-R3. Each address register A0-A3 contains
a segment descriptor consisting of a base and a length eld. Memory addresses are speci ed by
an o set and an address register. For example, the operands [R0,A1] and [3,A2] specify an
indexed access to the segment described by A1 and a displacement of 3 into A2's segment. ID
registers are less accessible general registers that by convention are used to hold object IDs. The
instruction pointer includes process status bits that control virtual addressing, type checking, and
fault handling. Placing these bits in the instruction pointer enables control and execution state to
be changed by loading a single register. Quick task switching within an execution level is facilitated
by the relatively small size of each register set.
    1 The background register set does not include ID registers. They only exist at P0 and P1 .
