# P9

## Reference
Tu, T., Liu, X., Song, L., Zhang, Y. (2019). *Understanding Real-World Concurrency Bugs in Go*. Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS '19), ACM, pp. 865–878. https://doi.org/10.1145/3297858.3304069. P ID: P9 (row R0-009). Included under I3.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Empirical study of real-world concurrency bugs: "the first systematic study on concurrency bugs in real Go programs", 171 bugs from six applications (P9, p. 1).
- **Context:** Builds on earlier real-world bug studies, mainly of C, C++ and Java (Lu et al. ASPLOS '08 [45], TaxDC [40], Node.js [57]), and on deadlock and race detection work (P9, pp. 5, 12). It sets out to test Go's claim that "explicit message passing is less error-prone" than shared memory (P9, p. 2). It cites earlier static checkers for Go channels (Lange et al. [38, 39], Ng and Yoshida [49]) (P9, p. 12).
- **Correctness:** The assumptions are mostly sound, but the sampling is under-reported. Bugs were found by searching commit logs for keywords (3211 matching commits), then randomly sampling those commits and studying them by hand (P9, p. 5). The paper does not say how many commits were sampled. It does not say who classified each bug, and it gives no agreement figure between classifiers. Only bugs that were fixed and well documented were kept (P9, p. 6). One claim, that message passing is "even more likely" to cause blocking bugs, divides bug counts by static counts of primitive use (Table 4). It does not measure how often each primitive is exercised at run time (P9, pp. 4, 6).
- **Contributions:** (1) The first empirical study of Go concurrency bugs, in six production applications. (2) Nine observations and eight implications about bug causes, fixes and detection. (3) A taxonomy along two orthogonal dimensions: behaviour (blocking or non-blocking) and cause (shared memory or message passing). Study data is published at github.com/system-pclub/go-concurrency-bugs (P9, p. 2).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised. Each section ends with numbered Observations and Implications, and counts are in Tables 5–12 (P9, pp. 5–11). The numbers in the tables match the numbers in the text.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The aim and a three-item contribution list are stated in the introduction (P9, pp. 1–2). |
| Q2 | partly | The channel mechanism is described for the studied programs. It covers naming (the channel value), behaviour when the receiver is busy (unbuffered channels block, buffered channels block only when full) and ordering in `select` (random choice). Message format is not described (P9, p. 3). |
| Q3 | yes | Defects come from the GitHub commit histories and linked bug reports of six real applications (P9, p. 5). |
| Q4 | partly | The defect comparisons name their baseline. Shared-memory bugs are the baseline in the same applications, and gRPC-C is the baseline for goroutine use (P9, pp. 4, 6). The fix and detector results give no baseline (P9, pp. 8, 11). |
| Q5 | partly | The paper gives the programs and why they were chosen (P9, p. 3), and sample sizes and run counts (171 bugs; 41 reproduced; each race test run 100 times) (P9, pp. 5–6, 11). It gives no hardware configuration for the gRPC runs or the detector runs. |
| Q6 | yes | The abstract's 171 bugs are in Table 5 (P9, p. 5). Its "more than half … Go-specific" can be derived from Tables 6 and 9 (P9, pp. 6, 9), but the paper never adds it up. The conclusions' claims are in Tables 6 and 9 (P9, p. 12). |
| Q7 | no | Causes are asserted, not isolated. Examples: "we suspect Go's new programming model" (P9, p. 7); the detector failures are put down to design goals (P9, p. 9); "possible reasons" for the race detector's misses (P9, p. 12); "we suspect" that programmers see channels as safer (P9, p. 11). |
| Q8 | yes | A dedicated "Threats to validity" paragraph (P9, p. 6). |
| Q9 | yes | The evaluated systems are Go's built-in deadlock detector and race detector (P9, pp. 8, 11). No author is listed as a designer of Go or of these detectors. Whether Q9 applies to I3 studies at all is open (see Notes). |

Local variables declared before an anonymous function are shared between parent and child goroutines. Shared memory is reachable through Mutex, RWMutex, Cond, atomic, Once and WaitGroup. A reference sent over a channel lets both goroutines reach the same variable (Docker#22985, CockroachDB#6111). | pp. 3, 9 |
| Message mechanism | Channels (`chan`). Unbuffered: send or receive blocks until the other side acts (synchronous). Buffered: send blocks only when the buffer is full. The receiver is named by the channel value. `select` waits on several channel operations and picks at random when more than one is ready. Rules: a nil channel blocks forever; sending to a closed channel, or closing a channel twice, panics at run time. `context`, `Pipe` and the `time` library are other forms of message passing. | p. 3 |
| Non-message primitives | At the language and library level: Mutex, RWMutex (in Go, write requests take priority over read requests, unlike `pthread_rwlock_t`), Cond, atomic, Once, WaitGroup, and shared local variables through anonymous functions. The paper gives no reason why Go keeps them; it only says Go "supports traditional shared memory accesses". | pp. 3, 6 |
| Self-definition | Not applicable: a defect study of applications; the paper does not discuss how the language or runtime is implemented. | — |
| Interposition | Not stated. | — |
| Operating system functions | Not applicable: a defect study; no operating system functions are discussed. | — |
| Cost of message primitives | Not measured. | — |
| Performance results | No performance result is measured. Table 3 gives goroutine counts and lifetimes, not performance. On three gRPC benchmarks, gRPC-Go creates 2.67–201.46 times as many goroutines as gRPC-C creates threads. The average goroutine lifetime is 63.23–92.73% of total run time, against 100% for gRPC-C threads. "gRPC-C is faster than gRPC-Go" is quoted from [22], not measured. | p. 4 |
| Scaling | Not applicable: no scaling measured. | — |
| Attributed causes | Not applicable for performance. Related cause, stated by third parties (the authors, not Go's designers): the built-in deadlock detector's limits are "largely due to the design goal of the built-in detector—minimal runtime overhead". This is inherent to detecting deadlocks in the scheduler. No measurement isolates it. | pp. 8–9 |
| Fate and reasons | Not applicable: no system is evaluated for fate. Go was the 9th most popular language on GitHub in 2017, with 187K repositories. | p. 3 |
| Concurrency defects | **Population:** six Go applications; 3211 commits matched keywords, and a random sample of them gave 171 bugs (p. 5). **Categories:** behaviour, either blocking (broader than deadlock: it includes waiting with no circular wait) or non-blocking; cause, either shared memory or message passing (p. 5). **Totals:** 85 blocking, 86 non-blocking; 105 shared memory, 66 message passing (Table 5, p. 5). **Blocking** (Table 6, p. 6): shared memory 36 (Mutex 28, RWMutex 5, Wait 3), about 42%; message passing 49 (Chan 29, Chan with other primitives 16, messaging libraries 4), about 58%. **Non-blocking** (Table 9, p. 9; p. 10): shared memory 69, about 80% (traditional 46, anonymous function 11, WaitGroup 6, library 6); message passing 17, about 20% (channel 16, library 1). Message-order defects: 3 bugs from `select`'s random choice (p. 10). Protocol violations: closing a channel twice, missing send, receive or close (pp. 7, 10). **Fixes:** blocking-bug patches average 6.8 lines, and about 90% adjust synchronization primitives (p. 8). About 69% of non-blocking bugs are fixed by restricting timing (p. 11). Channels also fix shared-memory bugs (Table 11, p. 11). **Detection:** the built-in deadlock detector finds 2 of 21 reproduced blocking bugs (Table 8, p. 8). The race detector finds 10 of 20 non-blocking bugs within 100 runs (Table 12, p. 11). **By construction:** the paper claims no design prevents any of these defects. It tests the belief that message passing is less error-prone and refutes it for blocking bugs (Observation 3, p. 6). It supports the belief for non-blocking bugs "when used correctly" (Implication 6, p. 11). | pp. 5–11 |

Evidence: manual root-cause analysis of 171 real bugs. | pp. 2, 6, 9–10, 12 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Not applicable: hardware is not discussed. | — |
| Model equivalence | Not stated as one model built on the other. Freedom from data races is not kept: references passed through channels still race (p. 9). Channels are used to fix shared-memory bugs, and replacing a channel with shared variables is used to fix channel bugs (pp. 8, 11). | pp. 8–9, 11 |
| Model mixing | Shared memory is used more than message passing in every application. Mutex is 45.01–70.34% of primitive uses and `chan` 18.48–42.99% (Table 4). The mix is stable from Feb 2015 to May 2018 (Figs. 2–3). gRPC-Go uses 8 kinds of primitive in 786 places, against lock only in gRPC-C (746 places). 16 blocking bugs involve a channel combined with a lock or wait (Table 6). | Notes | See Notes. | — |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| New: blocking bug | One or more goroutines are unintentionally stuck and cannot move forward. This is broader than deadlock, because it includes waiting with no circular wait for a resource that no other goroutine supplies. | p. 5 |
| New: non-blocking bug | All goroutines finish their tasks, but their behaviour is not the one intended. | p. 5 |
| New: cause dimension (shared memory vs. message passing) | Bugs are classified by how goroutines communicate: by misprotecting shared memory or by misusing message passing. | pp. 2, 5 |
| New: message passing is less error-prone (common belief, refuted for blocking bugs) | "Contrary to the common belief", message passing causes 58% of blocking bugs, while shared-memory primitives are used more. Message passing causes fewer non-blocking bugs. | pp. 2, 6, 10–12 |
| New: mixing message passing with other synchronization | Using channels together with locks, wait, or libraries (`context`, `time`, `Pipe`) gives blocking bugs that are "very hard to detect". | pp. 2, 7, 12 |
| New: channel usage rules | The rules Go enforces on its channels: no use before initialization, no double close, no send on a closed channel, and every send or receive needs a matching partner. Breaking these rules is "one major reason" for concurrency bugs. | pp. 3, 12 |
| New: data race through a message-passed reference | Sending a reference to a shared variable over a channel can cause a data race. | p. 9 |
| New: Go's new implementation of existing primitives | The same primitives as in other languages can cause new bugs because Go implements them differently, for example RWMutex giving writers priority. | p. 6 |

## Notes
- **Source:** the authors' PDF at https://songlh.github.io/paper/go-study.pdf (14 pages; acmart LaTeX, created 2019-03-22). It has the same title, DOI and ASPLOS '19 copyright block as the ACM version. The ACM Digital Library PDF link returned an HTML page and was not used. The authors' PDF is saved as `research/papers/P9.pdf`.
- **Page convention:** page numbers in this record are the PDF's pages 1–14. The proceedings page is 864 plus the PDF page (865–878, per Crossref).
- **Checks:** the counts in Tables 5, 6 and 9 add up to the totals in the text (36 + 69 = 105 shared memory; 49 + 17 = 66 message passing). The 42% and 58% split is 36 and 49 of 85 blocking bugs (pp. 5–6, 9).
- **Q9 for I3:** `quality.md` defines Q9 for evaluating a system. Here the system evaluated is incidental: Go's built-in detectors (pp. 8, 11). Answered yes because no author built them, but an I3 study arguably "does not evaluate a system", which would make it "no".
- **SQ7 relevance:** this is a within-language comparison. Both mechanisms are in the same programs, and channels sit on top of a language that also has shared memory. It is not a system built on message passing only (pp. 2–3).
- **Extra artefact:** the authors built a detector for anonymous-function races that found new bugs, one confirmed by developers (p. 12). It is not evaluated in the paper.

# P12

## Reference
William J. Dally, J.A. Stuart Fiske, John S. Keen, Richard A. Lethin, Michael D. Noakes, Peter R. Nuth, Roy E. Davison, Gregory A. Fyler (1992). *The Message-Driven Processor: A Multicomputer Processing Node with Efficient Mechanisms*. IEEE Micro 12(2), 23–39. https://doi.org/10.1109/40.127581. P12, included under I1 (row R0-012). Pages below are those of the authors' 25-page preprint (see Notes), not the IEEE Micro pages.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and implementation description of a working processor chip (the MDP) and its multicomputer (the J-Machine), with cycle counts but no evaluation section (pp. 1–3, 13–18).
- **Context:** Message-passing multicomputers (Cosmic Cube, iPSC, N-CUBE, Ametek), shared-address machines (BBN Butterfly, IBM RP3), single-chip nodes (Transputer, MOSAIC, iWARP); the authors' earlier MDP architecture paper [11] and k-ary n-cube network work [10, 12–14] (pp. 2–3).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that sequential-processor mechanisms do not support synchronisation, communication and global naming efficiently, so these "must be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead" (p. 2). It is argued, and backed only by one comparison with iPSC message times (p. 2). The cycle counts are given as design facts, not as measurements (pp. 9–11).
- **Contributions:** A single-chip node in which message arrival creates and dispatches a task in hardware, with no receive instruction (p. 1). It adds SEND instructions, hardware message queues, presence tags (FUT/CFUT), name translation (XLATE/ENTER) and three priority register sets (pp. 5–9). The chip is running silicon (p. 16), and Concurrent Smalltalk and Id are implemented on it (pp. 20–23).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with worked assembly examples (combining tree, CALL handler, size-of-tree; pp. 5, 10–11, 22). In this preprint most figures are blank and only their captions remain (see Notes).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The two design goals are listed in the introduction (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Message format (p. 9, Fig. 12 p. 13), receiver naming (p. 9) and busy-receiver behaviour (queue, priorities; pp. 6, 9) are described. Ordering guarantees are not stated; only deadlock freedom is (p. 12). |
| Q3 | yes | Silicon since June 1991, running programs; J-Machine boards and a 128-node machine are operational (pp. 16, 23–24). |
| Q4 | partly | Only the message-plus-dispatch time names a baseline (iPSC-1 5 ms, iPSC-2 300 µs; p. 2). The claim of being competitive with iWARP and Transputer names baselines but gives no values (p. 23). |
| Q5 | partly | Hardware configuration is given (62.5 ns cycle, 1K-node prototype; pp. 11–12). Workloads are only illustrative examples, with no reason for choosing them and no runs (pp. 10, 23). |
| Q6 | partly | The transistor count (Fig. 18 p. 18) and the June 1991 silicon date (p. 16) are in the body. "Competitive with iWARP/Transputer" and "2.5 years, < 8 people" (pp. 23–24) have no supporting data in the body. |
| Q7 | no | Causes of low overhead are asserted, e.g. dispatch avoids control-transfer overhead (pp. 10–11). No breakdown or ablation isolates them. |
| Q8 | partly | Open software questions, 12 hardware bugs and a "very conservative" implementation are mentioned in passing (pp. 16, 18, 23–24). There is no dedicated section. |
| Q9 | no | All authors designed or built the MDP (p. 3, p. 16). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See Reference above; I1 (I1(a) SEND instructions; I1(b) hardware message buffering and dispatch). | p. 1, 7 |
| Paper type | design (with an implementation section and silicon status; no evaluation section) | pp. 1–3, 13–18 |
| System | Message-Driven Processor (MDP), a 36-bit single-chip node with 1.1M transistors. Built by MIT AI Lab with Intel and funded by DARPA. Architecture studies began in October 1986; first silicon was June 1991, with a second revision sent in January 1992. Status: silicon. | pp. 1, 3, 16 |
| System | J-Machine multicomputer built from MDPs. The 64-node board and 1024-node chassis were designed; a 128-node machine is operational; J-Machines have been on-line since July 1991. Status: silicon / running system. | pp. 1, 16–18, 23–24 |
| System | COSMOS, a small run-time kernel for Concurrent Smalltalk (CST). Status: running on the J-Machine. | p. 20 |
| Levels with message semantics | Hardware: message arrival is the only way a task is created ("There is no receive instruction. A task is created to handle each arriving message"). Not every state change is a message, since tasks change local memory with ordinary instructions. → no. | pp. 1, 9 |
| Levels with message semantics | Instruction set: SEND, SENDE, SEND2, SEND2E are instructions, but the ISA "extends a conventional microprocessor ISA" with READ/WRITE, arithmetic and branches acting on local state. → no. | pp. 6, 8 |
| Levels with message semantics | Kernel (COSMOS): how COSMOS parts communicate is not stated. Compiled code calls it by CALL, a procedure call, not a message. → not stated. | pp. 20, 22 |
| Levels with message semantics | Language (CST): "Method or function invocation is performed by sending a message to the first argument." A non-message path was added later: when the compiler can infer the type, "a method invocation is optimized directly to the correct function invocation." → no. | p. 20 (fn. 5) |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Hardware: the node (MDP), which creates a task per message. Any task on the node reads and writes node memory through segment descriptors, and a console processor can read or write any location through the diagnostic port. | pp. 5, 6, 9 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | CST level: the object that is the first argument. Its state can be moved or copied to another node by COSMOS when XLATE faults, and immutable objects (functions, selectors) are copied. | pp. 20–21 |
| Message mechanism | Asynchronous: SEND injects words and the sender continues, and CST has "asynchronous message send". | pp. 9, 20, 21 |
| Message mechanism | Naming: the first word is the absolute destination node address <x,y,z>. Object IDs are translated to a node and to segment descriptors with XLATE. | pp. 7, 9, 22 |
| Message mechanism | Ordering and delivery: deterministic dimension-order (e-cube) routing, "provably deadlock free". End-to-end delivery is in hardware with no processor use at intermediate nodes. An order guarantee between sender–receiver pairs is not stated. | pp. 11, 12 |
| Message mechanism | Buffering: a hardware-managed FIFO queue in on-chip RAM, one per priority (P0, P1), circular, located by the QBM/QHL registers. Buffer memory is allocated automatically on the receiver. Network blocking flow control compresses blocked messages into routers. Queue overflow behaviour is not stated. | pp. 2, 9, 13, 15 |
| Message mechanism | Busy receiver: the message waits in the queue until it reaches the head. A P1 message preempts a P0 task (separate register sets). The next message is dispatched 2 cycles after SUSPEND. | pp. 6, 9, 11 |
| Message mechanism | Dispatch: the header opcode is loaded into the IP and A3 is set to the message segment (3 cycles). Remote procedure call messages go to a CALL handler that translates the method ID with XLATE. In CST, COSMOS selects the function from a selector object by the receiver's class. | pp. 9–10, 20–21 |
| Non-message primitives | Instruction set: local memory and register read/write (READ, WRITE, MOVE), arithmetic, branches and CALL. Reason not stated (the MDP "extends a conventional microprocessor ISA"). | pp. 6, 8 |
| Non-message primitives | Hardware: presence and type tags with fault handlers (CFUT/FUT faults, type exceptions, EARLY fault). Reason: "makes software more efficient and robust"; only exceptional cases pay for the handler. | pp. 7, 15 |
| Non-message primitives | Hardware: diagnostic port, through which a console processor can read or write any location and reset, interrupt, halt or single-step the processor. Reason: supervisory commands. | pp. 3, 5 |
| Non-message primitives | Hardware: segment descriptors in address registers, with relocation, bounds checks and invalidation on object move. Reason: naming, relocation and protection. | pp. 6, 7, 15 |
| Non-message primitives | Hardware: a background execution level with no message, and IP status bits that control virtual addressing, type checking and faults. Reason: so state can be changed by loading one register. | p. 6 |
| Non-message primitives | Hardware: a translation table (set-associative) mapped into on-chip memory, written by ENTER and read by XLATE. Reason: global naming. | pp. 7, 15 |
| Self-definition | Message handling (buffering, dispatch, routing) is in hardware. Handlers and COSMOS are MDP assembly, and CST is compiled to MDP assembly. Whether a running program can inspect or change these levels is not stated. The paper does not discuss what the hardware base costs or prevents. | pp. 9, 13–15, 20 |
| Interposition | Not stated. The nearest mechanism is name translation: an XLATE miss or fault goes to COSMOS, which finds the object and moves or copies it. This makes object location transparent to the caller, at the instruction-set and kernel levels. Cost not given. | pp. 7, 21 |
| Operating system functions | Protection: per-node segment descriptors with bounds checks, and IP status bits. No central component. A decentralised cost is not discussed. | pp. 6, 15 |
| Operating system functions | Scheduling: per-node hardware dispatch from the priority queues, with the highest priority first. No central component. Load balancing and scheduling policy are "open questions". | pp. 6, 9, 18 |
| Operating system functions | Resource allocation: the message buffer is allocated automatically on the receiving node. COSMOS provides object-based memory management and garbage collection. Whether a central component is involved: not stated. | pp. 2, 20 |
| Operating system functions | Naming: per-node translation tables, and a global virtual namespace from COSMOS. Whether a central component is involved: not stated. | pp. 7, 20 |
| Operating system functions | Failure handling: ECC on DRAM only. Otherwise not stated. | p. 3 |
| Operating system functions | Central element: a console processor reaches every node through the diagnostic port for supervisory commands. The paper does not say whether it is used at run time. | pp. 3, 5 |
| Cost of message primitives | Send of a 4-word message: 4 cycles (250 ns), on MDP silicon at a 62.5 ns cycle. These are design figures; the paper does not say whether they were measured. | pp. 9, 12 |
| Cost of message primitives | Dispatch (task creation on arrival): 3 cycles. Next queued message: dispatched 2 cycles after SUSPEND. Message delivery plus dispatch: under 2 µs on the J-Machine (under 2 µs to any node of a 4K machine, under 1 µs dispatch). | pp. 2, 9, 11 |
| Cost of message primitives | Network latency T = Tc(2L + D). For a 6-word message over 10 hops on a 1K machine this is 22 cycles (1.4 µs), at one cycle per hop. | p. 12 |
| Cost of message primitives | Context switch: three register sets (background, P0, P1), so switching between levels is a register-set switch. No cycle count is given. Combine handler: 12 instructions, 21 cycles. | pp. 6, 10 |
| Performance results | Message delivery plus task dispatch: J-Machine < 2 µs; baselines iPSC-1 5 ms and iPSC-2 300 µs (versions as named; configuration not given). | p. 2 |
| Performance results | Network bandwidth: 288 Mbit/s per channel and 864 Mbit/s per node. For a 1K-node machine: bisection 18.4 Gbit/s, aggregate 864 Gbit/s, I/O 184 Gbit/s. No baseline. | pp. 11–12 |
| Performance results | A two-input dataflow node takes 20 MDP instructions to simulate. No baseline. | p. 23 |
| Performance results | Standard cells cost a factor of 3–4 in area and 2–3 in performance against full custom (designers' estimate). | p. 16 |
| Scaling | Not measured. The network addresses up to 64K nodes; the prototype is 1K nodes and a 128-node machine is operational. The latency model T = Tc(2L + D) grows with distance. | pp. 11–12, 23 |
| Attributed causes | "sequential machines require hundreds of instructions to create a new process", so these functions "must be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead". Designers; inherent to sequential mechanisms; not isolated. | p. 2 |
| Attributed causes | Low handler overhead comes from hardware dispatch setting the IP and A3, which "avoids the overhead otherwise associated with control transfer and with setting up an addressing environment". It also comes from sending directly from registers "without any need to first format it in memory". Designers; inherent to the design; not isolated. | pp. 10–11 |
| Attributed causes | Tags make the no-fault case faster than "test and branch instructions". Designers; inherent to the design; not isolated. | p. 7 |
| Attributed causes | The low overhead against iPSC allows "concurrency at a much finer grain". Designers; inherent to the design; not isolated. | p. 2 |
| Attributed causes | Standard cells cost 3–4x area and 2–3x performance, and the implementation is "very conservative". Designers; due to the implementation; not isolated. | pp. 16, 24 |
| Fate and reasons | Research system. Twelve silicon bugs led to a second revision in January 1992 "for performance reasons". Several thousand chips are planned for MIT research multicomputers. A commercial product based on the mechanisms is "very plausible". It is succeeded by the MIT M-Machine, which extends the mechanisms to intra-node concurrency. All stated by the designers. | pp. 16, 24 |
| Concurrency defects | Not applicable: no defect study. The 12 bugs reported are hardware design bugs, not categorised. | p. 16 |
| What shapes programs | "most parallel programs are very biased by the mechanisms (or lack thereof) of the machines for which they were initially written"; also, fine-grain parallelism is hard to extract from C or FORTRAN programs. Evidence: designers' assertion. | pp. 18, 24 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | The MDP provides general primitive mechanisms rather than specialising for one model, to support shared memory, data parallel, dataflow, actors and message passing. The authors claim performance competitive with nodes specialised to one model (iWARP systolic, Transputer CSP). This applies to the message send as primitive (SEND plus hardware dispatch). Argued, not measured. | pp. 1–2, 23 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Benefit: hardware tags remove type and presence checks from the common case. | p. 7 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Cost: in a multicomputer, features with small returns (large caches) are dropped for more nodes. A design cost of specialisation is not quantified. | pp. 2, 7 |
| Model equivalence | Shared memory on messages: "one can build a shared memory model that gives the application programmer a single, shared address space", and a global virtual address space via translation. CST and dataflow run "using a shared address space". Properties and performance kept or lost: not stated. | pp. 5, 7, 23 |
| Model mixing | CST compiler: method invocation is turned into a direct function call when the type is known or declared (reason: optimisation). Compiled code calls COSMOS by CALL. Futures (CFUT tags) are used for replies. How often: not stated. | pp. 20–22 |
| Runtime limits | Open questions about the cost of the model: spawning locally versus remotely depends on overhead; object placement and migration to reduce communication; throttling parallelism when the machine is saturated. For dataflow, scheduling overhead motivates larger grains. The hardware shared-memory model is not named as a cause. | p. 23 |
| Many-core scaling | Up to 64K nodes in a 3-D mesh, each node with local memory. There is no hardware shared memory or coherence; a global address space comes from translation. Inter-node communication uses hardware message routing. No scaling result. Named limits: wire density and component pinout (topology choice) and network hot spots (P1 priority). Future work proposes many processing units per chip (M-Machine). | pp. 2, 11, 13, 24 |
| Adoption factors | MDP: not adopted commercially at the time of writing, research only; a commercial product is "very plausible". Factors stated: cost-effectiveness of fine-grain nodes (argued), no established parallel benchmarks, and programs biased to their original machines' mechanisms. | pp. 23–24 |
| Quality | See Quality table above. | — |
| Notes | See Notes. | — |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| message-driven processing (new) | "processing is performed in response to messages (via the dispatch mechanism). There is no receive instruction. A task is created to handle each arriving message." | p. 1 |
| primitive mechanisms vs programming models (new) | Mechanisms are the hardware's primitive operations from which programming abstractions are built. The MDP gives general communication, synchronisation and naming mechanisms instead of specialising for one model. | pp. 1–2 |
| message dispatch as task creation (new) | The header opcode is loaded into the IP and a message segment descriptor goes into A3, creating a task in 3 cycles. | p. 9 |
| presence tags / futures (FUT, CFUT) (new) | Tagged locations are marked empty, and reading one faults and suspends the task until a value is written. Used for synchronisation. | pp. 6–7 |
| name translation (XLATE/ENTER) (new) | A hardware associative table maps arbitrary keys to values (segment descriptors or node numbers) to support a global virtual address space. | p. 7 |
| fine-grain multicomputer / jellybean node (new) | An inexpensive node with small memory, many per system, giving more performance per unit cost. Tasks are about 20 instructions and objects about 8 words. | pp. 1–2, 23 |
| global virtual address space over message passing (new) | The same IDs name local and remote objects. A shared-memory model can be built on the mechanisms. | pp. 3, 5 |
| selector-object dispatch (new) | CST method invocation is a message to the first argument. COSMOS picks the function by class from a selector object; known types bypass it with a direct call. | pp. 20–21 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** the authors' preprint "micro.dvi", PostScript (`ieee-micro92.ps.Z`) from the Stanford Concurrent VLSI Architecture group publications page, http://cva.stanford.edu/publications/1992/ieee-micro92.ps.Z, fetched 2026-10-06. I converted it to PDF with Ghostscript ps2pdf and saved it as `research/papers/P12.pdf` (25 pages). It is not the IEEE Micro typeset version, which is closed access (OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar: closed).
- **Page numbers:** all pages cited are preprint pages 1–25, not IEEE Micro pp. 23–39. Wording may differ slightly from the published text.
- **Figures:** the preprint has no embedded images. Figures 1–4, 7, 9, 11, 13–17, 19 and 20 are blank apart from their captions. Figures 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 18 and 21–23 are text or tables and were read.
- **Author list:** the preprint lists the authors as Dally, Davison, Fiske, Fyler, Keen, Lethin, Noakes, Nuth (Davison and Fyler at Intel). The Stanford CVA citation gives the published order Dally, Fiske, Keen, Lethin, Noakes, Nuth, Davison, Fyler, which is used in Reference.
- **X8 (ICCD 1992 version, 10.1109/iccd.1992.276304):** not read in this run. I cannot say which version is longer or whether the ICCD version adds anything.
- **Measured or designed figures:** the cycle counts (4-cycle send, 3-cycle dispatch, 21-cycle combine) read as design figures for the silicon. The paper does not say they were measured.
- **SQ8:** the claim that "most parallel programs are very biased by the mechanisms (or lack thereof) of the machines for which they were initially written" (p. 24) bears directly on SQ8, but only as an assertion.
- **Deepest pass:** pass 2. The whole text was read in detail for extraction; assumptions were not re-derived (no pass 3).

In anticipation of the promise of tremendous hardware advances, software researchers have fashioned expansive programming environments to improve programmer productivity. Even with the march of technology, exploratory programming environments such as Smalltalk-80 require such expensive computers that few programmers can afford them. With the hope of increasing that community, a research project at the University of California created a reduced instruction set computer for Smalltalk called SOAR, which stands for Smalltalk on a RISC. The authors are now able to estimate the performance implications of the Smalltalk-80 programming environment. In the next section the authors list the demands that Smalltalk-80 places on traditional computer systems, then present software and hardware ideas that answer those demands.

Abstract

Keywords Go; Concurrency Bug; Bug Study

Go is a statically-typed programming language that aims
to provide a simple, efficient, and safe way to build multithreaded software. Since its creation in 2009, Go has matured and gained significant adoption in production and
open-source software. Go advocates for the usage of message passing as the means of inter-thread communication
and provides several new concurrency mechanisms and libraries to ease multi-threading programming. It is important
to understand the implication of these new proposals and the
comparison of message passing and shared memory synchronization in terms of program errors, or bugs. Unfortunately,
as far as we know, there has been no study on Go’s concurrency bugs.
In this paper, we perform the first systematic study on
concurrency bugs in real Go programs. We studied six popular Go software including Docker, Kubernetes, and gRPC.
We analyzed 171 concurrency bugs in total, with more than
half of them caused by non-traditional, Go-specific problems.
Apart from root causes of these bugs, we also studied their
fixes, performed experiments to reproduce them, and evaluated them with two publicly-available Go bug detectors.
Overall, our study provides a better understanding on Go’s
concurrency models and can guide future researchers and
practitioners in writing better, more reliable Go software
and in developing debugging and diagnosis tools for Go.

Introduction

Go [20] is a statically typed language originally developed
by Google in 2009. Over the past few years, it has quickly
gained attraction and is now adopted by many types of software in real production. These Go applications range from
libraries [19] and high-level software [26] to cloud infrastructure software like container systems [13, 36] and key-value
databases [10, 15].
A major design goal of Go is to improve traditional multithreaded programming languages and make concurrent programming easier and less error-prone. For this purpose, Go
centers its multi-threading design around two principles:
1) making threads (called goroutines) lightweight and easy
to create and 2) using explicit messaging (called channel)
to communicate across threads. With these design principles, Go proposes not only a set of new primitives and new
libraries but also new implementation of existing semantics.
It is crucial to understand how Go’s new concurrency primitives and mechanisms impact concurrency bugs, the type of
bugs that is the most difficult to debug and the most widely
studied [40, 43, 45, 57, 61] in traditional multi-threaded programming languages. Unfortunately, there has been no prior
work in studying Go concurrency bugs. As a result, to date,
it is still unclear if these concurrency mechanisms actually
make Go easier to program and less error-prone to concurrency bugs than traditional languages.
In this paper, we conduct the first empirical study on
Go concurrency bugs using six open-source, productiongrade Go applications: Docker [13] and Kubernetes [36],
two datacenter container systems, etcd [15], a distributed
key-value store system, gRPC [19], an RPC library, and CockroachDB [10] and BoltDB [6], two database systems.
In total, we have studied 171 concurrency bugs in these applications. We analyzed the root causes of them, performed
experiments to reproduce them, and examined their fixing

 === PAGE 2
patches. Finally, we tested them with two existing Go concurrency bug detectors (the only publicly available ones).
Our study focuses on a long-standing and fundamental
question in concurrent programming: between message passing [27, 37] and shared memory, which of these inter-thread
communication mechanisms is less error-prone [2, 11, 48].
Go is a perfect language to study this question, since it provides frameworks for both shared memory and message
passing. However, it encourages the use of channels over
shared memory with the belief that explicit message passing
is less error-prone [1, 2, 21].
To understand Go concurrency bugs and the comparison
between message passing and shared memory, we propose
to categorize concurrency bugs along two orthogonal dimensions: the cause of bugs and their behavior. Along the cause
dimension, we categorize bugs into those that are caused
by misuse of shared memory and those caused by misuse of
message passing. Along the second dimension, we separate
bugs into those that involve (any number of) goroutines that
cannot proceed (we call them blocking bugs) and those that
do not involve any blocking (non-blocking bugs).
Surprisingly, our study shows that it is as easy to make concurrency bugs with message passing as with shared memory,
sometimes even more. For example, around 58% of blocking
bugs are caused by message passing. In addition to the violation of Go’s channel usage rules (e.g., waiting on a channel
that no one sends data to or close), many concurrency bugs
are caused by the mixed usage of message passing and other
new semantics and new libraries in Go, which can easily be
overlooked but hard to detect.
To demonstrate errors in message passing, we use a blocking bug from Kubernetes in Figure 1. The finishReq function creates a child goroutine using an anonymous function at line 4 to handle a request—a common practice in
Go server programs. The child goroutine executes fn() and
sends result back to the parent goroutine through channel
ch at line 6. The child will block at line 6 until the parent
pulls result from ch at line 9. Meanwhile, the parent will
block at select until either when the child sends result to ch
(line 9) or when a timeout happens (line 11). If timeout happens earlier or if Go runtime (non-deterministically) chooses
the case at line 11 when both cases are valid, the parent will
return from requestReq() at line 12, and no one else can
pull result from ch any more, resulting in the child being
blocked forever. The fix is to change ch from an unbuffered
channel to a buffered one, so that the child goroutine can
always send the result even when the parent has exit.
This bug demonstrates the complexity of using new features in Go and the difficulty in writing correct Go programs
like this. Programmers have to have a clear understanding
of goroutine creation with anonymous function, a feature
Go proposes to ease the creation of goroutines, the usage
of buffered vs. unbuffered channels, the non-determinism
of waiting for multiple channel operations using select,

Background and Applications

Go is a statically-typed programming language that is designed for concurrent programming from day one [60]. Almost all major Go revisions include improvements in its concurrency packages [23]. This section gives a brief background
on Go’s concurrency mechanisms, including its thread model,
inter-thread communication methods, and thread synchronization mechanisms. We also introduce the six Go applications we chose for this study.
2.1

Goroutine

Go uses a concept called goroutine as its concurrency unit.
Goroutines are lightweight user-level threads that the Go

 === PAGE 3
runtime library manages and maps to kernel-level threads
in an M-to-N way. A goroutine can be created by simply
adding the keyword go before a function call.
To make goroutines easy to create, Go also supports creating a new goroutine using an anonymous function, a function
definition that has no identifier, or “name”. All local variables
declared before an anonymous function are accessible to the
anonymous function, and are potentially shared between
a parent goroutine and a child goroutine created using the
anonymous function, causing data race (Section 6).
2.2

Synchronization with Shared Memory

Go supports traditional shared memory accesses across
goroutines. It supports various traditional synchronization primitives like lock/unlock (Mutex), read/write lock
(RWMutex), condition variable (Cond), and atomic read/write
(atomic). Go’s implementation of RWMutex is different from
pthread_rwlock_t in C. Write lock requests in Go have a
higher privilege than read lock requests.
As a new primitive introduced by Go, Once is designed
to guarantee a function is only executed once. It has a Do
method, with a function f as argument. When Once.Do(f)
is invoked many times, only for the first time, f is executed.
Once is widely used to ensure a shared variable only be
initialized once by multiple goroutines.
Similar to pthread_join in C, Go uses WaitGroup to allow multiple goroutines to finish their shared variable accesses before a waiting goroutine. Goroutines are added to
a WaitGroup by calling Add. Goroutines in a WaitGroup use
Done to notify their completion, and a goroutine calls Wait
to wait for the completion notification of all goroutines in
a WaitGroup. Misusing WaitGroup can cause both blocking
bugs (Section 5) and non-blocking bugs (Section 6).
2.3

Synchronization with Message Passing

Channel (chan) is a new concurrency primitive introduced
by Go to send data and states across goroutines and to build
more complex functionalities [3, 50]. Go supports two types
of channels: buffered and unbuffered. Sending data to (or
receiving data from) an unbuffered channel will block a goroutine, until another goroutine receives data from (or sends
data to) the channel. Sending to a buffered channel will only
block, when the buffer is full. There are several underlying
rules in using channels and the violation of them can create
concurrency bugs. For example, channel can only be used
after initialization, and sending data to (or receiving data
from) a nil channel will block a goroutine forever. Sending
data to a closed channel or close an already closed channel
can trigger a runtime panic.
The select statement allows a goroutine to wait on multiple channel operations. A select will block until one of its
cases can make progress or when it can execute a default
branch. When more than one cases in a select are valid, Go

will randomly choose one to execute. This randomness can
cause concurrency bugs as will be discussed in Section 6.
Go introduces several new semantics to ease the interaction across multiple goroutines. For example, to assist the
programming model of serving a user request by spawning a set of goroutines that work together, Go introduces
context to carry request-specific data or metadata across
goroutines. As another example, Pipe is designed to stream
data between a Reader and a Writer. Both context and
Pipe are new forms of passing messages and misusing them
can create new types of concurrency bugs (Section 5).

Bug taxonomy. We propose a new method to categorize Go
concurrency bugs according to two orthogonal dimensions.

The first dimension is based on the behavior of bugs. If one or
more goroutines are unintentionally stuck in their execution
and cannot move forward, we call such concurrency issues
blocking bugs. If instead all goroutines can finish their tasks
but their behaviors are not desired, we call them non-blocking
ones. Most previous concurrency bug studies [24, 43, 45]
categorize bugs into deadlock bugs and non-deadlock bugs,
where deadlocks include situations where there is a circular
wait across multiple threads. Our definition of blocking is
broader than deadlocks and include situations where there
is no circular wait but one (or more) goroutines wait for
resources that no other goroutines supply. As we will show
in Section 5, quite a few Go concurrency bugs are of this
kind. We believe that with new programming habits and
semantics with new languages like Go, we should pay more
attention to these non-deadlock blocking bugs and extend
the traditional concurrency bug categorization mechanism.
The second dimension is along the cause of concurrency
bugs. Concurrency bugs happen when multiple threads try to
communicate and errors happen during such communication.
Our idea is thus to categorize causes of concurrency bugs by
how different goroutines communicate: by accessing shared
memory or by passing messages. This categorization can
help programmers and researchers choose better ways to
perform inter-thread communication and to detect and avoid
potential errors when performing such communication.
According to our categorization method, there are a total
of 85 blocking bugs and 86 non-blocking bugs, and there
are a total of 105 bugs caused by wrong shared memory
protection and 66 bugs caused by wrong message passing.
Table 5 shows the detailed breakdown of bug categories
across each application.
We further analyzed the life time of our studied bugs, i.e.,
the time from when the buggy code was added (committed)
to the software to when it is being fixed in the software (a bugfixing patch is committed). As shown in Figure 4, most bugs
we study (both shared memory and message passing) have
long life time. We also found the time when these bugs were
report to be close to when they were fixed. These results
show that most of the bugs we study are not easy to be

soon. Thus, we believe these bugs are non-trivial and worth
close examination.
Reproducing concurrency bugs. In order to evaluate the
built-in deadlock and data-race detection techniques, we
reproduced 21 blocking bugs and 20 non-blocking bugs. To
reproduce a bug, we rolled the application back to the buggy
version, built the buggy version, and ran the built program
using the bug-triggering input described in the bug report.
We leveraged the symptom mentioned in the bug report
to decide whether we have successfully reproduced a bug.
Due to their non-deterministic nature, concurrency bugs
are difficult to reproduce. Sometimes, we needed to run a
buggy program a lot of times or manually add sleep to a
buggy program. For a bug that is not reproduced, it is either
because we do not find some dependent libraries, or because
we fail to observe the described symptom.
Threats to validity. Threats to the validity of our study
could come from many aspects. We selected six representative Go applications. There are many other applications
implemented in Go and they may not share the same concurrency problems. We only studied concurrency bugs that
have been fixed. There could be other concurrency bugs
that are rarely reproduced and are never fixed by developers.
For some fixed concurrency bugs, there is too little information provided, making them hard to understand. We do
not include these bugs in our study. Despite these limitations, we have made our best efforts in collecting real-world
Go concurrency bugs and in conducting a comprehensive
and unbiased study. We believe that our findings are general
enough to motivate and guide future research on fighting
Go concurrency bugs.

5

Blocking Bugs

This section presents our study results on blocking bugs,
including their root causes, fixes, and the effectiveness of the
built-in runtime Go deadlock detector on detecting blocking
situations.
5.1

Root Causes of Blocking Bugs

Blocking bugs manifest when one or more goroutines conduct operations that wait for resources, and these resources

are never available. To detect and avoid blocking bugs, it is
important to understand their root causes. We study blocking bugs’ root causes by examining which operation blocks
a goroutine and why the operation is not unblocked by other
goroutines. Using our second dimension of bug categorization, we separate blocking bugs into those that are caused by
stuck operations that are intended to protect shared memory accesses and those that are caused by message passing
operations. Table 6 summarizes the root causes of all the
blocking bugs.
Overall, we found that there are around 42% blocking bugs
caused by errors in protecting shared memory, and 58% are
caused by errors in message passing. Considering that shared
memory primitives are used more frequently than message
passing ones (Section 3.2), message passing operations are
even more likely to cause blocking bugs.
Observation 3: Contrary to the common belief that message
passing is less error-prone, more blocking bugs in our studied
Go applications are caused by wrong message passing than by
wrong shared memory protection.
5.1.1

(mis)Protection of Shared Memory

Shared memory accesses are notoriously hard to program
correctly and have always been one of the major focuses
on deadlock research [35, 51, 54]. They continue to cause
blocking bugs in Go, both with traditional patterns and new,
Go-specific reasons.
Mutex 28 blocking bugs are caused by misusing locks
(Mutex), including double locking, acquiring locks in conflicting orders, and forgetting to unlock. All bugs in this category
are traditional bugs, and we believe traditional deadlock detection algorithms should be able to detect these bugs with
static program analysis.
RWMutex As explained in Section 2.2, Go’s write lock requests have a higher privilege than read lock requests. This
unique lock implementation can lead to a blocking bug when
a goroutine (th-A) acquires one RWMutex twice with read
locking, and these two read lock operations are interleaved
by a write lock operation from another goroutine (th-B).
When th-A’s first read lock operation succeeds, it will block
th-B’s write lock operation, since write locking is exclusive.
However, th-B’s write lock operation will also block th-A’s
second read lock operation, since the write lock request has
a higher privilege in Go’s implementation. Neither th-A nor
th-B will be able to proceed.
Five blocking bugs are caused by this reason. Note that the
same interleaving locking pattern will not cause blocking
bugs for pthread_rwlock_t in C, since pthread_rwlock_t
prioritize read lock requests under the default setting. The
RWMutex blocking bug type implies that even when Go uses
the same concurrency semantics as traditional languages,
there can still be new types of bugs because of Go’s new
implementation of the semantics.

# P22

## Reference
Milo M. K. Martin, Mark D. Hill, Daniel J. Sorin (2012). *Why On-Chip Cache Coherence Is Here to Stay*. Communications of the ACM 55(7), pp. 78–89. https://doi.org/10.1145/2209249.2209269. Included under I4 (SQ14), row R0-025.

All pages below are pages 1–9 of the authors' near-final version (`papers/P22.pdf`), not the CACM pages 78–89 (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
3. I read every section, the sidebar, Table 1 and Figures 2, 4 and 5, and checked the analyses (amortized traffic, storage growth, latency formulas, non-inclusive overhead) against the paper's own numbers. I did not rerun the recall simulation, because its inputs are not published.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position paper backed by analysis. It presents a proof-of-concept coherence design built from known techniques, then analyses it with analytical models and one small simulation. It reports no silicon or benchmark measurements (p. 1, p. 8).
- **Context:** It answers predictions that on-chip coherence will not scale and will give way to software-managed coherence, scratchpads or message passing without shared memory. It cites DeNovo [5], Intel's 48-core message-passing processor [10] and Cohesion [13] (p. 1, p. 3). It builds on directory protocols [1, 8], the SGI Origin 2000 [14], Intel Core i7 [17], AMD HT-Assist [6] and Linux scalability studies [2, 3] (p. 1, pp. 4–6).
- **Correctness:** Some assumptions are stated: coherence does not change the number of misses, though false sharing and poor synchronization may change it (p. 4). Others are stated too: an inclusive shared cache (p. 2), a single chip (p. 9), and no queuing or contention modelled (p. 8). Some are left implicit: the cost model counts bytes per miss and ignores how invalidation bursts are spread over time, and the energy analysis is inferred from the traffic and storage results, not modelled (pp. 7–8).
- **Contributions:** (1) An amortized argument that traffic per miss does not depend on core count when sharers are tracked exactly (p. 3, Fig. 2b p. 4). (2) Coherence traffic is at most 20% above a cache system without coherence (Table 1, p. 4). (3) With a hierarchy of inclusive caches, storage grows as √C (two levels) or ∛C (three levels) (p. 6, Fig. 4). (4) With explicit eviction notifications, recalls are rare: below 0.1% at a 4× capacity ratio with 8 ways (p. 7, Fig. 5). (5) Latency and energy arguments (pp. 7–8). (6) An extension to non-inclusive caches (p. 8).
- **Clarity:** Clear. There is one "Concern" section per scalability worry, and each ends with a boxed conclusion (pp. 3–8). There is a dedicated caveats section (pp. 8–9). One numeric inconsistency: the abstract says storage is "2% of total cache size for even 512 cores" (p. 1). The summary says 5% with two cache levels or 2% with three (p. 8). The abstract does not say that the 2% figure needs three levels.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim in one place: "refutes this conventional wisdom by showing one way to scale on-chip cache coherence with bounded costs" (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Two of four are given. Message format: request and ack 8 B, data 72 B, holding block address and type (Table 1, p. 4). Addressing: shared cache banked by address, per-core tracking bits, forwarding to sharers (p. 2). Delivery or ordering guarantees and busy-receiver behaviour are not stated. |
| Q3 | partly | Almost all evidence is analytical. The only executed artefact is a recall simulation on a synthetic random miss stream (p. 7). There is no silicon, FPGA or real-program run (p. 8). |
| Q4 | partly | Traffic and latency are compared with a named but hypothetical baseline: "caches but no hardware coherence" (p. 4, p. 7). Inexact encoding is compared with the Origin 2000 scheme (p. 5). The energy claim has no baseline or measurement (pp. 7–8). |
| Q5 | partly | Two of three are reported for the recall simulation. Workload: a random miss stream, justified by [9]. Configuration: fully associative private caches, associativities and capacity ratios swept. The number of runs or samples is not reported (p. 7). |
| Q6 | yes | Each number in the abstract and conclusions appears in the body. 20% traffic: Table 1 (p. 4). √C storage and 2% at 512 cores: Fig. 4 (p. 6). Zero latency for non-shared misses: p. 7. 2–9% non-inclusive overhead: p. 8. |
| Q7 | partly | The traffic spike is isolated to inexact encoding (Fig. 2a vs 2b, p. 4). The recall rate is isolated to capacity ratio and associativity (Fig. 5, p. 7). Causes in the energy and complexity arguments are only asserted (pp. 8–9). |
| Q8 | yes | A dedicated section, "Summary, Caveats, and Criticisms", lists five limitations (pp. 8–9). |
| Q9 | no | All three authors designed the evaluated protocol ("we synergistically combine known techniques", p. 1). The paper also discloses: "Hill has a significant financial interest in AMD" (p. 9). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Martin, Hill, Sorin (2012), *Why On-Chip Cache Coherence Is Here to Stay*, CACM 55(7):78–89; P22; included by I4 (SQ14), R0-025 | p. 1 |
| Paper type | design. A proof-of-concept design with analytical evaluation, argued as a position ("existence proof of a scalable coherence protocol, but we do not claim it to be the best"). | p. 1, p. 8 |
| System | (a) The authors' proof-of-concept protocol: a hierarchy of inclusive caches with embedded tracking bits and explicit eviction notifications. Status: design only, analytical model plus one simulation. Built by the authors, 2011–2012. (b) Its base protocol is "loosely based upon" Intel Core i7 (Nehalem): silicon, deployed commercially. (c) Also discussed: SGI Origin 2000 (silicon, commercial), Sun/Oracle UltraSPARC T2, NVIDIA Fermi, AMD Bulldozer and AMD HT-Assist (silicon). | p. 1, p. 2, pp. 5–6, p. 8 |
| Levels with message semantics | Instruction set: no. Cores "communicate via loads and stores to a shared address space". Hardware (cache controllers): yes for coherence actions only. A private-cache miss "issues a coherence request message"; the shared cache forwards, invalidates or sends recall messages; "communication involves only point-to-point messages". Cache hits change state with no message. Microcode, kernel, runtime, language: not stated. Message-based start later extended: not stated. | p. 1, p. 2, p. 3 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Receivers are cache controllers: shared-cache banks, cluster caches and private caches. A private cache's block state can be changed from outside: on a recall message "the private cache is forced to evict the block"; on a write miss the shared cache's forwarded request makes private caches "invalidate their copies". Each core's private cache is also read and written by its own core's loads and stores. | p. 2, p. 3 |
| Message mechanism | Coherence messages between caches. Sync/async: not stated, but requests are forwarded and "responses are typically sent directly to the original requester (… three-hop protocol)" (p. 7). Naming: by block address to an address-interleaved shared-cache bank; the bank names sharers by per-core tracking bits (p. 2). Ordering and delivery guarantees: not stated. Buffering: not stated. Busy receiver: not stated. Dispatch: by the block's coherence state (M/S/I) and tracking bits (p. 2, sidebar). | p. 2, p. 7 |
| Non-message primitives | At the instruction-set level: loads and stores to shared memory are the communication primitive. Reason: coherence makes caches "functionally invisible to software" and keeps backward compatibility for software "written for cache-coherent shared memory systems" (p. 1). Cache hits: served locally with no message (p. 7). Interrupts, traps, DMA, I/O: not stated. | p. 1, p. 7 |
| Self-definition | Not applicable: the paper describes hardware coherence, not a system written in its own objects and messages. | p. 1 |
| Interposition | not stated. The paper does not discuss placing a component between sender and receiver. | none |
| Operating system functions | Not addressed for the paper's own design. The paper claims conventional operating systems "have been shown to scale using cache coherence [2, 3]". It quotes Boyd-Wickizer et al.: "there is no scalability reason to give up on traditional operating system organizations just yet". On centralization: a single shared last-level cache tracks sharers per block (one directory entry per block, distributed across banks). Protection, scheduling, naming and failure handling are not stated. | p. 1, p. 2, p. 8 |
| Cost of message primitives | No measured latency or cycles. Analytical sizes: request and ack messages 8 B, data message 72 B (64 B block + 8 B address). Latency formulas: t_direct = t_noncoherent = 2·t_interconnect + t_cache; t_indirect = 3·t_interconnect + 2·t_cache. | p. 4 (Table 1), p. 7 |
| Performance results | (1) Traffic, bytes/miss, analytical model, coherent vs "without coherence" (64-bit address, 64-byte block): clean 96 vs 80 B/miss (+20%); dirty 160 vs 152 B/miss (+5%) (Table 1, p. 4). (2) Traffic with Origin-style inexact encoding (32 bits/block) vs exact: spike of "almost 6x" at 1024 cores (Fig. 2a, p. 4; text p. 5). (3) Storage overhead, % of cache storage, exact tracking: 16 cores ~3% (p. 3). 1024-core two-level: 6%. 4096-core three-level: 3% (p. 6). 512 cores: 5% two-level, 2% three-level (p. 8). (4) Recall rate, % of misses, synthetic random miss stream: below 0.1% for an 8-way shared cache at 4× capacity ratio; Core i7 is 16-way at 8× (Fig. 5, p. 7). (5) Indirect-miss latency vs non-coherent miss: 1.5× to 2× (p. 7). (6) Non-inclusive directory storage overhead, 16 cores: 2% at S2/S1=8; 4%, 6%, 9% at 4, 2, 1. Hierarchical, 256 cores: 2% at Z=8; 5%, 10%, 18% at Z=4, 2, 1 (p. 8). | p. 3, p. 4, p. 5, p. 6, p. 7, p. 8 |
| Scaling | Analytical, not measured. Core counts modelled: 1–1024 for traffic (Fig. 2, p. 4); 1–4096 for storage (Fig. 4, p. 6); 256 for non-inclusive storage (p. 8). Results: traffic per miss with exact tracking is independent of core count (p. 3–4). Flat storage overhead grows linearly with C (passes 20% before 128 cores in Fig. 4). Two-level storage grows as √C; three-level as ∛C (p. 6). The latency ratio is independent of core count (p. 7). Baseline: a system with caches and no coherence (p. 4), and flat vs hierarchical designs (p. 6). | p. 3, p. 4, p. 6, p. 7, p. 8 |
| Attributed causes | (a) "Coherence's alleged lack of scalability is believed to be due to the poor scaling of the storage and traffic … as well as concerns about latency and energy". Stated by the authors (third party to the predictions) as others' belief, which the paper disputes (p. 1). (b) Traffic does not grow because "for every write that invalidates N caches, it must have been preceded by N read misses". Designers; inherent to exact tracking; argued by amortization and shown in Fig. 2b (p. 3–4). (c) The traffic spike in inexact encoding comes from "unnecessary invalidations". Designers; inherent to the encoding; isolated by Fig. 2a vs 2b (p. 5). (d) Recalls come from shared-cache capacity and associativity, and from silent clean evictions that leave the shared cache "ambiguous". Designers; due to implementation; isolated by Fig. 5 (pp. 6–7). (e) Many applications do not scale, but the root cause may be "the algorithm, program implementation, or coherence"; this is asserted with no measurement (p. 1). | p. 1, pp. 3–7 |
| Fate and reasons | Cache coherence is commercial and dominant: "provided by mainstream servers, desktops, laptops, and even mobile devices … Intel, AMD, ARM, IBM, and Oracle (Sun)". It "has come to dominate the market for both technical and legacy reasons": better performance than software coherence, and backward compatibility. Stated by the authors (third party to the vendors). The paper's own protocol: research only (existence proof). | p. 1, p. 8 |
| Concurrency defects | Not applicable: no defect study. The sidebar gives one constructed example: without coherence, a lock variable could let "multiple cores into a critical section or prevent cores waiting … from making forward progress". | p. 2 |
| What shapes programs | The hardware model, by argument only. "At least with hardware coherence, programmers can concentrate on choreographing independent work rather than handling low-level mechanics" (p. 1). Coherence frees developers "from re-implementing coherence … or orchestrating explicit communication via message passing" (p. 9). Evidence kind: argument, no study of programs or programmers. | p. 1, p. 9 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Not addressed as such. The closest claim: "Forcing software to use software-managed coherence or explicit message passing does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". Message send as the hardware primitive: argued against for mainstream chips. | p. 9 |
| Model equivalence | Messages on shared memory: "any program that works for scratchpad systems (e.g., Cell processor) or message passing systems (e.g., MPI cluster) can easily map to a shared memory system with caches". This is asserted, with no performance or property analysis. The reverse also appears inside the design: the shared-memory abstraction is implemented by point-to-point coherence messages in hardware. Encapsulation and data-race freedom: not discussed. | p. 2, p. 3, p. 8 |
| Model mixing | At the system level, not the program level. Message passing (for "scale out high performance computing") and incoherent scratchpads (for "real-time systems") "will persist" and "coexist with on-chip cache-coherent shared memory". No frequency data or developer reasons. | p. 1, p. 8 |
| Runtime limits | Not addressed: no actor or message runtime is discussed. | none |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts: 1–4096, modelled. Shared memory and coherence: yes, hardware coherence. Inter-core communication: loads and stores, carried by point-to-point coherence messages over an on-chip interconnect, with a hierarchy of cluster caches (p. 2, pp. 5–6). Result: traffic per miss is constant, storage grows as √C or ∛C, the latency ratio is constant, and energy overhead is argued not to grow (pp. 3–8). Limits named but not addressed: interconnect scalability, "the critical problem of software non-scalability", queuing and contention, multi-socket coherence, and verification effort (p. 8–9). Prior claims of a coherence limit come from [5, 10, 13] (p. 1, p. 3). | pp. 1–9 |
| Adoption factors | For alternatives to coherent shared memory (no caches, or no shared address space; scratchpads; message passing): "successful in high-performance computing … they have not been common in mainstream multicore systems". Factors given: software compatibility ("Computer systems tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs", p. 1); existing scalable operating systems on coherence (p. 1, p. 8); programmability (p. 9); kind of workload (HPC, real-time) (p. 1). Economics: not stated. | p. 1, p. 8, p. 9 |
| Quality | See the Quality table: Q1 yes, Q2 partly, Q3 partly, Q4 partly, Q5 partly, Q6 yes, Q7 partly, Q8 yes, Q9 no. | p. 1–9 |
| Notes | Complexity: the authors say coherence protocol complexity "does not necessarily scale up with increasing numbers of cores". Hierarchical protocols can be "formally verified with an amount of effort that is independent of the number of cores [19]" (p. 9). This bears on SQ14 and on any cost argument against hardware coherence. | p. 9 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant | All coherence protocols ensure that, per block, there is either one core with write permission or any number with read permission. | p. 2 |
| new: scalable coherence | Coherence is "scalable" when its cost "grows (at most) slowly as core count increases". Five costs are examined: traffic, storage, inclusion, latency, energy. | p. 3 |
| new: amortized coherence traffic | A write that invalidates N sharers must follow N read misses, so average traffic per miss is constant in core count. | p. 3 |
| new: exact vs inexact encoding of sharers | Exact encoding uses one bit per core and gives constant traffic. Inexact (coarse-vector, limited-pointer) encoding bounds storage but causes "unnecessary invalidations", up to ~6× traffic at 1024 cores. | pp. 4–5 |
| new: hierarchical inclusive coherence | Cluster caches track their cores and the last-level cache tracks clusters. This gives fan-out invalidation, acknowledgment combining, and storage proportional to √C or ∛C. | pp. 5–6 |
| new: explicit eviction notifications | Private caches notify the shared cache on every eviction, including clean ones, so tracking is exact and recalls become rare. The cost is extra small messages. | p. 3, p. 6 |
| new: recall (back-invalidation) | When an inclusive shared cache evicts a block with sharers, it forces their eviction. This is rare (<0.1%) at a 4× capacity ratio. | p. 3, pp. 6–7 |
| new: direct vs indirect miss | Coherence adds latency only to indirect misses (blocks cached elsewhere), 1.5–2× a non-coherent miss, and the ratio does not depend on core count. | p. 7 |
| new: coherence messages implement shared memory | The coherent shared-memory abstraction is carried by point-to-point request, forward, invalidation, recall and ack messages between cache controllers. | pp. 2–3 |
| new: complexity shifting | Removing hardware coherence "does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". | p. 9 |
| new: compatibility as reason for coherence | Coherence dominates for "technical and legacy reasons", and systems "tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs". | p. 1 |
| new: coexistence of communication paradigms | Message passing and scratchpads persist in HPC and real-time niches but "coexist with" coherent shared memory, which dominates mainstream chips. | p. 1, p. 8 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** the authors' near-final manuscript, 9 pages, pdfTeX, dated 5 Dec 2011, headed "A final revision of this manuscript will appear in Communications of the ACM, TBD 2012". I downloaded it from https://research.cs.wisc.edu/multifacet/papers/cacm2012_coherence_nearfinal.pdf and saved it as `papers/P22.pdf` (sha256 b0a1e474…6df).
- **Why not the published version:** the ACM Digital Library PDF (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/2209249.2209269) returned HTTP 403. A Penn URL tried returned 404 or HTML. Crossref gives the published version as CACM 55(7):78–89, July 2012.
- **What this means for pages:** every page in this record is the manuscript's page (1–9), not the CACM page. The final CACM text may differ in wording or numbers from this manuscript.
- **No C IDs reused:** no concept files were among my inputs, so every concept is marked new.
- **Selection checks:** X5 is satisfied (ACM magazine article). X9 does not apply: the paper is not a survey, and it reports its own analysis and one simulation.

(4) With explicit eviction notifications, recalls are rare: below 0.1% at a 4× capacity ratio with 8 ways (p. 7, Fig. 5). (5) Latency and energy arguments (pp. 7–8). ## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant | All coherence protocols ensure that, per block, there is either one core with write permission or any number with read permission. | p. 2 |
| new: scalable coherence | Coherence is "scalable" when its cost "grows (at most) slowly as core count increases". Five costs are examined: traffic, storage, inclusion, latency, energy. | p. 3 |
| new: amortized coherence traffic | A write that invalidates N sharers must follow N read misses, so average traffic per miss is constant in core count. | p. 3 |
| new: exact vs inexact encoding of sharers | Exact encoding uses one bit per core and gives constant traffic. Inexact (coarse-vector, limited-pointer) encoding bounds storage but causes "unnecessary invalidations", up to ~6× traffic at 1024 cores. | pp. 4–5 |
| new: hierarchical inclusive coherence | Cluster caches track their cores and the last-level cache tracks clusters. This gives fan-out invalidation, acknowledgment combining, and storage proportional to √C or ∛C. | pp. 5–6 |
| new: explicit eviction notifications | Private caches notify the shared cache on every eviction, including clean ones, so tracking is exact and recalls become rare. The cost is extra small messages. | p. 3, p. 6 |
| new: recall (back-invalidation) | When an inclusive shared cache evicts a block with sharers, it forces their eviction. This is rare (<0.1%) at a 4× capacity ratio. | p. 3, pp. 6–7 |
| new: direct vs indirect miss | Coherence adds latency only to indirect misses (blocks cached elsewhere), 1.5–2× a non-coherent miss, and the ratio does not depend on core count. | p. 7 |
| new: coherence messages implement shared memory | The coherent shared-memory abstraction is carried by point-to-point request, forward, invalidation, recall and ack messages between cache controllers. | pp. 2–3 |
| new: complexity shifting | Removing hardware coherence "does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". | p. 9 |
| new: compatibility as reason for coherence | Coherence dominates for "technical and legacy reasons", and systems "tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs". | p. 1 |
| new: coexistence of communication paradigms | Message passing and scratchpads persist in HPC and real-time niches but "coexist with" coherent shared memory, which dominates mainstream chips. | p. 1, p. 8 |

5.2

Fixes of Blocking Bugs

After understanding the causes of blocking bugs in Go, we
now analyze how Go programmers fixed these bugs in the
real world.
Eliminating the blocking cause of a hanging goroutine
will unblock it and this is the general approach to fix blocking bugs. To achieve this goal, Go developers often adjust
synchronization operations, including adding missing ones,
moving or changing misplaced/misused ones, and removing
extra ones. Table 7 summarizes these fixes.
Most blocking bugs caused by mistakenly protecting
shared memory accesses were fixed by methods similar to
traditional deadlock fixes. For example, among the 33 Mutexor RWMutex-related bugs, 8 were fixed by adding a missing
unlock; 9 were fixed by moving lock or unlock operations
to proper locations; and 11 were fixed by removing an extra
lock operation.
11 blocking bugs caused by wrong message passing were
fixed by adding a missing message or closing operation to
a channel (and on two occasions, to a pipe) on a goroutine
different from the blocking one. 8 blocking bugs were fixed
by adding a select with a default option (e.g., Figure 7)
or a case with operation on a different channel. Another
common fix of channel-related blocking bugs is to replace an
unbuffered channel with a buffered channel (e.g., Figure 1).
Other channel-related blocking bugs can be fixed by strategies such as moving a channel operation out of a critical
section and replacing channel with shared variables.
To understand the relationship between the cause of
a blocking bug and its fix, we apply a statistical metric
called lift, following previous empirical studies on real-world
(AB)
bugs [29, 41]. lift is calculated as lift(A, B) = P P(A)P
(B) , where
A denotes a root cause category, B denotes a fix strategy category, P (AB) denotes the probability that a blocking is caused

cause is independent with B fix strategy. When lift value is

5.3

Detection of Blocking Bugs

Go provides a built-in deadlock detector that is implemented
in the goroutine scheduler. The detector is always enabled
during Go runtime and it reports deadlock when no goroutines in a running process can make progress. We tested all
our reproduced blocking bugs with Go’s built-in deadlock
detector to evaluate what bugs it can find. For every tested
bug, the blocking can be triggered deterministically in every run. Therefore, for each bug, we only ran it once in this
experiment. Table 8 summarizes our test results.
The built-in deadlock detector can only detect two blocking bugs, BoltDB#392 and BoltDB#240, and fail in all other
cases (although the detector does not report any false positives [38, 39]). There are two reasons why the built-in detector failed to detect other blocking bugs. First, it does not consider the monitored system as blocking when there are still
some running goroutines. Second, it only examines whether
or not goroutines are blocked at Go concurrency primitives
but does not consider goroutines that wait for other systems

+## First pass: the five Cs

+- **Category:** A position paper backed by analysis. It presents a proof-of-concept coherence design built from known techniques, then analyses it with analytical models and one small simulation. It reports no silicon or benchmark measurements (p. 1, p. 8).

+- **Context:** It answers predictions that on-chip coherence will not scale and will give way to software-managed coherence, scratchpads or message passing without shared memory. It cites DeNovo [5], Intel's 48-core message-passing processor [10] and Cohesion [13] (p. 1, p. 3). It builds on directory protocols [1, 8], the SGI Origin 2000 [14], Intel Core i7 [17], AMD HT-Assist [6] and Linux scalability studies [2, 3] (p. 1, pp. 4–6).

+- **Correctness:** Some assumptions are stated: coherence does not change the number of misses, though false sharing and poor synchronization may change it (p. 4). Others are stated too: an inclusive shared cache (p. 2), a single chip (p. 9), and no queuing or contention modelled (p. 8). Some are left implicit: the cost model counts bytes per miss and ignores how invalidation bursts are spread over time, and the energy analysis is inferred from the traffic and storage results, not modelled (pp. 7–8).

+- **Contributions:** (1) An amortized argument that traffic per miss does not depend on core count when sharers are tracked exactly (p. 3, Fig. 2b p. 4). (2) Coherence traffic is at most 20% above a cache system without coherence (Table 1, p. 4). (3) With a hierarchy of inclusive caches, storage grows as √C (two levels) or ∛C (three levels) (p. 6, Fig. 4). (4) With explicit eviction notifications, recalls are rare: below 0.1% at a 4× capacity ratio with 8 ways (p. 7, Fig. 5). (5) Latency and energy arguments (pp. 7–8). (6) An extension to non-inclusive caches (p. 8).

+- **Clarity:** Clear. There is one "Concern" section per scalability worry, and each ends with a boxed conclusion (pp. 3–8). There is a dedicated caveats section (pp. 8–9). One numeric inconsistency: the abstract says storage is "2% of total cache size for even 512 cores" (p. 1). The summary says 5% with two cache levels or 2% with three (p. 8).
