+| Receiving unit and state ownership | Receivers are cache controllers: shared-cache banks, cluster caches and private caches. A private cache's block state can be changed from outside: on a recall message "the private cache is forced to evict the block"; on a write miss the shared cache's forwarded request makes private caches "invalidate their copies". Each core's private cache is also read and written by its own core's loads and stores. | p. 2, p. 3 |

+| Message mechanism | Coherence messages between caches. Sync/async: not stated, but requests are forwarded and "responses are typically sent directly to the original requester (… three-hop protocol)" (p. 7). Naming: by block address to an address-interleaved shared-cache bank; the bank names sharers by per-core tracking bits (p. 2). Ordering and delivery guarantees: not stated. Buffering: not stated. Busy receiver: not stated. Dispatch: by the block's coherence state (M/S/I) and tracking bits (p. 2, sidebar). | p. 2, p. 7 |

+| Non-message primitives | At the instruction-set level: loads and stores to shared memory are the communication primitive. Reason: coherence makes caches "functionally invisible to software" and keeps backward compatibility for software "written for cache-coherent shared memory systems" (p. 1). Cache hits: served locally with no message (p. 7). Interrupts, traps, DMA, I/O: not stated. | p. 1, p. 7 |
+| Self-definition | Not applicable: the paper describes hardware coherence, not a system written in its own objects and messages. | p. 1 |
+| Interposition | not stated. The paper does not discuss placing a component between sender and receiver. | none |

+| Operating system functions | Not addressed for the paper's own design. The paper claims conventional operating systems "have been shown to scale using cache coherence [2, 3]". It quotes Boyd-Wickizer et al.: "there is no scalability reason to give up on traditional operating system organizations just yet". On centralization: a single shared last-level cache tracks sharers per block (one directory entry per block, distributed across banks). Protection, scheduling, naming and failure handling are not stated. | p. 1, p. 2, p. 8 |

+| Cost of message primitives | No measured latency or cycles. Analytical sizes: request and ack messages 8 B, data message 72 B (64 B block + 8 B address). Latency formulas: t_direct = t_noncoherent = 2·t_interconnect + t_cache; t_indirect = 3·t_interconnect + 2·t_cache. | p. 4 (Table 1), p. 7 |

+| Performance results | (1) Traffic, bytes/miss, analytical model, coherent vs "without coherence" (64-bit address, 64-byte block): clean 96 vs 80 B/miss (+20%); dirty 160 vs 152 B/miss (+5%) (Table 1, p. 4). (2) Traffic with Origin-style inexact encoding (32 bits/block) vs exact: spike of "almost 6x" at 1024 cores (Fig. 2a, p. 4; text p. 5). (3) Storage overhead, % of cache storage, exact tracking: 16 cores ~3% (p. 3). 1024-core two-level: 6%. 4096-core three-level: 3% (p. 6). 512 cores: 5% two-level, 2% three-level (p. 8). (4) Recall rate, % of misses, synthetic random miss stream: below 0.1% for an 8-way shared cache at 4× capacity ratio; Core i7 is 16-way at 8× (Fig. 5, p. 7). (5) Indirect-miss latency vs non-coherent miss: 1.5× to 2× (p. 7). (6) Non-inclusive directory storage overhead, 16 cores: 2% at S2/S1=8; 4%, 6%, 9% at 4, 2, 1. Hierarchical, 256 cores: 2% at Z=8; 5%, 10%, 18% at Z=4, 2, 1 (p. 8). | p. 3, p. 4, p. 5, p. 6, p. 7, p. 8 |

+| Scaling | Analytical, not measured. Core counts modelled: 1–1024 for traffic (Fig. 2, p. 4); 1–4096 for storage (Fig. 4, p. 6); 256 for non-inclusive storage (p. 8). Results: traffic per miss with exact tracking is independent of core count (p. 3–4). Flat storage overhead grows linearly with C (reaches the 20% top of the Fig. 4 axis at about 128 cores). Two-level storage grows as √C; three-level as ∛C (p. 6). The latency ratio is independent of core count (p. 7). Baseline: a system with caches and no coherence (p. 4), and flat vs hierarchical designs (p. 6). | p. 3, p. 4, p. 6, p. 7, p. 8 |

+| Attributed causes | (a) "Coherence's alleged lack of scalability is believed to be due to the poor scaling of the storage and traffic … as well as concerns about latency and energy". Stated by the authors (third party to the predictions) as others' belief, which the paper disputes (p. 1). (b) Traffic does not grow because "for every write that invalidates N caches, it must have been preceded by N read misses". Designers; inherent to exact tracking; argued by amortization and shown in Fig. 2b (p. 3–4). (c) The traffic spike in inexact encoding comes from "unnecessary invalidations". Designers; inherent to the encoding; isolated by Fig. 2a vs 2b (p. 5). (d) Recalls come from shared-cache capacity and associativity, and from silent clean evictions that leave the shared cache "ambiguous". Designers; due to implementation; isolated by Fig. 5 (pp. 6–7). (e) Many applications do not scale, but the root cause may be "the algorithm, program implementation, or coherence"; this is asserted with no measurement (p. 1). | p. 1, pp. 3–7 |

+| Fate and reasons | Cache coherence is commercial and dominant: "provided by mainstream servers, desktops, laptops, and even mobile devices … Intel, AMD, ARM, IBM, and Oracle (Sun)". It "has come to dominate the market for both technical and legacy reasons": better performance than software coherence, and backward compatibility. Stated by the authors (third party to the vendors). The paper's own protocol: research only (existence proof). | p. 1, p. 8 |

+| Concurrency defects | Not applicable: no defect study. The sidebar gives one constructed example: without coherence, a lock variable could let "multiple cores into a critical section or prevent cores waiting … from making forward progress". | p. 2 |

+| What shapes programs | The hardware model, by argument only. "At least with hardware coherence, programmers can concentrate on choreographing independent work rather than handling low-level mechanics" (p. 1). Coherence frees developers "from re-implementing coherence … or orchestrating explicit communication via message passing" (p. 9). Evidence kind: argument, no study of programs or programmers. | p. 1, p. 9 |

+| Hardware–language trade-off | Not addressed as such. The closest claim: "Forcing software to use software-managed coherence or explicit message passing does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". Message send as the hardware primitive: argued against for mainstream chips. | p. 9 |

+| Model equivalence | Messages on shared memory: "any program that works for scratchpad systems (e.g., Cell processor) or message passing systems (e.g., MPI cluster) can easily map to a shared memory system with caches". This is asserted, with no performance or property analysis. The reverse also appears inside the design: the shared-memory abstraction is implemented by point-to-point coherence messages in hardware. Encapsulation and data-race freedom: not discussed. | p. 2, p. 3, p. 8 |

+| Model mixing | At the system level, not the program level. Message passing (for "scale out high performance computing") and incoherent scratchpads (for "real-time systems") "will persist" and "coexist with on-chip cache-coherent shared memory". No frequency data or developer reasons. | p. 1, p. 8 |
+| Runtime limits | Not addressed: no actor or message runtime is discussed. | none |

+| Many-core scaling | Core counts: 1–4096, modelled. Shared memory and coherence: yes, hardware coherence. Inter-core communication: loads and stores, carried by point-to-point coherence messages over an on-chip interconnect, with a hierarchy of cluster caches (p. 2, pp. 5–6). Result: traffic per miss is constant, storage grows as √C or ∛C, the latency ratio is constant, and energy overhead is argued not to grow (pp. 3–8). Limits named but not addressed: interconnect scalability, "the critical problem of software non-scalability", queuing and contention, multi-socket coherence, and verification effort (p. 8–9). Prior claims of a coherence limit come from [5, 10, 13] (p. 1, p. 3). | pp. 1–9 |

+| Adoption factors | For alternatives to coherent shared memory (no caches, or no shared address space; scratchpads; message passing): "successful in high-performance computing … they have not been common in mainstream multicore systems". Factors given: software compatibility ("Computer systems tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs", p. 1); existing scalable operating systems on coherence (p. 1, p. 8); programmability (p. 9); kind of workload (HPC, real-time) (p. 1). Economics: not stated. | p. 1, p. 8, p. 9 |
+| Quality | See the Quality table: Q1 yes, Q2 partly, Q3 partly, Q4 partly, Q5 partly, Q6 yes, Q7 partly, Q8 yes, Q9 no. | p. 1–9 |

+| Notes | Complexity: the authors say coherence protocol complexity "does not necessarily scale up with increasing numbers of cores". Hierarchical protocols can be "formally verified with an amount of effort that is independent of the number of cores [19]" (p. 9). This bears on SQ14 and on any cost argument against hardware coherence. | p. 9 |
+## Concepts
+| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
+| new: single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant | All coherence protocols ensure that, per block, there is either one core with write permission or any number with read permission. | p. 2 |
+| new: scalable coherence | Coherence is "scalable" when its cost "grows (at most) slowly as core count increases". Five costs are examined: traffic, storage, inclusion, latency, energy. | p. 3 |
+| new: amortized coherence traffic | A write that invalidates N sharers must follow N read misses, so average traffic per miss is constant in core count. | p. 3 |

+| new: exact vs inexact encoding of sharers | Exact encoding uses one bit per core and gives constant traffic. Inexact (coarse-vector, limited-pointer) encoding bounds storage but causes "unnecessary invalidations", up to ~6× traffic at 1024 cores. | pp. 4–5 |

+| new: hierarchical inclusive coherence | Cluster caches track their cores and the last-level cache tracks clusters. This gives fan-out invalidation, acknowledgment combining, and storage proportional to √C or ∛C. | pp. 5–6 |

+| new: explicit eviction notifications | Private caches notify the shared cache on every eviction, including clean ones, so tracking is exact and recalls become rare. The cost is extra small messages. | p. 3, p. 6 |
+| new: recall (back-invalidation) | When an inclusive shared cache evicts a block with sharers, it forces their eviction. This is rare (<0.1%) at a 4× capacity ratio. | p. 3, pp. 6–7 |
+| new: direct vs indirect miss | Coherence adds latency only to indirect misses (blocks cached elsewhere), 1.5–2× a non-coherent miss, and the ratio does not depend on core count. | p. 7 |

+| new: coherence messages implement shared memory | The coherent shared-memory abstraction is carried by point-to-point request, forward, invalidation, recall and ack messages between cache controllers. | pp. 2–3 |
+| new: complexity shifting | Removing hardware coherence "does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". | p. 9 |
+| new: compatibility as reason for coherence | Coherence dominates for "technical and legacy reasons", and systems "tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs". | p. 1 |

+| new: coexistence of communication paradigms | Message passing and scratchpads persist in HPC and real-time niches but "coexist with" coherent shared memory, which dominates mainstream chips. | p. 1, p. 8 |
+## Notes

+- **Source read:** the authors' near-final manuscript, 9 pages, pdfTeX, dated 5 Dec 2011, headed "A final revision of this manuscript will appear in Communications of the ACM, TBD 2012". I downloaded it from https://research.cs.wisc.edu/multifacet/papers/cacm2012_coherence_nearfinal.pdf and saved it as `papers/P22.pdf` (sha256 b0a1e474…6df).

+- **Why not the published version:** the ACM Digital Library PDF (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/2209249.2209269) returned HTTP 403. A Penn URL tried returned 404 or HTML. Crossref gives the published version as CACM 55(7):78–89, July 2012.
+- **What this means for pages:** every page in this record is the manuscript's page (1–9), not the CACM page. The final CACM text may differ in wording or numbers from this manuscript.
+- **No C IDs reused:** no concept files were among my inputs, so every concept is marked new.
+- **Selection checks:** X5 is satisfied (ACM magazine article). X9 does not apply: the paper is not a survey, and it reports its own analysis and one simulation.

# P8

## Reference
Andrew Baumann, Paul Barham, Pierre-Evariste Dagand, Tim Harris, Rebecca Isaacs, Simon Peter, Timothy Roscoe, Adrian Schüpbach, Akhilesh Singhania (2009). *The Multikernel: A New OS Architecture for Scalable Multicore Systems*. Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 22nd Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '09), pp. 29–44 (Crossref). https://doi.org/10.1145/1629575.1629579. P8, from row R0-008. Included under I1(c): a kernel in which "all inter-core communication is performed using explicit messages" (p. 5).

Page numbers below are the PDF pages of the 20-page copy on sigops.org. Each page also carries that number at the foot. They are not the ACM proceedings pages 29–44.

## Deepest pass
3

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A new OS architecture (the multikernel), a prototype that implements it (Barrelfish), and a measured evaluation on x86-64 multiprocessors (pp. 1–2).
- **Context:** Distributed systems applied to OS structure. The paper builds on Lauer and Needham's duality of message and shared-memory OSes (p. 3), URPC/LRPC (pp. 3, 8–9), exokernel (p. 8), seL4 capabilities (p. 10), Tornado/K42 clustered objects and Corey (p. 17), microkernels (L4) and Disco (p. 17), and fos (p. 17).
- **Correctness:** Its assumptions are that hardware is becoming a network (pp. 3, 5), that cores are becoming diverse (p. 3), that cache coherence will grow costly or disappear (pp. 4–5) and that messages cost less than shared memory as more cache lines are touched (pp. 3–4). The first three are argued from trends and citations. Only the last is measured (Fig. 3, on 16 cores of one machine).
- **Contributions:** (1) the multikernel model and its three principles: explicit communication, hardware-neutral structure and replicated state; (2) Barrelfish, a concrete multikernel; (3) measurements showing scalability, adaptability to hardware and competitive performance (p. 2).
- **Clarity:** Well written and clearly structured. Design choices that follow from the model are kept apart from engineering choices (pp. 7, 11). Some figure values can only be read off plots.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The contributions are stated as a three-item list in the introduction (p. 2), and the goals as a five-item list (p. 7). |
| Q2 | partly | Addressing is described: a name service, channel setup by monitors, and point-to-point dispatcher channels (pp. 9–10). Busy-receiver handling is described: poll, then block and ask the monitor for notification (p. 9). The message format is described only as cache-line sized with stub-compiled marshalling (pp. 9–10). Ordering and delivery are mentioned only in passing ("reliable in-order message delivery", p. 17), and full-queue behaviour is not stated. |
| Q3 | yes | Barrelfish runs real programs (OpenMP, SPLASH-2, a web server, SQLite) on four real x86-64 machines (pp. 8, 15–16). |
| Q4 | partly | Most claims name a versioned baseline: Linux 2.6.26, Windows Server 2008 R2 Beta, L4Ka::Pistachio 2009-02-25 and lighttpd 1.4.23 (pp. 10, 13, 16). The IP-loopback and OpenMP comparisons say only "Linux", without a version or configuration in their sections (pp. 14–15). |
| Q5 | partly | Workloads and why they were chosen are reported (pp. 12, 14–15), and so is the hardware (p. 8). The number of runs is stated only for Fig. 9 (five runs, p. 15). Other experiments give σ or error bars without a run count, or nothing (Table 4, web server). |
| Q6 | yes | The abstract and conclusions make only qualitative claims ("comparable", "scale better", "competitive"; pp. 1, 18). Each is backed by Figs. 7–9 and Tables 1–4 (pp. 9–16). |
| Q7 | partly | Table 4's cache-miss and HyperTransport counters support the loopback cause (p. 14). Other causes are only asserted: the dispatch loop as the cause of unmap overhead (p. 13), the threads library for the Fig. 9 differences (p. 15), kernel crossings for the web server (p. 16), and "likely" the stride prefetcher (p. 13). |
| Q8 | yes | The Summary has a dedicated paragraph on what the evaluation does not show (p. 16). Further limits are stated on pp. 11–12 and 17. |
| Q9 | no | All nine authors are Barrelfish's designers and builders ("We have implemented a multikernel OS", p. 1; "our implementation", p. 7). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See *Reference* above. P8; I1(c). | p. 1, p. 5 |
| Paper type | Design (a new OS model), with implementation (Barrelfish) and evaluation in the same paper. | pp. 2, 5, 7, 12 |
| System | Barrelfish, a multikernel OS, built in 2009 by ETH Zurich Systems Group and Microsoft Research Cambridge (the author affiliations). Status: running kernel on x86-64 multiprocessors, with an ARM port in progress. Source released at barrelfish.org. | pp. 1, 8, 18 |
| Levels with message semantics | Hardware: no. On the test machines "the only inter-core communication mechanism available … is cache-coherent memory" (p. 9), although the interconnect itself "resembles a message-passing network" (p. 3). Microcode: not stated. Instruction set: no; x86-64, with messages built from stores and polling (p. 9). Kernel: inter-core, yes: "all inter-core communication is performed using explicit messages … no memory is shared … except for that used for messaging channels" (p. 5). Kernel as a whole, no under the form's definition: the per-core CPU driver handles traps, interrupts and system calls (p. 8), and capability changes are made by system calls (p. 10). Runtime: no; user threads share an address space (p. 11). Language: not stated; the CPU driver is C and assembly (p. 8). Later non-message paths: the model allows a replica to be shared under spinlocks as an optimisation (p. 7), and the authors call this "a next step" (p. 18). Neither is implemented in this paper. | pp. 3, 5, 7–11, 18 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | The receiver is a dispatcher. A process is a set of dispatcher objects, one per core, and "communication … is not actually between processes but between dispatchers (and hence cores)" (p. 9). Monitors, one per core, receive inter-core coordination messages (p. 9). The CPU driver "shares no state with other cores" (p. 8). The OS keeps global state as replicas kept consistent by agreement between monitors (pp. 7, 9). Others can still reach the state: the channel memory is shared memory (p. 9), and applications may share memory and even a hardware page table across cores (pp. 5, 11). | pp. 5, 7–9, 11 |
| Message mechanism | Inter-core transport: URPC, a shared-memory region used as a point-to-point channel for cache-line-sized messages between one writer and one reader. The receiver polls the last word of the line (p. 9). Prefetching for pipelined throughput can be chosen at channel setup (p. 9). The model is asynchronous and split-phase (pp. 6–7). Same-core IPC is an asynchronous, fixed-size message from the CPU driver, with an optional synchronous LRPC/L4-like call (p. 8). Naming: a name service maps service names to a service reference, used to set up a channel through the monitors (p. 10). All transports sit behind a common interface, with marshalling generated by a stub compiler (p. 10). Ordering and delivery: "a multikernel may exploit reliable in-order message delivery" (p. 17); no further guarantee is stated. Buffering: the throughput test uses a queue of 16 messages (p. 10); full-queue behaviour is not stated. Busy or absent receiver: the dispatcher polls for a fixed time, then blocks and asks its monitor for notification, and an IPI wakes it (pp. 9, 14). Remote monitors handle messages when "convenient" (p. 12). Dispatch: user-level message dispatching and event demultiplexing code in the threads package (pp. 9, 13). | pp. 6–10, 12–14, 17 |
| Non-message primitives | (1) Cache-coherent shared memory as the hardware carrier of every inter-core message. Reason: it is the only mechanism on current hardware (p. 9). (2) Shared memory for the message channels themselves (p. 5). Same-core, "more complex communication channels are built over this using shared memory" (p. 8). (3) Application shared memory and shared address spaces across cores, optionally one shared hardware page table. Reason: most current programs need it, and the shared table is "typically more efficient" (pp. 5, 11). (4) Traps and system calls into the privileged CPU driver; capability operations are system calls (pp. 8, 10). (5) Device interrupts are routed in hardware, then demultiplexed by the CPU driver and turned into messages (p. 8). (6) IPIs and MONITOR/MWAIT to wake or idle a core, used instead of spinning forever (pp. 9, 14). (7) Cache prefetch instructions in URPC (p. 9). (8) DMA by the NIC (p. 15). (9) Future work: a replica shared by closely coupled cores under spinlocks, to use shared caches (pp. 7, 18). | pp. 5, 7–11, 14–15, 18 |
| Self-definition | Not object-based. The OS is split into a privileged CPU driver, written in C and assembly and specialised for x86-64 (7135 + 337 lines), and user-level monitors and services that talk by messages (p. 8). The CPU driver lies outside the message model and is the base: it serially processes traps and interrupts (p. 8). Whether a running program can inspect or change these levels: not stated. The closest mechanism is the system knowledge base, which holds hardware facts in first-order logic for queries such as transport selection (p. 11). Cost of the split: OS invocations become local RPCs with two context switches, "several thousand cycles" (pp. 11–12). | pp. 8, 11–12 |
| Interposition | Not stated as interposition. Related mechanisms: all transports sit behind a common interface (p. 10), the protocol and transport are late-bound (p. 6), and the name service maps a name to a service reference (p. 10). These suggest a transport or service could be swapped without changing the sender or receiver, but the paper neither claims nor measures this. | pp. 6, 10 |
| Operating system functions | *Protection*: each core's CPU driver enforces protection and authorisation (p. 8), and capabilities are modelled on seL4 (p. 10). Coordination is involved: yes, because all cores must keep their capability lists consistent (p. 10). *Scheduling*: the CPU driver time-slices locally and runs dispatchers by upcalls, with user-level thread schedulers (pp. 8–9). Cross-core threads are handled by messages, and CPU drivers can be coordinated for gang scheduling (p. 11). Central component: not stated. *Memory*: virtual memory is managed at user level through capabilities (p. 10). Unmap uses a one-phase commit and retype a two-phase commit between all monitors (p. 11). That is coordination: yes. *Devices*: drivers are user-level processes (p. 8), placed on cores by the system knowledge base (p. 11). Whether the SKB is one instance: not stated. *Naming*: a name service (p. 10); centralisation not stated. *Failure*: none; "the complete system is a failure unit" (p. 17). *Costs of decentralising*: the capability scheme "was a mistake … unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient than scalable per-processor memory managers" (p. 10). Replica consistency adds latency and developer burden (p. 7). Two-phase commit "serializes more messages" than shootdown (p. 14). | pp. 7–11, 14, 17 |
| Cost of message primitives | Same-core LRPC, one way (Table 1): 845 cycles on 2×4 Intel, 757 on 2×2 AMD, 1463 on 4×4 AMD, 1549 on 8×4 AMD (p. 9). L4 raw IPC is about 420 cycles on 2×2 AMD (p. 8). Inter-core URPC latency (Table 2): 180 cycles (shared cache) to 618 cycles (two hops, 8×4 AMD) (p. 10). URPC against L4 IPC on 2×2 AMD (Table 3): 450 vs 424 cycles; 3.42 vs 2.36 messages per kcycle; 9 vs 25 I-cache lines; 8 vs 13 D-cache lines (p. 10). IPI wake cost C ≈ 6000 cycles (p. 14). A trap costs ≈ 800 cycles (p. 12). | pp. 8–10, 12, 14 |
| Performance results | (a) Update shared state, 4×4 AMD: SHM costs ~12,000 extra cycles per update at 16 cores, against under 30 on one core. MSG beats SHM for 4 or more cache lines (Fig. 3, pp. 3–4). (b) URPC pipelined throughput: 2.75–11.97 messages per kcycle (Table 2, p. 10). (c) Unmap latency, 8×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux 2.6.26 mprotect vs Windows Server 2008 R2 Beta VirtualProtect: at 32 cores, about 18k vs 29k vs 45k cycles, read off Fig. 7. Barrelfish is slower at 2 cores (≈10k vs ≈5–6k) (p. 13). (d) Two-phase commit, 8×4 AMD: ≈14k to ≈28k cycles single-operation and ≈8k to ≈19k pipelined, 2 to 32 cores, read off Fig. 8 (p. 14). (e) IP loopback, 2×2 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux (version not stated): 2154 vs 1823 Mbit/s; 21 vs 77 D-cache misses per packet; HyperTransport link utilisation 8%/3% vs 11%/9% (Table 4, p. 14). (f) OpenMP (CG, FT, IS) and SPLASH-2 (Barnes-Hut, radiosity), 4×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux with GCC 4.3.3 and GOMP: similar on FT, Barnes-Hut and radiosity. Barrelfish is better on CG at 12–16 cores and worse on IS (Fig. 9, p. 15). (g) UDP echo, 2×4 Intel, e1000: 951.7 vs 951 Mbit/s for Linux 2.6.26 (p. 16). (h) Static web page, 2×2 AMD: 18697 req/s (640 Mbit/s) vs 8924 req/s (316 Mbit/s) for lighttpd 1.4.23 on Linux 2.6.26 (tuned). Web-plus-SQLite: 3417 req/s, with no baseline (p. 16). | pp. 3–4, 10, 13–16 |
| Scaling | Fig. 3: 2–16 cores, against shared-memory updates (p. 3). Figs. 6–8: 2–32 cores on 8×4 AMD. NUMA-aware multicast is near flat at ≈3k cycles; broadcast and unicast grow linearly to ≈13–14k (Fig. 6, read off the plot). For unmap and two-phase commit see *Performance results* (pp. 13–14). Fig. 9: 1–16 cores against Linux (p. 15). The authors: "It would be wrong to draw any quantitative conclusions from our large-scale benchmarks" (p. 16). | pp. 3, 13–16 |
| Attributed causes | All are stated by the designers. (1) SHM cost: "All of these extra cycles are spent with the core stalled on cache misses". Inherent to coherent shared memory; not isolated beyond the SHM/MSG contrast (p. 3). (2) Broadcast shootdown is slow "due to the cache-coherence protocol used by AMD64": the line crosses the interconnect N times. Hardware cause; explained, not separately measured (p. 12). (3) The flat unicast curve below 8 cores is "likely" the stride prefetcher. Speculation (p. 13). (4) Multicast wins because the shared L3 removes interconnect traffic and eight processors send in parallel. Design; shown by the protocol comparison in Fig. 6 (p. 13). (5) Unmap overhead above the base protocol is "largely due to inefficiencies in the message dispatch loop of the user-level threads package". Implementation; not isolated (p. 13). (6) Linux and Windows unmap scale worse because of "serially sending IPIs" (p. 13). Not isolated. (7) Loopback gain: URPC avoids shared memory except the channel and payload, while "Linux causes more cache-coherence traffic"; also kernel crossings. Design; partly isolated by the miss and HyperTransport counters (p. 14). (8) Fig. 9 differences come from "our user-space threads library vs. the Linux in-kernel implementation". Implementation; not isolated (p. 15). (9) Web server gain is "mainly due to avoiding kernel-user crossings". Design; not isolated (p. 16). (10) The CPU-driver/monitor split costs several thousand cycles per OS call. Implementation choice; not measured in a figure (p. 12). | pp. 3, 12–16 |
| Fate and reasons | The paper reports a research prototype, "not by any means yet a mature system" (p. 17). Its source is released (p. 18), and an ARM port to programmable NICs is in progress (p. 17). It states no later fate. | pp. 17–18 |
| Concurrency defects | Not applicable; not a defect study. Related qualitative remarks only: shared data has "correctness and performance pitfalls" (p. 4), and retyping one capability differently on two cores "leads to an inconsistent system", which the two-phase commit prevents (p. 11). | pp. 4, 11 |
| What shapes programs | Argument with examples, not a study. The knowledge for efficient sharing "is encoded implicitly in its implementation", so a shared-memory OS is tied to one hardware design (pp. 2, 4). Examples: the Windows 7 dispatcher-lock removal touched 6000 lines in 58 files; Linux RCU needed many iterations (p. 2). Programmers must reason about "messages sent by the cache-coherence protocol" (p. 4). Page numbers below are the PDF pages of the 20-page copy on sigops.org. Each page also carries that number at the foot. They are not the ACM proceedings pages 29–44.

## Deepest pass
3

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A new OS architecture (the multikernel), a prototype that implements it (Barrelfish), and a measured evaluation on x86-64 multiprocessors (pp. 1–2).
- **Context:** Distributed systems applied to OS structure. The paper builds on Lauer and Needham's duality of message and shared-memory OSes (p. 3), URPC/LRPC (pp. 3, 8–9), exokernel (p. 8), seL4 capabilities (p. 10), Tornado/K42 clustered objects and Corey (p. 17), microkernels (L4) and Disco (p. 17), and fos (p. 17).
- **Correctness:** Its assumptions are that hardware is becoming a network (pp. 3, 5), that cores are becoming diverse (p. 3), that cache coherence will grow costly or disappear (pp. 4–5) and that messages cost less than shared memory as more cache lines are touched (pp. 3–4). The first three are argued from trends and citations. Only the last is measured (Fig. 3, on 16 cores of one machine).
- **Contributions:** (1) the multikernel model and its three principles: explicit communication, hardware-neutral structure and replicated state; (2) Barrelfish, a concrete multikernel; (3) measurements showing scalability, adaptability to hardware and competitive performance (p. 2).
- **Clarity:** Well written and clearly structured. Design choices that follow from the model are kept apart from engineering choices (pp. 7, 11). Some figure values can only be read off plots.

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: multikernel | An OS structured "as a distributed system of cores that communicate using messages and share no memory". | p. 5 |
| new: explicit inter-core communication | All inter-core communication uses explicit messages; no memory is shared except message channels. | p. 5 |
| new: hardware-neutral OS structure | Only the message transports and the hardware interface are machine-specific. | p. 6 |
| new: replicated (not shared) state | Potentially shared state is accessed as a local replica, with consistency kept by messages and agreement protocols. | pp. 6–7 |
| new: split-phase operation | An operation sends a request and continues, and the reply arrives later. | p. 6 |
| new: late binding of protocol and transport | The protocol and transport are chosen at runtime to fit the hardware or workload. | p. 6 |
| new: pipelining and batching of messages | Several requests in flight, or several requests in one message, give more throughput per core. | pp. 2, 6 |
| new: CPU driver | Per-core, privileged, event-driven, single-threaded, nonpreemptable kernel part that shares no state with other cores. | p. 8 |
| new: monitor | Per-core user-level process that coordinates system-wide state through agreement protocols. | p. 9 |
| new: dispatcher | Per-core representative of a process; the unit that communicates. | p. 9 |
| new: URPC | User-level RPC: a shared-memory, cache-line, point-to-point channel received by polling. | p. 9 |
| new: system knowledge base (SKB) | Hardware facts in first-order logic, queried for policy (e.g. building multicast trees). | p. 11 |
| new: spectrum of sharing and locking | From a shared-state kernel with one big lock to replicated state with agreement; the multikernel sits at the replicated extreme. | p. 5 |
| new: multikernel vs microkernel | A microkernel uses messages between processes but "remains a shared-memory, multithreaded system in the kernel". | p. 17 |
| new: message-passing/shared-memory duality | Lauer and Needham: the two OS models are duals, and machine architecture decides between them. | p. 3 |

## Notes
- Source: full text, PDF from https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2009/papers/baumann-sosp09.pdf (20 pages, pdfTeX, created 2009-08-10), saved as `research/papers/P8.pdf`. It is the camera-ready layout, not the ACM DL version: Crossref gives pp. 29–44 for the ACM version, and all page numbers here are the 20-page copy's. All 20 pages were read (third pass), and the figure values marked "read off" were estimated from rendered plots of Figs. 6–9.
- No C IDs could be reused, because no `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` was among the inputs. All concepts are marked new.
- SQ-relevant point not captured above: the authors argue for a future where hardware drops cache coherence and an OS based on native message passing fits best (p. 5). Yet their own messages are built on coherence, and they tuned URPC to the coherence protocol (pp. 9, 17). The case for messages as a hardware primitive is therefore argued, not tested, in this paper.
- In hindsight the authors call the decentralised capability design "a mistake" (p. 10), which is evidence for SQ4/SQ15 on the cost of decentralised resource allocation.

bugs, in a similar way as a previous categorization of nonblocking bug fixes in C/C++ [43].
Around 69% of the non-blocking bugs were fixed by restricting timing, either through adding synchronization primitives like Mutex, or through moving existing primitives like
moving Add in Figure 9. 10 non-blocking bugs were fixed
by eliminating instructions accessing shared variables or by
bypassing the instructions (e.g., Figure 10). 14 bugs were
fixed by making a private copy of the shared variable (e.g.,
Figure 8) and these bugs are all shared-memory ones.
To have a better understanding of non-blocking bug fixes
and their relationship to bug causes, we further check what
primitives are leveraged inside patches. Table 11 lists the
fixes according to the type of primitives used in the patches.
Similar to the results of a previous study on patches of concurrency bugs in C/C++ [43], mutex is the most widely used
primitive to enforce mutual exclusion and fix non-blocking
bugs. Besides traditional bugs, mutex was also used to fix
races caused by anonymous function and by WaitGroup and
to replace misused channel.
As a new primitive, channel is the second most widelyused. Channel was leveraged to pass value between two

goroutines and to replace shared variable to fix data race. It
was also used to enforce the order between two operations
in different goroutines. There are also bugs where channel is
not properly used and is fixed in the patch (e.g., Figure 10).
Interestingly, channels were not only used to fix messagepassing bugs but also bugs caused by traditional shared memory synchronization. We suspect this is because some Go
programmers view message passing as a more reliable way
or easier-to-program way of performing inter-thread communication than shared memory synchronization.
Finally, 24 bugs were fixed by other concurrency primitives and 19 bugs were fixed without using any concurrency
primitives (e.g., Figure 8).
Similar to our lift analysis in Section 5.2, we calculate lift
between causes and fix strategies and between causes and
fix primitives for non-blocking bugs. Among bug categories
with more than 10 bugs, the strongest correlation is between
the cause misusing channel and fix primitive channel, with a
lift value of 2.7. The cause anonymous function and the fix
strategy data private has the second highest lift value of 2.23.

with lift value 2.21.

techniques remain to be the main fixes for non-blocking bugs in
Go, while channel is used widely to fix not only channel-related
bugs but also shared-memory bugs.
Implication 7: While Go programmers continue to use traditional shared memory protection mechanisms to fix nonblocking bugs, they prefer the use of message passing as a fix
in certain cases possibly because they view message passing as
a safer way to communicate across threads.
6.3

Detection of Non-Blocking Bugs

Go provides a data race detector which uses the same happenbefore algorithm as ThreadSanitizer [53]. It can be enabled
by building a program using the ‘-race’ flag. During program
execution, the race detector creates up to four shadow words
for every memory object to store historical accesses of the
object. It compares every new access with the stored shadow
word values to detect possible races.
We use our 20 reproduced non-blocking bugs to evaluate
how many bugs the detector can detect. We ran each buggy
program 100 times with the race detector turned on. Table 12
summarizes the number of bugs detected under each root
cause category. The detector reports no false positives.

 === PAGE 12
The data race detector successfully detected 7/13 traditional bugs and 3/4 bugs caused by anonymous functions.
For six of these successes, the data race detector reported
bugs on every run, while for the rest four, around 100 runs
were needed before the detector reported a bug.
There are three possible reasons why the data race detector failed to report many non-blocking bugs. First, not all
non-blocking bugs are data races; the race detector was not
designed to detect these other types. Second, the effectiveness of the underlying happen-before algorithm depends on
the interleaving of concurrent goroutines. Finally, with only
four shadow words for each memory object, the detector
cannot keep a long history and may miss data races.
Implication 8: Simple traditional data race detector cannot
effectively detect all types of Go non-blocking bugs. Future
research can leverage our bug analysis to develop more informative, Go-specific non-blocking bug detectors.

7

Discussion and Future Work

Go advocates for making thread creation easy and lightweight and for using message passing over shared memory
for inter-thread communication. Indeed, we saw more goroutines created in Go programs than traditional threads and
there are significant usages of Go channel and other message passing mechanisms. However, our study show that
if not used correctly, these two programming practices can
potentially cause concurrency bugs.
Shared memory vs. message passing. Our study found
that message passing does not necessarily make multithreaded programs less error-prone than shared memory.
In fact, message passing is the main cause of blocking bugs.
To make it worse, when combined with traditional synchronization primitives or with other new language features
and libraries, message passing can cause blocking bugs that
are very hard to detect. Message passing causes less nonblocking bugs than shared memory synchronization and surprisingly, was even used to fix bugs that are caused by wrong
shared memory synchronization. We believe that message
passing offers a clean form of inter-thread communication
and can be useful in passing data and signals. But they are
only useful if used correctly, which requires programmers
to not only understand message passing mechanisms well
but also other synchronization mechanisms of Go.
Implication on bug detection. Our study reveals many
buggy code patterns that can be leveraged to conduct concurrency bug detection. As a preliminary effort, we built a
detector targeting the non-blocking bugs caused by anonymous functions (e.g. Figure 8). Our detector has already discovered a few new bugs, one of which has been confirmed
by real application developers [12].
More generally, we believe that static analysis plus previous deadlock detection algorithms will still be useful in
detecting most Go blocking bugs caused by errors in shared
memory synchornization. Static technologies can also help

in detecting bugs that are caused by the combination of
channel and locks, such as the one in Figure 7.
Misusing Go libraries can cause both blocking and nonblocking bugs. We summarized several patterns about misusing Go libraries in our study. Detectors can leverage the
patterns we learned to reveal previously unknown bugs.
Our study also found the violation of rules Go enforces
with its concurrency primitives is one major reason for concurrency bugs. A novel dynamic technique can try to enforce
such rules and detect violation at runtime.

8

Related Works

Studying Real-World Bugs. There are many empirical
studies on real-world bugs [9, 24, 25, 29, 40, 44, 45]. These
studies have successfully guided the design of various bugcombating techniques. To the best of our knowledge, our
work is the first study focusing on concurrency bugs in Go
and the first to compare bugs caused by errors when accessing shared memory and errors when passing messages.
Combating Blocking Bugs. As a traditional problem, there
are many research works fighting deadlocks in C and
Java [7, 28, 33–35, 51, 54, 55, 58, 59]. Although useful, our
study shows that there are many non-deadlock blocking
bugs in Go, which are not the goal of these techniques. Some
techniques are proposed to detect blocking bugs caused by
misusing channel [38, 39, 49, 56]. However, blocking bugs
can be caused by other primitives. Our study reveals many
code patterns for blocking bugs that can serve the basis for
future blocking bug detection techniques.
Combating Non-Blocking Bugs. Many previous research
works are conducted to detect, diagnose and fix non-deadlock
bugs, caused by failing to synchronize shared memory accesses [4, 5, 8, 14, 16, 17, 30–32, 43, 46, 47, 52, 62–64]. They
are promising to be applied to Go concurrency bugs. However, our study finds that there is a non-negligible portion of
non-blocking bugs caused by errors during message passing,
and these bugs are not covered by previous works. Our study
emphasizes the need of new techniques to fight errors during
message passing.

9

Conclusion

As a programming language designed for concurrency, Go
provides lightweight goroutines and channel-based message
passing between goroutines. Facing the increasing usage of
Go in various types of applications, this paper conducts the
first comprehensive, empirical study on 171 real-world Go
concurrency bugs from two orthogonal dimensions. Many
interesting findings and implications are provided in our
study. We expect our study to deepen the understanding
of Go concurrency bugs and bring more attention to Go
concurrency bugs.

+## Reference

+Andrew Baumann, Paul Barham, Pierre-Evariste Dagand, Tim Harris, Rebecca Isaacs, Simon Peter, Timothy Roscoe, Adrian Schüpbach, Akhilesh Singhania (2009). *The Multikernel: A New OS Architecture for Scalable Multicore Systems*. Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 22nd Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '09), pp. 29–44 (Crossref). https://doi.org/10.1145/1629575.1629579. P8, from row R0-008. Included under I1(c): a kernel in which "all inter-core communication is performed using explicit messages" (p. 5).
+Page numbers below are the PDF pages of the 20-page copy on sigops.org. Each page also carries that number at the foot. They are not the ACM proceedings pages 29–44.
+## Deepest pass
+## First pass: the five Cs
+- **Category:** A new OS architecture (the multikernel), a prototype that implements it (Barrelfish), and a measured evaluation on x86-64 multiprocessors (pp. 1–2).

+- **Context:** Distributed systems applied to OS structure. The paper builds on Lauer and Needham's duality of message and shared-memory OSes (p. 3), URPC/LRPC (pp. 3, 8–9), exokernel (p. 8), seL4 capabilities (p. 10), Tornado/K42 clustered objects and Corey (p. 17), microkernels (L4) and Disco (p. 17), and fos (p. 17).

+- **Correctness:** Its assumptions are that hardware is becoming a network (pp. 3, 5), that cores are becoming diverse (p. 3), that cache coherence will grow costly or disappear (pp. 4–5) and that messages cost less than shared memory as more cache lines are touched (pp. 3–4). The first three are argued from trends and citations. Only the last is measured (Fig. 3, on 16 cores of one machine).

+- **Contributions:** (1) the multikernel model and its three principles: explicit communication, hardware-neutral structure and replicated state; (2) Barrelfish, a concrete multikernel; (3) measurements showing scalability, adaptability to hardware and competitive performance (p. 2).
+- **Clarity:** Well written and clearly structured. Design choices that follow from the model are kept apart from engineering choices (pp. 7, 11). Some figure values can only be read off plots.
+## Quality
+| Q | Answer | Why |
+| Q1 | yes | The contributions are stated as a three-item list in the introduction (p. 2), and the goals as a five-item list (p. 7). |

+| Q2 | partly | Addressing is described: a name service, channel setup by monitors, and point-to-point dispatcher channels (pp. 9–10). Busy-receiver handling is described: poll, then block and ask the monitor for notification (p. 9). The message format is described only as cache-line sized with stub-compiled marshalling (pp. 9–10). Ordering and delivery are mentioned only in passing ("reliable in-order message delivery", p. 17), and full-queue behaviour is not stated. |
+| Q3 | yes | Barrelfish runs real programs (OpenMP, SPLASH-2, a web server, SQLite) on four real x86-64 machines (pp. 8, 15–16). |

+| Q4 | partly | Most claims name a versioned baseline: Linux 2.6.26, Windows Server 2008 R2 Beta, L4Ka::Pistachio 2009-02-25 and lighttpd 1.4.23 (pp. 10, 13, 16). The IP-loopback and OpenMP comparisons say only "Linux", without a version or configuration in their sections (pp. 14–15). |

+| Q5 | partly | Workloads and why they were chosen are reported (pp. 12, 14–15), and so is the hardware (p. 8). The number of runs is stated only for Fig. 9 (five runs, p. 15). Other experiments give σ or error bars without a run count, or nothing (Table 4, web server). |
+| Q6 | yes | The abstract and conclusions make only qualitative claims ("comparable", "scale better", "competitive"; pp. 1, 18). Each is backed by Figs. 7–9 and Tables 1–4 (pp. 9–16). |

+| Q7 | partly | Table 4's cache-miss and HyperTransport counters support the loopback cause (p. 14). Other causes are only asserted: the dispatch loop as the cause of unmap overhead (p. 13), the threads library for the Fig. 9 differences (p. 15), kernel crossings for the web server (p. 16), and "likely" the stride prefetcher (p. 13). |
+| Q8 | yes | The Summary has a dedicated paragraph on what the evaluation does not show (p. 16). Further limits are stated on pp. 11–12 and 17. |
+| Q9 | no | All nine authors are Barrelfish's designers and builders ("We have implemented a multikernel OS", p. 1; "our implementation", p. 7). |
+## Extracted fields
+| Field | Value | Page |
+| Reference | See *Reference* above. P8; I1(c). | p. 1, p. 5 |
+| Paper type | Design (a new OS model), with implementation (Barrelfish) and evaluation in the same paper. | pp. 2, 5, 7, 12 |

+| System | Barrelfish, a multikernel OS, built in 2009 by ETH Zurich Systems Group and Microsoft Research Cambridge (the author affiliations). Status: running kernel on x86-64 multiprocessors, with an ARM port in progress. Source released at barrelfish.org. | pp. 1, 8, 18 |

+| Levels with message semantics | Hardware: no. On the test machines "the only inter-core communication mechanism available … is cache-coherent memory" (p. 9), although the interconnect itself "resembles a message-passing network" (p. 3). Microcode: not stated. Instruction set: no; x86-64, with messages built from stores and polling (p. 9). Kernel: inter-core, yes: "all inter-core communication is performed using explicit messages … no memory is shared … except for that used for messaging channels" (p. 5). Kernel as a whole, no under the form's definition: the per-core CPU driver handles traps, interrupts and system calls (p. 8), and capability changes are made by system calls (p. 10). Runtime: no; user threads share an address space (p. 11). Language: not stated; the CPU driver is C and assembly (p. 8). Later non-message paths: the model allows a replica to be shared under spinlocks as an optimisation (p. 7), and the authors call this "a next step" (p. 18). Neither is implemented in this paper. | pp. 3, 5, 7–11, 18 |

+| Receiving unit and state ownership | The receiver is a dispatcher. A process is a set of dispatcher objects, one per core, and "communication … is not actually between processes but between dispatchers (and hence cores)" (p. 9). Monitors, one per core, receive inter-core coordination messages (p. 9). The CPU driver "shares no state with other cores" (p. 8). The OS keeps global state as replicas kept consistent by agreement between monitors (pp. 7, 9). Others can still reach the state: the channel memory is shared memory (p. 9), and applications may share memory and even a hardware page table across cores (pp. 5, 11). | pp. 5, 7–9, 11 |

+| Message mechanism | Inter-core transport: URPC, a shared-memory region used as a point-to-point channel for cache-line-sized messages between one writer and one reader. The receiver polls the last word of the line (p. 9). Prefetching for pipelined throughput can be chosen at channel setup (p. 9). The model is asynchronous and split-phase (pp. 6–7). Same-core IPC is an asynchronous, fixed-size message from the CPU driver, with an optional synchronous LRPC/L4-like call (p. 8). Naming: a name service maps service names to a service reference, used to set up a channel through the monitors (p. 10). All transports sit behind a common interface, with marshalling generated by a stub compiler (p. 10). Ordering and delivery: "a multikernel may exploit reliable in-order message delivery" (p. 17); no further guarantee is stated. Buffering: the throughput test uses a queue of 16 messages (p. 10); full-queue behaviour is not stated. Busy or absent receiver: the dispatcher polls for a fixed time, then blocks and asks its monitor for notification, and an IPI wakes it (pp. 9, 14). Remote monitors handle messages when "convenient" (p. 12). Dispatch: user-level message dispatching and event demultiplexing code in the threads package (pp. 9, 13). | pp. 6–10, 12–14, 17 |

+| Non-message primitives | (1) Cache-coherent shared memory as the hardware carrier of every inter-core message. Reason: it is the only mechanism on current hardware (p. 9). (2) Shared memory for the message channels themselves (p. 5). Same-core, "more complex communication channels are built over this using shared memory" (p. 8). (3) Application shared memory and shared address spaces across cores, optionally one shared hardware page table. Reason: most current programs need it, and the shared table is "typically more efficient" (pp. 5, 11). (4) Traps and system calls into the privileged CPU driver; capability operations are system calls (pp. 8, 10). (5) Device interrupts are routed in hardware, then demultiplexed by the CPU driver and turned into messages (p. 8). (6) IPIs and MONITOR/MWAIT to wake or idle a core, used instead of spinning forever (pp. 9, 14). (7) Cache prefetch instructions in URPC (p. 9). (8) DMA by the NIC (p. 15). (9) Future work: a replica shared by closely coupled cores under spinlocks, to use shared caches (pp. 7, 18). | pp. 5, 7–11, 14–15, 18 |

+| Self-definition | Not object-based. The OS is split into a privileged CPU driver, written in C and assembly and specialised for x86-64 (7135 + 337 lines), and user-level monitors and services that talk by messages (p. 8). The CPU driver lies outside the message model and is the base: it serially processes traps and interrupts (p. 8). Whether a running program can inspect or change these levels: not stated. The closest mechanism is the system knowledge base, which holds hardware facts in first-order logic for queries such as transport selection (p. 11). Cost of the split: OS invocations become local RPCs with two context switches, "several thousand cycles" (pp. 11–12). | pp. 8, 11–12 |

+| Interposition | Not stated as interposition. Related mechanisms: all transports sit behind a common interface (p. 10), the protocol and transport are late-bound (p. 6), and the name service maps a name to a service reference (p. 10). These suggest a transport or service could be swapped without changing the sender or receiver, but the paper neither claims nor measures this. | pp. 6, 10 |

+| Operating system functions | *Protection*: each core's CPU driver enforces protection and authorisation (p. 8), and capabilities are modelled on seL4 (p. 10). Coordination is involved: yes, because all cores must keep their capability lists consistent (p. 10). *Scheduling*: the CPU driver time-slices locally and runs dispatchers by upcalls, with user-level thread schedulers (pp. 8–9). Cross-core threads are handled by messages, and CPU drivers can be coordinated for gang scheduling (p. 11). Central component: not stated. *Memory*: virtual memory is managed at user level through capabilities (p. 10). Unmap uses a one-phase commit and retype a two-phase commit between all monitors (p. 11). That is coordination: yes. *Devices*: drivers are user-level processes (p. 8), placed on cores by the system knowledge base (p. 11). Whether the SKB is one instance: not stated. *Naming*: a name service (p. 10); centralisation not stated. *Failure*: none; "the complete system is a failure unit" (p. 17). *Costs of decentralising*: the capability scheme "was a mistake … unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient than scalable per-processor memory managers" (p. 10). Replica consistency adds latency and developer burden (p. 7). Two-phase commit "serializes more messages" than shootdown (p. 14). | pp. 7–11, 14, 17 |

+| Cost of message primitives | Same-core LRPC, one way (Table 1): 845 cycles on 2×4 Intel, 757 on 2×2 AMD, 1463 on 4×4 AMD, 1549 on 8×4 AMD (p. 9). L4 raw IPC is about 420 cycles on 2×2 AMD (p. 8). Inter-core URPC latency (Table 2): 180 cycles (shared cache) to 618 cycles (two hops, 8×4 AMD) (p. 10). URPC against L4 IPC on 2×2 AMD (Table 3): 450 vs 424 cycles; 3.42 vs 2.36 messages per kcycle; 9 vs 25 I-cache lines; 8 vs 13 D-cache lines (p. 10). IPI wake cost C ≈ 6000 cycles (p. 14). A trap costs ≈ 800 cycles (p. 12). | pp. 8–10, 12, 14 |

+| Performance results | (a) Update shared state, 4×4 AMD: SHM costs ~12,000 extra cycles per update at 16 cores, against under 30 on one core. MSG beats SHM for 4 or more cache lines (Fig. 3, pp. 3–4). (b) URPC pipelined throughput: 2.75–11.97 messages per kcycle (Table 2, p. 10). (c) Unmap latency, 8×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux 2.6.26 mprotect vs Windows Server 2008 R2 Beta VirtualProtect: at 32 cores, about 18k vs 29k vs 45k cycles, read off Fig. 7. Barrelfish is slower at 2 cores (≈10k vs ≈5–6k) (p. 13). (d) Two-phase commit, 8×4 AMD: ≈14k to ≈28k cycles single-operation and ≈8k to ≈19k pipelined, 2 to 32 cores, read off Fig. 8 (p. 14). (e) IP loopback, 2×2 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux (version not stated): 2154 vs 1823 Mbit/s; 21 vs 77 D-cache misses per packet; HyperTransport link utilisation 8%/3% vs 11%/9% (Table 4, p. 14). (f) OpenMP (CG, FT, IS) and SPLASH-2 (Barnes-Hut, radiosity), 4×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux with GCC 4.3.3 and GOMP: similar on FT, Barnes-Hut and radiosity. Barrelfish is better on CG at 12–16 cores and worse on IS (Fig. 9, p. 15). (g) UDP echo, 2×4 Intel, e1000: 951.7 vs 951 Mbit/s for Linux 2.6.26 (p. 16). (h) Static web page, 2×2 AMD: 18697 req/s (640 Mbit/s) vs 8924 req/s (316 Mbit/s) for lighttpd 1.4.23 on Linux 2.6.26 (tuned). Web-plus-SQLite: 3417 req/s, with no baseline (p. 16). | pp. 3–4, 10, 13–16 |

+| Scaling | Fig. 3: 2–16 cores, against shared-memory updates (p. 3). Figs. 6–8: 2–32 cores on 8×4 AMD. NUMA-aware multicast is near flat at ≈3k cycles; broadcast and unicast grow linearly to ≈13–14k (Fig. 6, read off the plot). For unmap and two-phase commit see *Performance results* (pp. 13–14). Fig. 9: 1–16 cores against Linux (p. 15). The authors: "It would be wrong to draw any quantitative conclusions from our large-scale benchmarks" (p. 16). | pp. 3, 13–16 |

+| Attributed causes | All are stated by the designers. (1) SHM cost: "All of these extra cycles are spent with the core stalled on cache misses". Inherent to coherent shared memory; not isolated beyond the SHM/MSG contrast (p. 3). (2) Broadcast shootdown is slow "due to the cache-coherence protocol used by AMD64": the line crosses the interconnect N times. Hardware cause; explained, not separately measured (p. 12). (3) The flat unicast curve below 8 cores is "likely" the stride prefetcher. Speculation (p. 13). (4) Multicast wins because the shared L3 removes interconnect traffic and eight processors send in parallel. Design; shown by the protocol comparison in Fig. 6 (p. 13). (5) Unmap overhead above the base protocol is "largely due to inefficiencies in the message dispatch loop of the user-level threads package". Implementation; not isolated (p. 13). (6) Linux and Windows unmap scale worse because of "serially sending IPIs" (p. 13). Not isolated. (7) Loopback gain: URPC avoids shared memory except the channel and payload, while "Linux causes more cache-coherence traffic"; also kernel crossings. Design; partly isolated by the miss and HyperTransport counters (p. 14). (8) Fig. 9 differences come from "our user-space threads library vs. the Linux in-kernel implementation". Implementation; not isolated (p. 15). (9) Web server gain is "mainly due to avoiding kernel-user crossings". Design; not isolated (p. 16). (10) The CPU-driver/monitor split costs several thousand cycles per OS call. Implementation choice; not measured in a figure (p. 12). | pp. 3, 12–16 |

+| Fate and reasons | The paper reports a research prototype, "not by any means yet a mature system" (p. 17). Its source is released (p. 18), and an ARM port to programmable NICs is in progress (p. 17). It states no later fate. | pp. 17–18 |

+| Concurrency defects | Not applicable; not a defect study. Related qualitative remarks only: shared data has "correctness and performance pitfalls" (p. 4), and retyping one capability differently on two cores "leads to an inconsistent system", which the two-phase commit prevents (p. 11). | pp. 4, 11 |

+| What shapes programs | Argument with examples, not a study. The knowledge for efficient sharing "is encoded implicitly in its implementation", so a shared-memory OS is tied to one hardware design (pp. 2, 4). Examples: the Windows 7 dispatcher-lock removal touched 6000 lines in 58 files; Linux RCU needed many iterations (p. 2). Programmers must reason about "messages sent by the cache-coherence protocol" (p. 4). Message passing brings "stack ripping" and event-driven style; the authors argue OS developers already work this way (p. 4). | pp. 2, 4 |

+| Hardware–language trade-off | Not addressed for languages. On hardware the paper argues only that future systems may "drop [cache coherence] entirely in favor of a message-passing model. An OS that can exploit native message-passing would be the natural fit" (p. 5). It does not measure hardware message support. | p. 5 |

+| Model equivalence | Messages are built on shared memory: URPC over cache-coherent memory, tuned to the coherence protocol, at two interconnect round trips per message (p. 9). Shared memory is also built on messages: a shared virtual address space can use replicated page tables kept consistent by message protocols (p. 11). Kept: no OS state shared outside channels (p. 5). Not kept: applications can still share memory (p. 11). Performance: URPC costs about the same as L4 IPC, 450 vs 424 cycles (p. 10). The paper cites Lauer and Needham's duality (p. 3). | pp. 3, 5, 9–11 |

+| Model mixing | Barrelfish applications use POSIX-like threads sharing an address space, because "most current programs" need it (p. 11), and the OpenMP and SPLASH-2 benchmarks run that way (p. 15). The paper gives no frequency data. | pp. 11, 15 |

+| Runtime limits | Not an actor runtime. Message-system limits the paper names: "extreme sensitivity to message queue lengths" (p. 17), unoptimised user-level dispatch (p. 13), and cost tied to the coherence protocol underneath URPC (pp. 9, 17). The hardware shared-memory model is named as the source of shared-memory OS costs (pp. 3–4). | pp. 3–4, 9, 13, 17 |

+| Many-core scaling | Up to 32 cores (8×4 AMD), all with cache-coherent shared memory (p. 8). Inter-core communication is URPC over coherent memory across HyperTransport (pp. 3, 9). For results see *Scaling*. Limits named: coherence cost as core counts grow (p. 4, citing Mattson et al. that coherence restricts scaling "to even 80 cores"), and queueing effects (pp. 4, 17). The paper does not evaluate beyond commodity hardware or heterogeneous cores (p. 16). | pp. 3–4, 8–9, 16–17 |

+| Adoption factors | Barrelfish's adoption is not reported. Factors the paper gives: POSIX subsets and C libraries make porting "mostly straightforward" (p. 16); there is "enormous investment" in Linux and Windows (p. 16); a scalability problem "must affect a substantial group of users" before it gets attention (p. 1). Distributed shared virtual memory saw limited use because of "performance and scalability problems" (p. 17). | pp. 1, 16–17 |
+| Quality | See *Quality* above. | pp. 1–18 |
+| Notes | See *Notes* below. | — |
+## Concepts
+| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
+| new: multikernel | An OS structured "as a distributed system of cores that communicate using messages and share no memory". | p. 5 |
+| new: explicit inter-core communication | All inter-core communication uses explicit messages; no memory is shared except message channels. | p. 5 |
+| new: hardware-neutral OS structure | Only the message transports and the hardware interface are machine-specific. | p. 6 |
+| new: replicated (not shared) state | Potentially shared state is accessed as a local replica, with consistency kept by messages and agreement protocols. | pp. 6–7 |
+| new: split-phase operation | An operation sends a request and continues, and the reply arrives later. | p. 6 |
+| new: late binding of protocol and transport | The protocol and transport are chosen at runtime to fit the hardware or workload. | p. 6 |
+| new: pipelining and batching of messages | Several requests in flight, or several requests in one message, give more throughput per core. | pp. 2, 6 |
+| new: CPU driver | Per-core, privileged, event-driven, single-threaded, nonpreemptable kernel part that shares no state with other cores. | p. 8 |
+| new: monitor | Per-core user-level process that coordinates system-wide state through agreement protocols. | p. 9 |
+| new: dispatcher | Per-core representative of a process; the unit that communicates. | p. 9 |
+| new: URPC | User-level RPC: a shared-memory, cache-line, point-to-point channel received by polling. | p. 9 |
+| new: system knowledge base (SKB) | Hardware facts in first-order logic, queried for policy (e.g. building multicast trees). | p. 11 |

+| new: spectrum of sharing and locking | Traditional OSes moved from the far left towards finer-grained locking and more replication. The multikernel sits at the extreme right, where all state is replicated and kept consistent by agreement protocols. | p. 5 |
+| new: multikernel vs microkernel | A microkernel uses messages between processes but "remains a shared-memory, multithreaded system in the kernel". | p. 17 |
+| new: message-passing/shared-memory duality | Lauer and Needham: the two OS models are duals, and machine architecture decides between them. | p. 3 |
+## Notes

+- Source: full text, PDF from https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2009/papers/baumann-sosp09.pdf (20 pages, pdfTeX, created 2009-08-10), saved as `research/papers/P8.pdf`. It is the camera-ready layout, not the ACM DL version: Crossref gives pp. 29–44 for the ACM version, and all page numbers here are the 20-page copy's. All 20 pages were read (third pass), and the figure values marked "read off" were estimated from rendered plots of Figs. 6–9.
+- No C IDs could be reused, because no `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` was among the inputs. All concepts are marked new.

+- SQ-relevant point not captured above: the authors argue for a future where hardware drops cache coherence and an OS based on native message passing fits best (p. 5). Yet their own messages are built on coherence, and they tuned URPC to the coherence protocol (pp. 9, 17). The case for messages as a hardware primitive is therefore argued, not tested, in this paper.
+- In hindsight the authors call the decentralised capability design "a mistake" (p. 10), which is evidence for SQ4/SQ15 on the cost of decentralised resource allocation.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).
# Template

The shape of every file the workflow produces. The folders mirror `research/`, where the filled copies are saved. Each template is the spec of its file: frontmatter, sections, and a `{placeholder}` with what goes there.

## How to use

# P12

## Reference
William J. Dally, J.A. Stuart Fiske, John S. Keen, Richard A. Lethin, Michael D. Noakes, Peter R. Nuth, Roy E. Davison, Gregory A. Fyler (1992). *The Message-Driven Processor: A Multicomputer Processing Node with Efficient Mechanisms*. IEEE Micro 12(2), 23–39. https://doi.org/10.1109/40.127581. P12, included under I1 (row R0-012). Pages below are those of the authors' 25-page preprint (see Notes), not the IEEE Micro pages.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and implementation description of a working processor chip (the MDP) and its multicomputer (the J-Machine), with cycle counts but no evaluation section (pp. 1–3, 13–18).
- **Context:** Message-passing multicomputers (Cosmic Cube, iPSC, N-CUBE, Ametek), shared-address machines (BBN Butterfly, IBM RP3), single-chip nodes (Transputer, MOSAIC, iWARP); the authors' earlier MDP architecture paper [11] and k-ary n-cube network work [10, 12–14] (pp. 2–3).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that sequential-processor mechanisms do not support synchronisation, communication and global naming efficiently, so these "must be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead" (p. 2). It is argued, and backed only by one comparison with iPSC message times (p. 2). The cycle counts are given as design facts, not as measurements (pp. 9–11).
- **Contributions:** A single-chip node in which message arrival creates and dispatches a task in hardware, with no receive instruction (p. 1). It adds SEND instructions, hardware message queues, presence tags (FUT/CFUT), name translation (XLATE/ENTER) and three priority register sets (pp. 5–9). The chip is running silicon (p. 16), and Concurrent Smalltalk and Id are implemented on it (pp. 20–23).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with worked assembly examples (combining tree, CALL handler, size-of-tree; pp. 5, 10–11, 22). In this preprint most figures are blank and only their captions remain (see Notes).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The two design goals are listed in the introduction (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Message format (p. 9, Fig. 12 p. 13), receiver naming (p. 9) and busy-receiver behaviour (queue, priorities; pp. 6, 9) are described. Ordering guarantees are not stated; only deadlock freedom is (p. 12). |
| Q3 | yes | Silicon since June 1991, running programs; J-Machine boards and a 128-node machine are operational (pp. 16, 23–24). |
| Q4 | partly | Only the message-plus-dispatch time names a baseline (iPSC-1 5 ms, iPSC-2 300 µs; p. 2). The claim of being competitive with iWARP and Transputer names baselines but gives no values (p. 23). |
| Q5 | partly | Hardware configuration is given (62.5 ns cycle, 1K-node prototype; pp. 11–12). Workloads are only illustrative examples, with no reason for choosing them and no runs (pp. 10, 23). |
| Q6 | partly | The transistor count (Fig. 18 p. 18) and the June 1991 silicon date (p. 16) are in the body. "Competitive with iWARP/Transputer" and "2.5 years, < 8 people" (pp. 23–24) have no supporting data in the body. |
| Q7 | no | Causes of low overhead are asserted, e.g. dispatch avoids control-transfer overhead (pp. 10–11). No breakdown or ablation isolates them. |
| Q8 | partly | Open software questions, 12 hardware bugs and a "very conservative" implementation are mentioned in passing (pp. 16, 18, 23–24). There is no dedicated section. |
| Q9 | no | All authors designed or built the MDP (p. 3, p. 16). |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| message-driven processing (new) | "processing is performed in response to messages (via the dispatch mechanism). There is no receive instruction. A task is created to handle each arriving message." | p. 1 |
| primitive mechanisms vs programming models (new) | Mechanisms are the hardware's primitive operations from which programming abstractions are built. The MDP gives general communication, synchronisation and naming mechanisms instead of specialising for one model. | pp. 1–2 |
| message dispatch as task creation (new) | The header opcode is loaded into the IP and a message segment descriptor goes into A3, creating a task in 3 cycles. | p. 9 |
| presence tags / futures (FUT, CFUT) (new) | Tagged locations are marked empty, and reading one faults and suspends the task until a value is written. Used for synchronisation. | pp. 6–7 |
| name translation (XLATE/ENTER) (new) | A hardware associative table maps arbitrary keys to values (segment descriptors or node numbers) to support a global virtual address space. | p. 7 |
| fine-grain multicomputer / jellybean node (new) | An inexpensive node with small memory, many per system, giving more performance per unit cost. Tasks are about 20 instructions and objects about 8 words. | pp. 1–2, 23 |
| global virtual address space over message passing (new) | The same IDs name local and remote objects. A shared-memory model can be built on the mechanisms. | pp. 3, 5 |
| selector-object dispatch (new) | CST method invocation is a message to the first argument. COSMOS picks the function by class from a selector object; known types bypass it with a direct call. | pp. 20–21 |

I converted it to PDF with Ghostscript ps2pdf and saved it as `research/papers/P12.pdf` (25 pages). It is not the IEEE Micro typeset version, which is closed access (OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar: closed).

- **Figures:** the preprint has no embedded images. Figures 1–4, 7, 9, 11, 13–17, 19 and 20 are blank apart from their captions. Figures 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 18 and 21–23 are text or tables and were read.
- **Author list:** the preprint lists the authors as Dally, Davison, Fiske, Fyler, Keen, Lethin, Noakes, Nuth (Davison and Fyler at Intel). The Stanford CVA citation gives the published order Dally, Fiske, Keen, Lethin, Noakes, Nuth, Davison, Fyler, which is used in Reference.
