=== PAGE 1
 The Message-Driven Processor: A Multicomputer Processing Node
                   with Ecient Mechanisms
                     William J. Dally, Roy Davison? , J.A. Stuart Fiske, Greg Fyler? ,
                    John S. Keen, Richard A. Lethin, Michael Noakes, Peter R. Nuth




     Arti cial Intelligence Laboratory                              ?   Platform Architecture Group
     Massachusetts Institute of Technology                              Intel Corporation
     545 Technology Square                                              3065 Bowers Avenue
     Cambridge, MA 02139                                                Santa Clara, CA 95052-8131



                                               Abstract
         The Message-Driven Processor (MDP) is an integrated multicomputer node that provides
      ecient mechanisms for parallel computing. It incorporates a 36-bit integer processor, a mem-
      ory management unit, a router for a 3-D mesh network, a network interface, a 4K-word 2 36-bit
      SRAM, and an ECC DRAM controller in a single 1.1M transistor VLSI chip. Rather than being
      specialized for a single model of computation, the MDP incorporates ecient primitive mecha-
      nisms for communication, synchronization and naming. These mechanisms eciently support
      most proposed parallel programming models. Each processing node of the MIT J-Machine
      consists of an MDP with 1 MByte of DRAM. MDPs have been operational since June 1991
      and J-Machines built from them have been on-line since July 1991.


1     Introduction
The Message-Driven Processor (MDP) is a 36-bit single-chip microcomputer specialized to operate
eciently in a multicomputer. The MDP chip includes the processor, a 4K-word by 36-bit memory,
and a network port. An on-chip memory controller with ECC permits local memory to be expanded
to 1M-words by adding external DRAM chips.
    The processor is message driven in the sense that processing is performed in response to messages
(via the dispatch mechanism). There is no receive instruction. A task is created to handle each
arriving message. A computation is advanced (driven) by the messages carrying tasks about the
network.
    The design of the MDP was driven by two primary goals:

    1. To implement a general-purpose multicomputer processing node that provides the communica-
       tion, synchronization, and naming mechanisms required to eciently support several di erent
       parallel programming models.
    2. To create an inexpensive jellybean VLSI component that can be used to build cost-ecient
       parallel computers. The nodes should be inexpensive and plentiful VLSI commodity parts
       (like real jellybean candies) that can be networked together to form a Jellybean Machine
       (J-Machine) multicomputer.

Ecient Parallel Mechanisms Support Many Programming Models: Mechanisms are
the primitive operations provided by a computer's hardware. The abstractions that make up a
programming system are built from these mechanisms [15]. For example, most sequential machines
provide some mechanism for a push-down stack to support the last-in- rst-out (LIFO) storage

                                                    1
 === PAGE 2
allocation required by many sequential programming models. Most machines also provide some
form of memory relocation and protection to allow several processes to coexist in memory at a single
time without interference. The proper set of mechanisms can provide a signi cant improvement in
performance over a brute-force interpretation of a programming model.
    Over the past 40 years, sequential von Neumann processors have evolved a set of mechanisms
appropriate for supporting most sequential programming models. It is clear, however, from e orts to
build concurrent machines by wiring together many sequential processors, that these highly-evolved
sequential mechanisms are not adequate to support most parallel models of computation. These
mechanisms do not eciently support synchronization of events, communication of data, or global
naming of objects. As a result, these functions, inherent to any parallel model of computation, must
be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead. For example, sequential machines
require hundreds of instructions to create a new process. This cost prohibits the use of ne-grain
programming models where processes typically last only a few tens of instructions.
    The MDP supports a broad range of parallel programming models (including shared-memory [16],
data parallel [17], data ow [26], actors [1], and explicit message-passing [5]) by providing low-
overhead primitive mechanisms for communication, synchronization, and naming. Communication
mechanisms are provided that permit a user-level task on one node to send a message to any other
node in a 4K-node machine in < 2s. No processing resources on intermediate nodes are consumed
and bu er memory is automatically allocated on the receiving node. On message arrival, a task is
created and dispatched in < 1s. Synchronization is provided by presence tags on all storage loca-
tions. Three separate register sets allow fast task switching. The translation mechanism maintains
bindings between arbitrary names and values; it may be used to support a global virtual address
space. These mechanisms have been selected to be both general and amenable to ecient hard-
ware implementation. To support ne-grain concurrent programming systems, the mechanisms are
designed to eciently handle small objects (8 words) and small tasks (20 instructions).

A 3-D Array of Fine-Grain Processing Nodes is Physically Ecient: The MDP is an ex-
ample of an inexpensive ne-grain multicomputer building block. Being ne-grain does not mean a
node has a slow processor; a competent processor can be built in a fraction of a modern VLSI chip's
area. A ne-grain node implies an inexpensive node with a small amount of memory. The result is
greater arithmetic performance and local memory bandwidth per unit cost. The fast communica-
tion and global address space prevent the small local memories from limiting programmability or
performance.
    In a multicomputer, system cost is very sensitive to processor cost. A less expensive node results
in a comparably priced system with more processors and, to rst order, higher performance. In
these systems, costly features that give a small incremental return in processor performance (such
as large caches) are avoided in favor of building systems with more nodes, an option not available
to the designer of a sequential computer.
   The 3-D network that connects MDPs gives the highest throughput and lowest latency for a
given wire density [10]. This network makes use of all three dimensions of physical space. It allows
the processing nodes to be packed densely and results in uniformly short wires. No communication
bandwidth is wasted by embedding an esoteric topology into physical space. Messages traveling
through the network follow a Manhattan shortest path in physical space; they never backtrack.

Background: The MDP builds on previous work in multicomputer design. Like the Caltech
Cosmic Cube [4], the Intel iPSC [3], the N-CUBE [24], and the Ametek [2], each MDP in the J-
Machine has a local memory and communicates with other nodes by passing messages. Because of
its low overhead, the MDP can exploit concurrency at a much ner grain than these early message-
passing multicomputers. Delivering a message and dispatching a task in response to the message's
arrival takes < 2s on the J-Machine, as opposed to 5ms on an iPSC-1 or 300s on an iPSC-2.
Like the BBN Butter y [19] and the IBM RP3 [8], the MDP supports a global virtual address

                                                  2
 === PAGE 3
Figure 1: MDP Pinout: The MDP has a memory port (26 pins), six network ports (15 pins each)
and a diagnostic port (3 pins).


space. The same IDs (virtual addresses) are used to reference local (on the same node) and remote
(on a di erent node) objects. Like the InMOS transputer [6], the Caltech MOSAIC [20], and the
Intel iWARP [7], the MDP is a single chip processing element integrating a processor, memory, and
a communication unit. The MDP is unique in that it extends these previous e orts with ecient
primitive mechanisms for communication, synchronization and naming [15]. The MDP uses a direct
communication network based on the work reported in [12, 10, 14].
   The MDP was built as part of a collaborative project between MIT and Intel Corporation. The
project was funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

software points of view. Section 3 describes the MDP instruction set with emphasis on instructions
that support parallelism. The network architecture is discussed in Section 4. Section 5 brie y

the MDP's mechanisms. MDP software is addressed in Section 6.


2     System Architecture
Hardware View: To the hardware designer, the MDP appears as a component with a memory
port, six bidirectional network ports, and a diagnostic port as shown in Figure 1.
   The memory port provides a direct (no glue) interface to up to 1M-word of ECC DRAM memory
consisting of 11 multiplexed address lines, a 12-bit data bus, and 3 control signals. Static-column or
page mode DRAMs are cycled three times to access a 36-bit data word and a fourth time to check
or update the ECC check bits. Current J-Machines use 3 1Mx4 memory parts to form a 4-chip
processing node with 260KW of memory that measures 2x2.75 inches as shown in Figure 2.
    The network ports are used to connect MDPs together into a 3-dimensional mesh network. Each
of the six network ports corresponds to one of the six cardinal directions (+X; 0X; +Y; 0Y; +Z; 0Z )
and consists of nine data and six control lines. Each port connects directly to the opposite port on
an adjacent MDP. Details of the 3-D network are given in Section 4.
    The diagnostic port is used to issue supervisory commands and to read and write MDP memory

result to a combining node. When the message arrives at the processor containing the combining
node, a task is created that executes a combine routine. The routine adds the message value to the
node's value and decrements the count. When the count reaches zero, a combine message is sent
to the node's parent.
    The MDP supports communication using a SEND instruction for message formatting, a fast
network for delivery, automatic message bu ering, and task creation upon message arrival. A series
of SEND instructions is used to send a message of arbitrary length to any node in the machine.
Upon arrival, the message is bu ered in a hardware queue. When the message arrives at the head
of the queue, a task is dispatched to handle the message. In the combining tree example, a pair of
SEND instructions is used to send the combine message to a node. Upon message arrival, the MDP
bu ers the message and creates a task to execute the combine routine.
   Synchronization in the MDP is performed using message dispatch and presence tags on all state.

                                                  5
 === PAGE 6
The dispatch of a process on each message arrival allows messages to be used to signal events on
remote nodes. For example, in the combining tree example above, each combine message signals
its own arrival and causes the combine routine to be executed.
   Presence tags are used to synchronize on the arrival of data. For example, access to the value
produced by the combining tree may be synchronized by initially tagging as empty the location
that will hold this value. An attempt to read this location before the combining tree had written it
would raise an exception and cause the reading task to be suspended until the value is written by
the root of the tree. Synchronization on data availability in this manner is quite common in many
parallel programs.
    The MDP supports naming with segmented memory management and with translation instruc-
tions. In the combining tree example, a memory segment would be allocated to hold the state
of each combining node. Accesses to the node would be relocated and protected using a segment
descriptor. To make combining nodes relocatable across processing nodes, a node's virtual address
would be translated to nd the processing node on which it resides. Upon reaching this node, a
second translation would locate the segment descriptor for the combining node.


3      Instruction Set Architecture
The MDP extends a conventional microprocessor instruction-set architecture (ISA) with instruc-
tions to support parallel processing. Speci cally, the MDP provides ecient hardware mechanisms
for communication, synchronization and naming. This section describes the MDP ISA with partic-
ular emphasis on these mechanisms. Further details of the MDP ISA are described in [11].

Register Set: The MDP provides separate register sets to support rapid switching between three
execution levels: background, priority 0 (P0 ), and priority 1 (P1). The MDP executes at the
background level when there are no pending messages. Each arriving message creates a task and
initiates execution at P0 or P1 depending on the priority of the message. The MDP executes the
highest priority task at any point in time. Thus, the arrival of a P1 message while the MDP is
executing a P0 task will cause the MDP to switch execution levels (and thus register sets). When
the P1 task completes, execution at P0 is resumed by switching to the P0 register set which holds
the register state of the suspended task.
     The register set at each priority level includes:
      4 general-purpose data registers: R0-R3
      4 address registers:                  A0-A3
      4 ID registers:1                      ID0-ID3
      1 instruction pointer:                IP

    Most instructions operate on the general registers R0-R3. Each address register A0-A3 contains
a segment descriptor consisting of a base and a length eld. Memory addresses are speci ed by
an o set and an address register. For example, the operands [R0,A1] and [3,A2] specify an
indexed access to the segment described by A1 and a displacement of 3 into A2's segment. ID
registers are less accessible general registers that by convention are used to hold object IDs. The
instruction pointer includes process status bits that control virtual addressing, type checking, and
fault handling. Placing these bits in the instruction pointer enables control and execution state to
be changed by loading a single register. Quick task switching within an execution level is facilitated
by the relatively small size of each register set.
    1 The background register set does not include ID registers. They only exist at P0 and P1 .




                                                          6
 === PAGE 7
                                Figure 4: MDP Instruction Format


Tags: Tags in the MDP are used for type checking and synchronization. Every 36-bit word of
register and memory state holds a 32-bit value and a 4-bit tag that indicates the type of the value.
Tag values are de ned for primitive user data types (such as SYMBOL, INTEGER, BOOLEAN, etc.) and
for system data types (such as IP, ADDR (a segment descriptor), MSG (a message header), etc.).
Four tag values are user-de nable. If type checking is enabled, the MDP checks operand tags to
determine which form of an instruction to execute. An exception is raised if the operands are not
compatible with the instruction.
    Two tags, FUT and CFUT, support inter-task synchronization. A location is initially marked
empty by writing it with a CFUT tag. When a task produces the value for the location, it overwrites
the CFUT with the nal value and tag. Any attempt to read from the location before the value is
produced invokes the CFUT fault handler which typically suspends the reading task until the location
is written. FUT is used for global synchronization, and CFUT for local.
   Hardware support for tags makes software more ecient and robust. A program can perform
an operation without having to check that operands are present or of the correct type. For the
\normal" cases in which no fault occurs, execution proceeds more quickly than if special test and
branch instructions were required to check for type and presence. Only exceptional cases incur the
overhead of running a fault handler.

Instructions: The MDP executes 17-bit, xed format, three-address instructions with the format
shown in Figure 4. Each instruction speci es an operation, two register operands, and a third
operand that may be a register, a memory location, or a constant. Two 17-bit instructions are
packed in each 36-bit word. Any instruction-stream word not tagged as an instruction is loaded as
a constant into register R0. This provides a very ecient means to load arbitrary 36-bit constants.
The MDP instruction set is summarized by category in Figure 5.

Naming: Naming is supported in the MDP via translation instructions and segmented addressing.
Addressing memory through segment descriptors permits arbitrary sized objects to be relocated and
protected. The ENTER instruction enters an arbitrary translation from a 36-bit key to a 36-bit data
value in a set-associative cache (translation table) mapped into the on-chip memory. The XLATE
instruction looks up the data value (if any) associated with a key. These instructions can be used
to translate an object's name into a physical segment descriptor or a node number to support a
global virtual address space.

Communication: The MDP provides hardware support for end-to-end message delivery includ-
ing formatting, injection, delivery, bu er allocation, bu ering, and task scheduling.
   An MDP transmits a message using a series of SEND instructions each of which injects one or
two words into the network at either priority 0 or 1. A typical message send is shown in Figure 6.

   READ          WRITE         READR        WRITER        RTAG           WTAG        LDIP
   LDIPR         CHECK
Arithmetic and Logic Instructions:

   ROT           AND           OR           XOR           FFB            NOT         NEG
   LT            LE            GE           GT            EQUAL          NEQUAL      EQ
   NEQ
Network Instructions:
   SEND          SENDE         SEND2        SEND2E
Associative Lookup Table Instructions:
   XLATE         ENTER         PROBE
Special Instructions:
   NOP           INVAL         SUSPEND      CALL
Branches:

   SEND   R0,0            ; send net address (priority 0)
   SEND2 R1,R2,0          ; header and receiver (priority 0)
   SEND2E R3,[3,A3],0     ; selector and continuation - end msg. (priority 0)


Figure 6: MDP assembly code to send a 4 word message uses three variants of the SEND instruction.




                                                 8
 === PAGE 9
Figure 7: Message dispatch. In three clock cycles, a new task is created by (1) setting the IP to
change the thread of control and (2) creating a message segment to provide the initial addressing
environment.


The rst SEND instruction reads the absolute address of the destination node in < x; y; z > format
from R0 and forwards it to the network hardware. The SEND2 instruction reads the rst two words
of the message out of registers R1 and R2 and enqueues them for transmission. The nal instruction
enqueues two additional words of data, one from R3, and one from memory. The use of the SEND2E
instruction marks the end of the message and causes it to be transmitted into the network. This
sequence executes in 4 clock cycles (250ns).
   An injected message is delivered to the destination node by the network (Section 4). At the
destination, it is bu ered in a hardware-managed FIFO queue in the internal RAM of the MDP.
Separate queues are maintained for P0 and P1 messages.

Task Scheduling: When a message reaches the head of the highest priority non-empty queue,
a task is created to handle it by changing the thread of control and creating a new addressing
environment as shown in Figure 7. Every message header contains an opcode and the message
length. The message opcode is loaded into the IP to start a new thread of control. The length eld
is used along with the queue head to create a message segment descriptor (automatically written
to A3) that represents the initial addressing environment for the task. The message handler code
may open additional segments by translating object IDs in the message into segment descriptors.
Creating a task to handle a message takes 3 cycles.
    The dispatch mechanism is used directly to process messages requiring low latency (e.g., com-
bining and forwarding). Other messages (e.g., remote procedure call) specify a handler that locates
the required method, using the translation mechanism described above, and then transfers control
to it.

in Figure 8. The execution of this handler is depicted in Figure 9. The rst instruction gets the
method ID (o set 1 into the message segment referenced by A3). The next instruction translates
this method ID into a segment descriptor for the method and places this descriptor in A0. In one of
its operating modes, the MDP can use A0 as a pointer to a segment of code, and IP as an index into
that segment. This allows code to be easily relocated at runtime. The nal instruction of the CALL

4     Network Architecture
The Message Driven Processor contains a network interface and a router that support a commu-
nication network closely integrated with the processor. In a J-Machine composed of MDPs, the
network provides end-to-end message delivery with low latency (< 2s in a 4K-node network)
and high bandwidth (288 Mbits/sec per channel). Message delivery is handled entirely within the
routers of the machine and consumes no processor or memory resources at intermediate nodes.

Structure: The J-machine network is a three dimensional grid, with bidirectional channels,
dimension-order routing, and blocking ow control. (See Figure 11). Addressing limits the size
of the network to 64K nodes (32 2 32 2 64). Our initial prototype is a 1K node machine (8 2 8 2 16).
The faces of the network cube are left open for use as I/O ports to the machine. Each channel
can sustain a data-rate of 288Mbits/sec. All three dimensions may operate simultaneously for an
aggregate data rate of 864Mbits/sec per node.
   The network logic is composed of three modules as shown in Figure 14. The netout module
bu ers words and injects them into the network. The three routers, one for each dimension of
the network, route messages from node to node. The netin module reassembles messages at their
destination and bu ers them into a message queue. Section 5 contains more implementation details.

Engineering: The three-dimensional mesh topology of the J-Machine network was chosen as
the most ecient arrangement subject to constraints of wiring density and component pinout [10].
These constraints set the width of the six bidirectional channels per MDP node at 9 data bits plus 6
control bits. The J-machine is built as a stack of boards with dense board-to-board interconnections
(Section 5) to implement the 3-D network with short wires.



                                                11
 === PAGE 12
Figure 11: The J-Machine Network is a 3-D mesh or k-ary 3-cube. The network performs e-cube
or destination tag routing. Messages are routed in each dimension in turn to the proper coordinate
in that dimension. In this gure, a message is routed from (1,5,2) to (5,1,4) routing rst in x, then
y, then z.


    The MDP router is synchronous1 and operates at twice the rate of the processor sending a pair
of 9-bit phits between nodes each 62.5ns processor cycle2 . Each of the six bidirectional channels
can be turned around on alternate cycles with no contention penalty. A novel pad design tolerates
clock skew between routers and eliminates the potential for conduction overlap when the channel is
turned around [23]. Messages are routed through the network with a latency of one 62.5ns processor
cycle per hop. Thus message latency T is given by

                                                T = Tc (2L + D);                                                    (1)

    where Tc is the processor cycle time, L is message length in words, and D is the distance (number
of nodes) a message must traverse. For example, in a 1K-node machine, an L=6 word message to
a random destination traverses an average of D=10 nodes for a latency of T =22 cycles or 1.4s.
The bisection bandwidth3 of a 1K-node machine is 18.4Gbits/s, the aggregate bandwidth of the
network channels is 864Gbits/s, and the I/O bandwidth is 184Gbits/s.

e-cube routing). As shown in Figure 11, all messages are rst routed in the X dimension, then in Y,
then in Z. Since messages are routed in dimension order and messages running in opposite directions
along the same dimension do not block, there are no resource cycles, and the network is provably
deadlock free [13].

Y and Z addresses. At each node along the path, the address in the head it of the message is
compared with the node's index in the current dimension. If the two indices match, the head

The major subsystems in the MDP are shown in Figure 14. The chip includes a conventional
microprocessor with prefetch, control, register le and ALU (RALU), and memory blocks. The

cannot send message words as fast as the network can transmit them, the FIFO prevents bubbles
(absence of words) from entering the network pipeline and degrading performance.

the network arrives in 18-bit its, which are composed into a four word Queue Row Bu er (QRB).

row (4 2 36 bits) at a time reduces the number of memory cycles consumed by the network, leaving
more memory bandwidth for the CPU.

dimension of the network. Each router is split into two separate virtual networks with di erent
priorities that share the same physical channels. The priority 1 network can preempt the wires even
if the priority 0 network is congested or jammed.

Address Arithmetic Unit: The Address Arithmetic Unit (AAU), the largest logic block in
the MDP, performs all functions associated with memory addressing. To support naming, the
AAU contains the address registers, performs relocation and protection of memory accesses, and
implements the translation instructions. Each memory reference is o set by the selected address
register's base eld and checked against its length eld. An attempt to access through an invalid
address register (which may occur when an object is relocated) or to access beyond the end of
an object raises an exception. A translation base-mask (TBM) register is used to de ne an area of
memory to be a two-way set-associative translation bu er used by the XLATE and ENTER instructions.
The AAU hashes the keys used to access this table using an exclusive-or network to improve hit-rate
in the translation bu er.

encompasses exactly all of the messages currently in the queue. When a task is dispatched to
handle a message, the A3 register is loaded with a segment descriptor for the message. The MDP
dispatches a task as soon as the rst four words of a message are written. If the task attempts to

increase in productivity which was essential to completing the chip successfully with our small
design team.
    About 35K standard cells containing  210K transistors4 were used in the  700 sheets of
schematics drafted at MIT. These schematics were transferred to Intel for layout. Many of the
datapaths were laid out by hand to exploit the regularity of the design. Less regular collections of
logic were laid out using automatic place and route CAD tools.
    Architecture studies leading to the MDP were started in October 1986. Work on the RTL model
of the microarchitecture began in June 1988. Schematic entry at MIT started in November 1988.
The task of translating schematics into layout commenced in June 1989. Layout was completed in
December 1990. First silicon was received in June 1991 and was running programs within a few
hours.

but for performance reasons a second revision of the layout with modi ed control logic and some
metal xes was sent for fabrication in January 1992. We plan to use several thousand of these chips
to build research multicomputers at MIT.

System Design: A photograph of a J-Machine processor board is shown in Figure 19. The board
measures 20.5 by 24 inches and contains 64 processing nodes. Each node consists of an MDP chip
(in a 168-pin PGA package) and three 4Mbit DRAMs. Each pair of nodes shares a set of elastomeric
connectors to communicate with the corresponding nodes on the boards above or below the board

# P13

## Reference
Ungar, D., Patterson, D. (1987). *What Price Smalltalk?*. IEEE Computer 20(1), pp. 67–74. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.1987.1663359. Included under I2 (R0-015).

## Deepest pass
1 (incomplete: only the abstract was available; title, abstract and the abstract's statement of the article's structure were read; section headings, conclusions and references were not reachable)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Evaluation of a built system: a reduced instruction set computer for Smalltalk (SOAR), used to "estimate the performance implications of the Smalltalk-80 programming environment" (P13, abstract). Probably also a retrospective, as R0-015 proposes, but the abstract does not say so.
- **Context:** Exploratory programming environments such as Smalltalk-80 "require such expensive computers that few programmers can afford them"; SOAR ("Smalltalk on a RISC") was built by a research project at the University of California to widen that community (P13, abstract). Related work cited by the paper: not reachable.
- **Correctness:** Not assessable from the abstract. The abstract claims the authors "are now able to estimate" performance implications, which implies measurement on SOAR, but no figures, baselines or setup are given (P13, abstract).
- **Contributions:** (1) a list of "the demands that Smalltalk-80 places on traditional computer systems"; (2) "software and hardware ideas that answer those demands"; (3) an estimate of the performance implications of Smalltalk-80 (P13, abstract).
- **Clarity:** The abstract is clear about the aim and the structure of the article; the body was not read.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.

# P22

## Reference
Milo M. K. Martin, Mark D. Hill, Daniel J. Sorin (2012). *Why On-Chip Cache Coherence Is Here to Stay*. Communications of the ACM 55(7), pp. 78–89. https://doi.org/10.1145/2209249.2209269. Included under I4 (SQ14), row R0-025.

All pages below are pages 1–9 of the authors' near-final version (`papers/P22.pdf`), not the CACM pages 78–89 (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
3. I read every section, the sidebar, Table 1 and Figures 2, 4 and 5, and checked the analyses (amortized traffic, storage growth, latency formulas, non-inclusive overhead) against the paper's own numbers. I did not rerun the recall simulation, because its inputs are not published.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position paper backed by analysis. It presents a proof-of-concept coherence design built from known techniques, then analyses it with analytical models and one small simulation. It reports no silicon or benchmark measurements (p. 1, p. 8).
- **Context:** It answers predictions that on-chip coherence will not scale and will give way to software-managed coherence, scratchpads or message passing without shared memory. It cites DeNovo [5], Intel's 48-core message-passing processor [10] and Cohesion [13] (p. 1, p. 3). It builds on directory protocols [1, 8], the SGI Origin 2000 [14], Intel Core i7 [17], AMD HT-Assist [6] and Linux scalability studies [2, 3] (p. 1, pp. 4–6).
- **Correctness:** Some assumptions are stated: coherence does not change the number of misses, though false sharing and poor synchronization may change it (p. 4). Others are stated too: an inclusive shared cache (p. 2), a single chip (p. 9), and no queuing or contention modelled (p. 8). Some are left implicit: the cost model counts bytes per miss and ignores how invalidation bursts are spread over time, and the energy analysis is inferred from the traffic and storage results, not modelled (pp. 7–8).
- **Contributions:** (1) An amortized argument that traffic per miss does not depend on core count when sharers are tracked exactly (p. 3, Fig. 2b p. 4). (2) Coherence traffic is at most 20% above a cache system without coherence (Table 1, p. 4). (3) With a hierarchy of inclusive caches, storage grows as √C (two levels) or ∛C (three levels) (p. 6, Fig. 4). (4) With explicit eviction notifications, recalls are rare: below 0.1% at a 4× capacity ratio with 8 ways (p. 7, Fig. 5). (5) Latency and energy arguments (pp. 7–8). (6) An extension to non-inclusive caches (p. 8).
- **Clarity:** Clear. There is one "Concern" section per scalability worry, and each ends with a boxed conclusion (pp. 3–8). There is a dedicated caveats section (pp. 8–9). One numeric inconsistency: the abstract says storage is "2% of total cache size for even 512 cores" (p. 1). The summary says 5% with two cache levels or 2% with three (p. 8). The abstract does not say that the 2% figure needs three levels.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim in one place: "refutes this conventional wisdom by showing one way to scale on-chip cache coherence with bounded costs" (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Two of four are given. Message format: request and ack 8 B, data 72 B, holding block address and type (Table 1, p. 4). Addressing: shared cache banked by address, per-core tracking bits, forwarding to sharers (p. 2). Delivery or ordering guarantees and busy-receiver behaviour are not stated. |
| Q3 | partly | Almost all evidence is analytical. The only executed artefact is a recall simulation on a synthetic random miss stream (p. 7). There is no silicon, FPGA or real-program run (p. 8). |
| Q4 | partly | Traffic and latency are compared with a named but hypothetical baseline: "caches but no hardware coherence" (p. 4, p. 7). Inexact encoding is compared with the Origin 2000 scheme (p. 5). The energy claim has no baseline or measurement (pp. 7–8). |
| Q5 | partly | Two of three are reported for the recall simulation. Workload: a random miss stream, justified by [9]. Configuration: fully associative private caches, associativities and capacity ratios swept. The number of runs or samples is not reported (p. 7). |
| Q6 | yes | Each number in the abstract and conclusions appears in the body. 20% traffic: Table 1 (p. 4). √C storage and 2% at 512 cores: Fig. 4 (p. 6). Zero latency for non-shared misses: p. 7. 2–9% non-inclusive overhead: p. 8. |
| Q7 | partly | The traffic spike is isolated to inexact encoding (Fig. 2a vs 2b, p. 4). The recall rate is isolated to capacity ratio and associativity (Fig. 5, p. 7). Causes in the energy and complexity arguments are only asserted (pp. 8–9). |
| Q8 | yes | A dedicated section, "Summary, Caveats, and Criticisms", lists five limitations (pp. 8–9). |
| Q9 | no | All three authors designed the evaluated protocol ("we synergistically combine known techniques", p. 1). The paper also discloses: "Hill has a significant financial interest in AMD" (p. 9). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Martin, Hill, Sorin (2012), *Why On-Chip Cache Coherence Is Here to Stay*, CACM 55(7):78–89; P22; included by I4 (SQ14), R0-025 | p. 1 |
| Paper type | design. A proof-of-concept design with analytical evaluation, argued as a position ("existence proof of a scalable coherence protocol, but we do not claim it to be the best"). | p. 1, p. 8 |
| System | (a) The authors' proof-of-concept protocol: a hierarchy of inclusive caches with embedded tracking bits and explicit eviction notifications. Status: design only, analytical model plus one simulation. Built by the authors, 2011–2012. (b) Its base protocol is "loosely based upon" Intel Core i7 (Nehalem): silicon, deployed commercially. (c) Also discussed: SGI Origin 2000 (silicon, commercial), Sun/Oracle UltraSPARC T2, NVIDIA Fermi, AMD Bulldozer and AMD HT-Assist (silicon). | p. 1, p. 2, pp. 5–6, p. 8 |
| Levels with message semantics | Instruction set: no. Cores "communicate via loads and stores to a shared address space". Hardware (cache controllers): yes for coherence actions only. A private-cache miss "issues a coherence request message"; the shared cache forwards, invalidates or sends recall messages; "communication involves only point-to-point messages". Cache hits change state with no message. Microcode, kernel, runtime, language: not stated. Message-based start later extended: not stated. | p. 1, p. 2, p. 3 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Receivers are cache controllers: shared-cache banks, cluster caches and private caches. A private cache's block state can be changed from outside: on a recall message "the private cache is forced to evict the block"; on a write miss the shared cache's forwarded request makes private caches "invalidate their copies". Each core's private cache is also read and written by its own core's loads and stores. | p. 2, p. 3 |
| Message mechanism | Coherence messages between caches. Sync/async: not stated, but requests are forwarded and "responses are typically sent directly to the original requester (… three-hop protocol)" (p. 7). Naming: by block address to an address-interleaved shared-cache bank; the bank names sharers by per-core tracking bits (p. 2). Ordering and delivery guarantees: not stated. Buffering: not stated. Busy receiver: not stated. Dispatch: by the block's coherence state (M/S/I) and tracking bits (p. 2, sidebar). | p. 2, p. 7 |
| Non-message primitives | At the instruction-set level: loads and stores to shared memory are the communication primitive. Reason: coherence makes caches "functionally invisible to software" and keeps backward compatibility for software "written for cache-coherent shared memory systems" (p. 1). Cache hits: served locally with no message (p. 7). Interrupts, traps, DMA, I/O: not stated. | p. 1, p. 7 |
| Self-definition | Not applicable: the paper describes hardware coherence, not a system written in its own objects and messages. | p. 1 |
| Interposition | not stated. The paper does not discuss placing a component between sender and receiver. | none |
| Operating system functions | Not addressed for the paper's own design. The paper claims conventional operating systems "have been shown to scale using cache coherence [2, 3]". It quotes Boyd-Wickizer et al.: "there is no scalability reason to give up on traditional operating system organizations just yet". On centralization: a single shared last-level cache tracks sharers per block (one directory entry per block, distributed across banks). Protection, scheduling, naming and failure handling are not stated. | p. 1, p. 2, p. 8 |
| Cost of message primitives | No measured latency or cycles. Analytical sizes: request and ack messages 8 B, data message 72 B (64 B block + 8 B address). Latency formulas: t_direct = t_noncoherent = 2·t_interconnect + t_cache; t_indirect = 3·t_interconnect + 2·t_cache. | p. 4 (Table 1), p. 7 |
| Performance results | (1) Traffic, bytes/miss, analytical model, coherent vs "without coherence" (64-bit address, 64-byte block): clean 96 vs 80 B/miss (+20%); dirty 160 vs 152 B/miss (+5%) (Table 1, p. 4). (2) Traffic with Origin-style inexact encoding (32 bits/block) vs exact: spike of "almost 6x" at 1024 cores (Fig. 2a, p. 4; text p. 5). (3) Storage overhead, % of cache storage, exact tracking: 16 cores ~3% (p. 3). 1024-core two-level: 6%. 4096-core three-level: 3% (p. 6). 512 cores: 5% two-level, 2% three-level (p. 8). (4) Recall rate, % of misses, synthetic random miss stream: below 0.1% for an 8-way shared cache at 4× capacity ratio; Core i7 is 16-way at 8× (Fig. 5, p. 7). (5) Indirect-miss latency vs non-coherent miss: 1.5× to 2× (p. 7). (6) Non-inclusive directory storage overhead, 16 cores: 2% at S2/S1=8; 4%, 6%, 9% at 4, 2, 1. Hierarchical, 256 cores: 2% at Z=8; 5%, 10%, 18% at Z=4, 2, 1 (p. 8). | p. 3, p. 4, p. 5, p. 6, p. 7, p. 8 |
| Scaling | Analytical, not measured. Core counts modelled: 1–1024 for traffic (Fig. 2, p. 4); 1–4096 for storage (Fig. 4, p. 6); 256 for non-inclusive storage (p. 8). Results: traffic per miss with exact tracking is independent of core count (p. 3–4). Flat storage overhead grows linearly with C (reaches the 20% top of the Fig. 4 axis at about 128 cores). Two-level storage grows as √C; three-level as ∛C (p. 6). The latency ratio is independent of core count (p. 7). Baseline: a system with caches and no coherence (p. 4), and flat vs hierarchical designs (p. 6). | p. 3, p. 4, p. 6, p. 7, p. 8 |
| Attributed causes | (a) "Coherence's alleged lack of scalability is believed to be due to the poor scaling of the storage and traffic … as well as concerns about latency and energy". Stated by the authors (third party to the predictions) as others' belief, which the paper disputes (p. 1). (b) Traffic does not grow because "for every write that invalidates N caches, it must have been preceded by N read misses". Designers; inherent to exact tracking; argued by amortization and shown in Fig. 2b (p. 3–4). (c) The traffic spike in inexact encoding comes from "unnecessary invalidations". Designers; inherent to the encoding; isolated by Fig. 2a vs 2b (p. 5). (d) Recalls come from shared-cache capacity and associativity, and from silent clean evictions that leave the shared cache "ambiguous". Designers; due to implementation; isolated by Fig. 5 (pp. 6–7). (e) Many applications do not scale, but the root cause may be "the algorithm, program implementation, or coherence"; this is asserted with no measurement (p. 1). | p. 1, pp. 3–7 |
| Fate and reasons | Cache coherence is commercial and dominant: "provided by mainstream servers, desktops, laptops, and even mobile devices … Intel, AMD, ARM, IBM, and Oracle (Sun)". It "has come to dominate the market for both technical and legacy reasons": better performance than software coherence, and backward compatibility. Stated by the authors (third party to the vendors). The paper's own protocol: research only (existence proof). | p. 1, p. 8 |
| Concurrency defects | Not applicable: no defect study. The sidebar gives one constructed example: without coherence, a lock variable could let "multiple cores into a critical section or prevent cores waiting … from making forward progress". | p. 2 |
| What shapes programs | The hardware model, by argument only. "At least with hardware coherence, programmers can concentrate on choreographing independent work rather than handling low-level mechanics" (p. 1). Coherence frees developers "from re-implementing coherence … or orchestrating explicit communication via message passing" (p. 9). Evidence kind: argument, no study of programs or programmers. | p. 1, p. 9 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Not addressed as such. The closest claim: "Forcing software to use software-managed coherence or explicit message passing does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". Message send as the hardware primitive: argued against for mainstream chips. | p. 9 |
| Model equivalence | Messages on shared memory: "any program that works for scratchpad systems (e.g., Cell processor) or message passing systems (e.g., MPI cluster) can easily map to a shared memory system with caches". This is asserted, with no performance or property analysis. The reverse also appears inside the design: the shared-memory abstraction is implemented by point-to-point coherence messages in hardware. Encapsulation and data-race freedom: not discussed. | p. 2, p. 3, p. 8 |
| Model mixing | At the system level, not the program level. Message passing (for "scale out high performance computing") and incoherent scratchpads (for "real-time systems") "will persist" and "coexist with on-chip cache-coherent shared memory". No frequency data or developer reasons. | p. 1, p. 8 |
| Runtime limits | Not addressed: no actor or message runtime is discussed. | none |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts: 1–4096, modelled. Shared memory and coherence: yes, hardware coherence. Inter-core communication: loads and stores, carried by point-to-point coherence messages over an on-chip interconnect, with a hierarchy of cluster caches (p. 2, pp. 5–6). Result: traffic per miss is constant, storage grows as √C or ∛C, the latency ratio is constant, and energy overhead is argued not to grow (pp. 3–8). Limits named but not addressed: interconnect scalability, "the critical problem of software non-scalability", queuing and contention, multi-socket coherence, and verification effort (p. 8–9). Prior claims of a coherence limit come from [5, 10, 13] (p. 1, p. 3). | pp. 1–9 |

Factors given: software compatibility ("Computer systems tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs", p. 1); existing scalable operating systems on coherence (p. 1, p. 8); programmability (p. 9); kind of workload (HPC, real-time) (p. 1). Economics: not stated. | p. 1, p. 8, p. 9 |

| Notes | Complexity: the authors say coherence protocol complexity "does not necessarily scale up with increasing numbers of cores". Hierarchical protocols can be "formally verified with an amount of effort that is independent of the number of cores [19]" (p. 9). This bears on SQ14 and on any cost argument against hardware coherence. | p. 9 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant | All coherence protocols ensure that, per block, there is either one core with write permission or any number with read permission. | p. 2 |
| new: scalable coherence | Coherence is "scalable" when its cost "grows (at most) slowly as core count increases". Five costs are examined: traffic, storage, inclusion, latency, energy. | p. 3 |
| new: amortized coherence traffic | A write that invalidates N sharers must follow N read misses, so average traffic per miss is constant in core count. | p. 3 |
| new: exact vs inexact encoding of sharers | Exact encoding uses one bit per core and gives constant traffic. Inexact (coarse-vector, limited-pointer) encoding bounds storage but causes "unnecessary invalidations", up to ~6× traffic at 1024 cores. | pp. 4–5 |
| new: hierarchical inclusive coherence | Cluster caches track their cores and the last-level cache tracks clusters. This gives fan-out invalidation, acknowledgment combining, and storage proportional to √C or ∛C. | pp. 5–6 |
| new: explicit eviction notifications | Private caches notify the shared cache on every eviction, including clean ones, so tracking is exact and recalls become rare. The cost is extra small messages. | p. 3, p. 6 |
| new: recall (back-invalidation) | When an inclusive shared cache evicts a block with sharers, it forces their eviction. This is rare (<0.1%) at a 4× capacity ratio. | p. 3, pp. 6–7 |
| new: direct vs indirect miss | Coherence adds latency only to indirect misses (blocks cached elsewhere), 1.5–2× a non-coherent miss, and the ratio does not depend on core count. | p. 7 |
| new: coherence messages implement shared memory | The coherent shared-memory abstraction is carried by point-to-point request, forward, invalidation, recall and ack messages between cache controllers. | pp. 2–3 |
| new: complexity shifting | Removing hardware coherence "does not remove the complexity, but rather shifts the complexity from hardware to software". | p. 9 |
| new: compatibility as reason for coherence | Coherence dominates for "technical and legacy reasons", and systems "tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate small costs". | p. 1 |
| new: coexistence of communication paradigms | Message passing and scratchpads persist in HPC and real-time niches but "coexist with" coherent shared memory, which dominates mainstream chips. | p. 1, p. 8 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** the authors' near-final manuscript, 9 pages, pdfTeX, dated 5 Dec 2011, headed "A final revision of this manuscript will appear in Communications of the ACM, TBD 2012". I downloaded it from https://research.cs.wisc.edu/multifacet/papers/cacm2012_coherence_nearfinal.pdf and saved it as `papers/P22.pdf` (sha256 b0a1e474…6df).
- **Why not the published version:** the ACM Digital Library PDF (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/2209249.2209269) returned HTTP 403. A Penn URL tried returned 404 or HTML. Crossref gives the published version as CACM 55(7):78–89, July 2012.
- **What this means for pages:** every page in this record is the manuscript's page (1–9), not the CACM page. The final CACM text may differ in wording or numbers from this manuscript.
- **No C IDs reused:** no concept files were among my inputs, so every concept is marked new.
- **Selection checks:** X5 is satisfied (ACM magazine article). X9 does not apply: the paper is not a survey, and it reports its own analysis and one simulation.

I wrote the full record for P8 (Baumann et al. 2009, *The Multikernel*). I found the full text online, saved it as the PDF, and read all 20 pages, so the deepest pass is 3. Every field has a page.

**Files**
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P8.md`: the record, `status: proposed`. It has every section of the template and no `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` left.
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/papers/P8.pdf`: the 20-page copy from https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2009/papers/baumann-sosp09.pdf, created 2009-08-10. It is not yet in the release; run `just papers-push` to publish it.

**Quality scores:** Q1 yes, Q2 partly, Q3 yes, Q4 partly, Q5 partly, Q6 yes, Q7 partly, Q8 yes, Q9 no. All nine authors designed and built Barrelfish.

**Open issues**
- **Page numbers:** the pages I cite are from this 20-page copy (each page shows that number at the foot). Crossref gives the ACM version as pp. 29–44, a different layout, so my pages do not map to the ACM ones. This is a decision for you (D1 below).
- **Values read off plots:** Figs. 6–9 give no numbers in the text. The values I give for them were estimated from rendered images and are marked "read off".
- **Concept IDs:** no `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` was among my inputs, so every concept is marked "new:" and none reuses a C ID.
- **Paper type:** the field allows one value, but the paper is design, implementation and evaluation at once. I recorded "design" with the other two noted. This is D2 below.

**Extraction-form fields that were hard or ambiguous (pilot feedback)**
1. **Paper type:** a single value does not fit papers that propose a model, build it and measure it.
2. **Levels with message semantics:** under the strict rule ("every state change … with no other path"), the kernel level gets "no", because traps, interrupts and system calls go into the CPU driver. Yet the paper's core claim is that all inter-core communication is messages. The form cannot say "yes between cores, no within a core", so I wrote both in the value.
3. **Self-definition:** it is phrased for object or reflective systems. For a C kernel with a non-reflective base, most of it comes out "not stated" or "not object-based".
4. **Interposition:** the paper never discusses it. Its transport abstraction and name service come close, so I had to choose between "not stated" and an inference. I chose "not stated" and listed the related mechanisms.
5. **Operating system functions:** the rule that replicated parts which must agree count as central makes protection and memory "yes, coordination", even though the system has no single central component. The value hides that difference.
6. **Performance results and Scaling:** these overlap, and the figure-only results have no exact values. Nothing in the form says how to record values read off a plot.
7. **Hardware–language trade-off, Model mixing, Runtime limits, Concurrency defects:** these mostly do not apply to a kernel paper. The form has no explicit "not applicable" value, so I wrote one-line reasons.
8. **Q5:** it is unclear whether "number of runs" must be reported for every experiment or for at least one. That decides partly versus yes; I chose partly.
9. **Q2:** P8 gives only "reliable in-order delivery" in passing (p. 17), and it is unclear whether that counts as describing ordering and delivery. I did not count it.

**Decisions that are yours**

D1. How pages are cited when the copy read is not the publisher's layout.
- (a) Keep the PDF page of the copy read and state the source copy in *Notes*, as P8.md does now. No file edit is needed.
- (b) Add a line to `research/sls/1-protocol/extraction-form.md`, *Reference* row: "Pages refer to the copy in `papers/P{n}.pdf`; if it is not the publisher's version, say so and give the publisher's page range."
- (c) Require publisher pagination, and have the reader get the ACM version for P8 (through the university library) and redo the pages in P8.md.
- **I recommend (b):** it makes (a) the rule for every reader, at no cost.

D2. The *Paper type* field.
- (a) Leave it as is. Readers pick the dominant type and note the others, as P8.md does.
- (b) In `extraction-form.md`, change the *Paper type* row to "One or more of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study; with page", and list all three in P8.md.
- **I recommend (b).**

D3. Fields that do not apply to a paper.
- (a) Keep one-line reasons, as now.
- (b) Add to the header of `extraction-form.md`: "A field that does not apply to the paper's type is filled `n/a: {reason}`." Then change P8.md's *Concurrency defects*, *Hardware–language trade-off*, *Model mixing* and *Runtime limits* rows to start with `n/a:`.
- **I recommend (b):** it makes not-applicable fields easy to filter in synthesis.

D4. The kernel level in *Levels with message semantics*.
- (a) Keep the strict "no" with the inter-core "yes" written beside it, as now.
- (b) Change the field in `extraction-form.md` to ask separately "between cores or nodes" and "within a core (traps, interrupts, system calls)".
- **I recommend (b):** multikernel and microkernel papers will all hit this split.

data ow architectures. An Id program can be converted into a data ow graph, in which operators
are represented by nodes and dependencies by arcs. Originally, these data ow graphs were executed
directly on specialized data ow machines; more recently, researchers have begun compiling data ow
graphs to run on general-purpose parallel machines[9]. Data ow programs are well-suited to large
parallel computers, because the abundance of ne-grained tasks, each of which can be as small as
a single data ow operator, makes it easy to mask communication latency with task switches. Con-
versely, the J-machine's ne-grained mechanisms make it an excellent target for data ow programs.
    We have experimented with several methods of executing data ow programs on the J-machine [25].
The simplest of the systems translates each node of the data ow graph into a sequence of MDP
instructions. A data ow node with two inputs takes 20 MDP instructions to simulate, i.e., to store
the rst data value, match it with the second value when it arrives, perform the data ow operation,
and send the resulting value to two destinations. This makes use of the CFUT tag and fault handler.
   A more ecient approach is to increase the granularity each task in order to reduce scheduling
overhead. We are currently building a system on top of the Berkeley TAM project[9] that addresses
the ineciencies of our earlier systems.


7     Concluding Remarks
The MDP has been built to demonstrate the utility of general-purpose communication, synchroniza-
tion and naming mechanisms in a multicomputer building block. Its mechanisms have been shown
to eciently support data ow [25] and object-oriented programming [18] models using a shared
address space. Our studies have shown that the use of a few simple mechanisms provides orders of
magnitude lower communication and synchronization overhead than is possible with multicomput-
ers built from o -the-shelf microprocessors. Communication and synchronization performance is
competitive with processing nodes specialized to a single model of computation such as iWARP [7]
(systolic) or the Transputer [6] (CSP).
    Computers built from ne-grain processing nodes, such as the MDP, consisting of a small but
powerful processor and a small amount of memory, are more cost-e ective than those built from
fewer coarse-grain nodes. Fine-grain nodes have a larger fraction of their silicon area devoted to
processing and have higher arithmetic, memory, and communication bandwidth per unit cost. Large
scale parallel machines built from ne-grained processors have a larger total amount of memory
within a given latency of a processor. An ecient network design provides global memory latency
and bandwidth competitive with coarse grain machines.
   The MDP is a component for building scalable computer systems. It is useful in con gurations
ranging from one node to 64K nodes. A 128-node Jellybean machine (J-Machine) is currently

operational and resources are in place to build several more machines, including a 1024-node system
at MIT and machines at a number of other research institutions.
    The MDP project has demonstrated the feasibility of building experimental computer systems
with limited resources. By concentrating on the novel mechanisms of the MDP and keeping the
design simple and modest in other respects we were able to complete the design of the chip, its
system level hardware, and several programming systems with a handful (< 8) of graduate students
and engineers in 2.5 years.
   With the MDP we have begun exploring mechanisms for parallel computers. Much work remains
to be done to tune the MDP's mechanisms and compare them to alternatives. The demands
of parallel software that drive these mechanisms are very di erent from the demands placed on
sequential computers. The design of mechanisms for parallel computers is particularly challenging
because there are no well established parallel benchmarks and most parallel programs are very
biased by the mechanisms (or lack thereof) of the machines for which they were initially written.
    Our software studies have suggested improvements that could be made to the MDP. More
registers, as well as better mapping mechanisms would be useful. The current implementation is very
conservative, so there are certainly opportunities for streamlining the implementation, decreasing
the cycle time and number of clocks per instruction. A commercial custom VLSI product based on
the architectural mechanisms in the MDP is very plausible.
    As technology scales, it becomes feasible to put many powerful processing units on a single
chip. An interesting direction for further research is to extend the MDP mechanisms to control
intra-node as well as inter-node concurrency. This is the approach taken in the MIT M-Machine
project, currently in its early phase, which employs a processor coupling mechanism to allow local
processors to interact with single-cycle latency.

Why On-Chip Cache Coherence is Here to Stay
A final revision of this manuscript will appear in Communications of the ACM, TBD 2012
Milo M. K. Martin
Mark D. Hill
University of Pennsylvania
University of Wisconsin
Duke University
milom@cis.upenn.edu
markhill@cs.wisc.edu
sorin@ee.duke.edu
Abstract
Today’s multicore chips commonly implement shared memory
with cache coherence as low-level support for operating systems
and application software. Technology trends continue to enable
the scaling of the number of (processor) cores per chip. Because
conventional wisdom says that the coherence does not scale well
to many cores, some prognosticators predict the end of coherence.
This paper refutes this conventional wisdom by showing one way
to scale on-chip cache coherence with bounded costs by combining known techniques such as: shared caches augmented to track
cached copies, explicit cache eviction notifications, and hierarchical design. Based upon our scalability analysis of this proof-ofconcept design, we predict that on-chip coherence and the programming convenience and compatibility it provides are here to stay.
1.
Introduction
Shared memory is the dominant low-level communication
paradigm in today’s mainstream multicore processors. In a shared
memory system, the (processor) cores communicate via loads and
stores to a shared address space. The cores use caches to both
reduce the average memory latency and reduce memory traffic.
Caches are thus beneficial, but private caches lead to the possibility
of cache incoherence. The current mainstream solution is to provide shared memory and to prevent incoherence using a hardware
cache coherence protocol, making caches functionally invisible to
software. The sidebar (Figure 1) reviews the incoherence problem
and the basic hardware coherence solution.
Cache-coherent shared memory is provided by mainstream
servers, desktops, laptops, and even mobile devices, and it is
available from all major vendors, including Intel, AMD, ARM,
IBM, and Oracle (Sun). Cache coherence has come to dominate
the market for both technical and legacy reasons. Technically,
hardware cache coherence provides performance that is generally
superior to that achievable with software-implemented coherence.
Cache coherence’s legacy advantage is that it provides backward
compatibility for a long history of software, including operating
systems, that is written for cache-coherent shared memory systems.
Although coherence provides value in today’s multicore systems,
the conventional wisdom is that on-chip cache coherence will not
scale to the large number of cores expected to be found on future
processor chips [5, 10, 13]. Coherence’s alleged lack of scalability
is believed to be due to the poor scaling of the storage and traffic on the interconnection network that coherence requires, as well
as concerns about latency and energy. Such arguments against coherence lead those authors to conclude that cores in future multicore chips will not employ coherence, but instead will communicate with software-managed coherence, loads/stores of scratchpad
memories, or message passing (without shared memory).
Daniel J. Sorin
This paper seeks to refute this conventional wisdom by presenting one way to scale on-chip cache coherence in which coherence
overheads (i.e., traffic, storage, latency, and energy) (a) grow slowly
with core count and (b) are similar to the overheads deemed acceptable in today’s systems. To do this, we synergistically combine known techniques such as: shared caches augmented to track
cached copies, explicit cache eviction notifications, and hierarchical design. Using amortized analysis, we show that interconnection
network traffic per miss need not grow with core count and that coherence uses at most 20% more traffic per miss than a system with
caches but not coherence. Using hierarchical design, we show that
storage overhead can be made to grow as the root of core count
and stay small, e.g., 2% of total cache size for even 512 cores. We
find negligible energy overhead and zero latency penalty for cache
misses to data that are not actively shared, and our analysis suggests the relative miss penalty and energy overheads of accessing
shared data do not increase appreciably with increasing core count.
Consequently, we predict that on-chip coherence is here to stay.
Computer systems tend not to abandon compatibility to eliminate
small costs, such as the costs we find for scaling coherence. In particular, systems will not likely wish to replace conventional operating systems now that they have been shown to scale using cache
coherence [2, 3]. Boyd-Wickizer et al. [2] concur: “there is no
scalability reason to give up on traditional operating system organizations just yet.”
Some might object to retaining coherence, because many applications do not yet scale well with coherence. True, but is the root
cause the algorithm, program implementation, or coherence? If, for
example, frequent updates must be communicated to many readers,
coherence and most alternatives will do poorly. At least with hardware coherence, programmers can concentrate on choreographing
independent work rather than handling low-level mechanics.
Our claim for the continued viability of on-chip cache coherence
does not imply that other communication paradigms will disappear.
There will continue to be applications for which message passing
is appropriate (e.g., scale out high performance computing) or for
which incoherent scratchpad memories are appropriate (e.g., realtime systems), and we believe those communication paradigms will
persist. However, we predict that they are likely to continue to
coexist with on-chip cache-coherent shared memory.
2.
Cache Coherence Today
To understand the issues involved in coherence’s future, we must
first understand today’s cache coherence protocols. Rather than
provide a survey of the coherence protocol design space, we instead
focus on describing one concrete coherence protocol loosely based
upon the on-chip cache coherence protocol used by Intel’s Core
i7 [17]. This system represents the state-of-the-art and can already

Sidebar: The Problem of Incoherence
Incoherence. To illustrate the incoherence problem, consider the multiple cores and corresponding private caches in the upper-right of the
diagram below. If core 1 writes the block labeled B by updating its private cache only, subsequent reads by core 2 would see the old value
indefinitely. This incoherence can lead to incorrect behavior. For example, if the block holds a synchronization variable for implementing
mutual exclusion using a lock, such incoherent behavior could allow multiple cores into a critical section or prevent cores waiting for the
release of the lock from making forward progress.
The coherence invariant. The mainstream solution to preventing incoherence is a hardware cache coherence protocol. Although there are
many possible coherence protocols, they all maintain coherence by ensuring the single-writer, multiple-reader (SWMR) invariant. That is,
for a given block, at any given moment in time, there is either:
• only a single core with write (and read) permission to the block (in state M for modified) or
• zero or more cores with read permission to the block (in state S for shared).
Enforcing coherence. The diagram below illustrates core 0 caching block A with read/write permission (state M) and cores 1 and 2
caching block B with read-only permission (state S). A write to block B by core 1 (which, in our example above, led to incoherence) is
not allowed to update its read-only copy of the block. Instead, core 1 must first obtain write permission to the block. Obtaining write
permission without violating the single-writer, multiple-reader invariant requires invalidating any copies of the block in other caches (core
2 in this case, as encoded by the tracking bits in the shared cache). Such actions are handled in hardware by cache coherence logic that is
integrated into the cache controllers. Section 2 presents a current protocol (and describes the rest of the diagram). For more background,
see Sorin et al. [18].

scale to a moderate number of cores (e.g., 16). In such a system, the
cores on the chip communicate via loads and stores to the shared
memory. Each core has its own private cache hierarchy (referred to
hereafter simply as “private cache”). There is a single, shared lastlevel cache (referred to hereafter as “shared cache”). Such shared
caches typically employ address-interleaved banking with one bank
per core, thus proportionally scaling the bandwidth of the shared
cache as the number of cores increases. Figure 1 illustrates this
system model.
To make our analysis simpler and more concrete, we assume
for now that the shared cache is inclusive with respect to all of
the private caches. Inclusion means that, at all times, the shared
cache contains a superset of the blocks in the private caches. Intel’s
Core i7 is one example of a chip with inclusive caches. Because
inclusion is not a universally adopted design decision, we discuss
extending our results to non-inclusive shared caches in Section 9.
With inclusion, cache coherence can be maintained with a coherence protocol that tracks copies of blocks in private caches using
state that is embedded in the shared cache. That is, each block in the
shared cache is augmented with a few bits of coherence state (e.g.,
to denote if the block is writable by any core) and per-core tracking
bits that denote which cores are privately caching the block (one bit
per core). As depicted in Figure 1, inclusion requires that block A

(cached by core 0) and block B (cached by cores 1 and 2) must be
present in the shared cache with appropriate tracking bits ({1000}
and {0110}, respectively. If the block size of the shared cache is
larger than the private cache’s block size, each entry in the shared
cache maintains coherence state and tracking bits at the granularity
of the private cache block size.
When a core issues a load or store that misses in its private cache,
it issues a coherence request message to the shared cache. Based on
the block’s coherence state and the block’s per-core tracking bits,
the shared cache either responds directly or forwards the request
to the one or more cores that need to respond to the request. For
example, if the request is for read/write access and one or more
cores are privately caching the block in a read-only state, then the
shared cache forwards the request to all private caches in the tracking list and these private caches all invalidate their copies of the
block. If no cores are caching the block, then a request has the negligible overhead of only looking up the coherence state bits in the
shared cache. This protocol is essentially a simple directory protocol in which the directory entries are co-located with the tags of
the shared cache. Inclusion ensures that each private block has a
corresponding shared block to hold its coherence tracking bits.
To maintain inclusion, when the shared cache wishes to evict a
block for which some per-core tracking bits are set, then the shared

=====PAGE 3
cache issues a recall request (also known as a back-invalidation
or notification) to any core that is currently caching that block (as
determined by the per-core tracking state). Upon receipt of a recall
message, the private cache is forced to evict the block.
This approach to coherence has many attractive features, which
helps to explain why current Intel systems resemble it. This protocol avoids the need for a snooping bus and it avoids broadcasting; communication involves only point-to-point messages. Because it embeds the per-core tracking bits in the shared cache, it
avoids adding additional structures dedicated solely to coherence.
For small-scale systems (e.g., 4-16 cores), the storage cost is negligible (a 16-core system adds just 16 bits for each 64-byte cache
block in the shared cache, or approximately 3% more bits). For a
miss to a block not cached by other private caches, the miss latency
and energy consumed incur the negligible overhead of checking a
couple of state bits in the shared cache rather than just a single valid
bit. As we show later, even when blocks are shared, the traffic per
miss is small and independent of the number of cores. Overall, this
approach is reasonably low-cost in terms of traffic, storage, latency,
and energy, and its design complexity is tractable. Nevertheless,
the question is: does this system model scale to future many-core
chips?
3.
Scalability Concerns
Some prognosticators forecast that the era of cache coherence
is nearing its end [5, 10, 13], primarily due to an alleged lack of
scalability. However, when we examined state-of-the-art coherence
mechanisms, we found them to be more scalable than one might
expect.
We consider a coherent system to be “scalable” when the cost
of providing coherence grows (at most) slowly as core count increases. We focus exclusively on the cache coherence aspects of
multicore scaling, whereas a fully scalable system (coherent or otherwise) also requires scalability from other hardware (e.g., memory
and interconnect) and software (operating system and applications)
components.
This paper examines five potential concerns raised when scaling
on-chip coherence:
1. traffic on the on-chip interconnection network,
2. storage cost for tracking sharers,
3. inefficiencies caused by maintaining inclusion (as inclusion
is assumed by our base system),
4. latency of cache misses, and
5. energy overheads.
The next five sections address these concerns in sequence
and present our analysis which indicates that existing design
approaches can be employed such that none of these concerns
present a fundamental barrier to scaling coherence. After this
analysis, we discuss extending the analysis to non-inclusive caches
and address some caveats and potential criticisms of this work.
4.
Concern #1: Traffic
We now tackle the concerns regarding the scalability of coherence’s traffic on the on-chip interconnection network. To perform
a traffic analysis, we consider for each cache miss how many bytes
need to be transferred to obtain and relinquish the given block.
We divide the analysis into two parts: in the absence of sharing
and then with sharing. This analysis shows that when sharers are
tracked precisely, the traffic per miss is independent of the number
of cores. Thus, if coherence’s traffic is acceptable for today’s systems with small numbers of cores, it will continue to be acceptable
as we scale up the number of cores. We conclude this section with
a discussion of how coherence’s per-miss traffic compares to that
of a system without coherence.
4.1
Without Sharing
We first analyze the worst-case traffic in the absence of sharing.
Each miss in a private cache requires at least two messages: (1)
a request from the private cache to the shared cache and (2) a response from the shared cache to provide the data to the requestor.
If the block is written during the time it is in the cache, the block is
dirty and must be explicitly written back to the shared cache upon
eviction.
Even without sharing, the traffic depends on the specific coherence protocol implementation. In particular, we consider protocols
that require a private cache to send an explicit eviction notification
message to the shared cache whenever it evicts a block, even when
evicting a clean block. (This decision to require explicit eviction
notifications benefits the implementation of inclusive caching, as
discussed in Section 6.) We also conservatively assume that coherence requires the shared cache to send an acknowledgment message in response to each eviction notification. Fortunately, clean
eviction messages are small (say, enough to hold a 64-bit address)
and can only occur subsequent to cache misses (which transfer, say,
a 512-bit cache block). Thus coherence’s additional traffic per miss
is modest (we will compare it to a system without coherence later
in this section) and, most importantly, independent of the number
of cores. Based on 64-byte cache blocks, Table 1 shows that coherence’s traffic is 96 bytes/miss for clean blocks and 160 bytes/miss
for dirty blocks.
4.2
With Sharing
In a coherent system, when a core reads a block that is shared,
the coherence protocol may need to forward the request, but to at
most one core (and thus the traffic for each read miss is independent
of the number of cores). However, when a core incurs a write miss
to a block that is cached by one or more other cores, the coherence
protocol generates extra messages to invalidate the block from the
other cores. These invalidation messages are often used to argue
for the non-scalability of cache coherence, because when all cores
are sharing a block, a coherent system must send an invalidation
message to all other cores. However, our analysis shows that when
sharers are tracked exactly, the overall traffic per miss of cache
coherence is independent of the number of cores (the storage cost
of exact tracking is addressed in Section 5).
Consider the access pattern in which a block is read by all cores
and then written by one core. The writer core will indeed be forced
to send an invalidation message to all cores, and each core will
respond with an acknowledgment message (i.e., a cost of 2N messages for N sharers). However, such an expensive write operation
can occur only after a read miss by each of those cores. More generally, for every write that invalidates N caches, it must have been
preceded by N read misses. The traffic cost of a read miss is independent of the number of cores (a read miss is forwarded to a single
core at most). Thus, by amortized analysis, the overall average traffic per miss is constant. (A write miss that causes N messages can
occur at most once every Nth miss).
In support of this general analysis, Figure 2(b) shows the traffic
(in average bytes per miss) over a range of core counts for an access pattern parameterized by the number of read misses to a block
between each write miss to the block. A workload consisting of
all write misses (zero read misses per write miss; far left of the
graph) has the highest traffic per miss because all blocks are dirty.
The traffic per miss is independent of the number of cores because
