1. INTRODUCTION           TO THE INTEL 432
The Intel 432 was conceived in 1975 with several goals in mind. The primary
objective was to produce a system that would improve the software programming
environment, thereby lowering system life cycle cost. To achieve this goal, the
432 incorporates architectural run-time support for both data abstraction (pro-
gramming with abstract data types) and domain-based operating systems. The
principal insight of the 432 architecture is that both objectives can be supported
by a common semantic model, known as the abject model [22, 271.
   Another goal, finding a design approach that would yield a range of performance
from a single implementation,    led to the concept of transparent multiprocessing.
By using the object model the 432 system is able to run with a variable number
of physical processors without recompiling the software. Supporting so many
different concepts for the first time in a new machine inevitably led to a complex
architecture. Moreover, initial measurements of the 432’s performance. were quite
discouraging. Subsequent architectural enhancements improved execution speed,
but not enough to satisfy either its champions or its critics. It is therefore
appropriate to examine the design of the 432 and to investigate the factors that
underlie its performance.

1 .l System Architecture
The Intel 432 is notable as an “object-oriented” or “object-based”l architecture.
Just as the Smalltalk language [12] encapsulates all data into objects that can be
manipulated in carefully constrained ways, the 432 imposes similar restrictions
on all online storage:
-All information     is encapsulated into protected sets called objects (instruction
   segments, data structures, processes, messages).
-Every    memory reference, whether an instruction fetch or operand access, is
   checked for read/write privilege and base/bounds validity.
-Pointers    to objects are protected. These pointers are not directly manipulated
   by the user program, but only by trusted hardware and microcode on behalf of
   the user.
The Intel 432 is also a shared-memory multiprocessor [l, 2, 17,18, 191. Figure 1
shows a simplified block-diagram     configuration. (More elaborate 432 system
architectures can readily be constructed for improved reliability or availability
WI.)
   The GDPs in Figure 1 perform essentially the same role as do the CPUs in
more conventional systems. The main differences are that the GDPs perform no
I/O (the IPs do that) and the GDPs are self-dispatching via routines provided in
their on-chip microcode.
   The 432 instruction set is notable for several reasons.
-Its   instruction set is bit-aligned         and encoded so that programs                will be as
    compact as possible.

’ The designers of the 432 referred to their system as “object-oriented,” hut more recently the term
“object-oriented” has become understood to mean that a language or system supports inheritance
1341.

1.2 Functional Migration in the 432
There are several types of functional migration present in the 432 architecture.
The first type could be classified as “object” related; for example, the base/length

and

This was expected to yield more compact and faster-executing code. For every
supported operation in the instruction set, all machine-defined data types are
supported (char, integer, short integer, ordinal, short ordinal, real, short real,
temporary real) in the expectation that this simplifies the compiler writer’s task.
Machines such as the VAX and the S-l have traditionally offered the same
justification for having complete and symmetric instruction sets, but substantial
doubt exists as to the overall importance of this design principle in light of the
current predominance of high-level language usage over assembly language [7,
391 and the prospects for automatic generation of compilers [24]. Since the HLL
users never see the machine’s native instruction set, one of the important
motivations for completeness is removed.
 A third type of function migrated in the 432 deals with applications. The 432
GDP implements the IEEE standard 754 for both single- and double-precision
floating-point formats.
 A fourth type of migrated function comes from operating systems. The 432
subsumes operations such as interprocess communications, process scheduling,
processor dispatching, virtual memory management, and I/O into its architecture.
Except for I/O, other machines almost always perform these operations in
software. The 432’s Interface Processor transacts all I/O, allowing the GDPs to
exist in an environment where there are only objects. To do this the IP performs
whatever conversions are necessary between that environment and the real world
of bytes, disks, and networks.
 The 432 hardware, microcode, and OS software together implement a distrib-
uted fault handler that handles faults arising from any source, hardware faults,
applications code run-time errors, explicit exceptions raised at the source code
level, or memory management faults. Such a unified fault model contrasts sharply
with the ad hoc, localized approaches found on machines such as the VAX, where
run-time errors may be caught by the run-time system, the hardware, the memory
management unit, or the operating system, each handling the fault in its own
way. Microcode devoted to fault handling constitutes another kind of functional
migration.

into performance. We do not assume here that any and all aspects of system
architecture or implementation are fair candidates for alteration or disposal as
long as overall system throughput on the benchmarks appears to be higher. Here

Measurements of a real computer system must be made under some processing
load. The art of benchmarking has evolved to provide programs that, taken as a
whole, are thought to be representative of the processing load seen by the machine
in actual use. Benchmarking is still an art, however. Little agreement exists on
how to even characterize typical processing loads, much less to create benchmarks
that accurately represent these loads. Even representative small-scale processes
do not capture or duplicate such important systems-level conditions as process
swap overhead and I/O interrupts. For systems with caches, small benchmarks
may fit entirely within the cache, exaggerating the performance benefits of such
caches [35].

by operating system code. Since there is wide variability in the use of OS
functions, it can be very difficult to characterize that load, but it is often estimated

typically dedicated to the operating system. Processing loads of that magnitude
cannot be ignored.

of great value in architectural design. If the benchmarks are constrained
to be implemented in a single language, and for a single architecture that is

argued to be representative and meaningful because those operations constitute
the bulk of a processor’s instruction executions.

3.1 Protected Pointers
The arcs in Figure 2 represent protected pointers. The concept of a protected
pointer is intrinsic to an object-based computer architectum3 A pointer is
“protected” in that the user program cannot manipulate it directly (as one could
in the C language; e.g., int *ptr; ptr++. The underlying architecture, often
microcode, manipulates these pointers on behalf of the user program according
to a set of rigid constraints, By structuring object accesses around this system-
controlled pointer mechanism, it becomes possible to perform rights checks,
operation type checks, and other system functions at the time when they are
needed and only on those objects that are immediately affected.
 Object-based machines must take special care that these pointers cannot be
forged, for the object addressing mechanism will be relied upon completely and
implicitly in ensuring system integrity. The 432, for example, does not even have
a machine instruction for creating a protected pointer; this operation is performed
by microcode. This is in sharp distinction to conventional architectures, where
user programs perform both address and data calculations on the same hardware
(registers and ALU). Barring microcode bugs in the 432 GDP, an errant user
program can crash itself but cannot bring down the 432’s operating system.

the pointers from data. Other systems, including the IBM Sys/38 and the Intel
432, permit these pointers (called “capabilities” in these systems) to reside in the
same address space as the data. They are distinguished from data via additional
information contained in object headers. A capability is a protected pointer that
has associated with it information on the range of operations that capability
possessesfor the object being referenced.

ramifications on the design of the underlying structure of the architecture. A
conventional architecture usually associates access rights with physical pages of
memory (for example, placing the object code for system utilities into pages
marked as “execute-only”). Capabilities provide a means to separate program-
level concerns, such as modules and data structures, from irrelevant details such
as physical memory sizes, paging characteristics, and disk structures. Advocates
of the object-based programming style cite this separation of concerns as essential
to improving the match between the programmer’s desired abstractions and the
machine on which his or her program must execute. However, the cost of memory

overhead is, and to what extent that overhead can be removed by architectural
support and other means.
3.2 The lntrinsics of 432 Object Orientation
The performance effects of the 432’s object orientation are manifested in three
major ways. First, procedure calls and returns are slowed substantially by the
increased amount of information that must be dealt with in an object-based
environment. Some of this information describes the types and access rights of
various objects, and some represents addressability information on those objects
needed immediately by the called procedure. Second, addressable domains (e.g.,
objects and procedures) must be made accessible via explicit enter operations.
This operation, or sequences of them, are needed when executing intermodule
calls or when traversing pointer chains. Third, every memory reference is checked
for read/write privileges on the object being accessed, and every reference is
checked to ensure that it lies within the physical boundaries of the object.

address of a datum or called procedure is correct unless the underlying memory
management mechanism indicates otherwise. This approach minimizes run-time
checks at the risk of yielding unauthorized or faulty accessto routines or data by
possibly malicious users. By contrast, the context in which a capability-based,
object-oriented procedure executes is such that it is not even possible to access
objects that have not been explicitly made available-a “need-to-know” arrange-
ment. This strategy aims to contain system damage from faulty or malicious
operations, and provides a closer semantic match to the programmer’s abstract
model of the processor. Since the object-based approach requires that all entities

here; interested readers are referred to [8, 17, 25, 261. Basically, a two-level
addressing scheme allows information such as the location, size, and type of an
object to be stored and manipulated independently of the rights various programs
have to those objects. Contrast this with the inflexible protection and sharing
available on standard architectures, which base their access checks on page tables
or other artifacts.

begins with two pieces of information: an Access Descriptor (AD) selector, which

name that Intel uses for “capability.“) The AD selector consists of an environment

base of that object is found by using the Directory and Segment fields of the AD

a great deal of information about the current state of the processing environment.

an object-table cache (the placement of these caches is shown in Figure 4), and
the rest are dedicated to holding information on various system object segments.
The caches are searched associatively and their contents managed according to
a least-recently used replacement algorithm.

3.6 Procedure Calls
Procedure calls and returns are potentially expensive operations in object-based
systems like the 432, due to the large amount of state information associated
with each context. On a conventional architecture, the graph structure of a
program’s call patterns and data structure accesses is represented in the form of
virtual addresses embedded in the object code. In object-based systems-at least
for intermodule calls-this graph information is explicitly preserved in the form
of capabilities for objects such as instruction segments, data structures, and
messages. These capabilities must be manipulated by machine instructions.
 The 432’s procedure calls are quite costly. A typical procedure call requires 16
read accesses to memory and 24 write accesses, and it consumes 982 machine
cycles. In terms of machine cycles, this makes it about ten times as slow as a call
on the MC68010 or VAX 11/780. The reasons for this complexity are discussed
in [lo]; object orientation is shown to be only a minor factor. Space does not
permit a recapitulation of the analysis here.

hope to run within a factor of two or three of conventional systems. The 432
represents a specific point in the design/implementation space, incorporating a
certain set of design decisions. What we have shown here implies that a designer
who builds in an equivalent set of decisions about object orientation into a new
machine will incur an overhead in performance that is similar. By approaching
object orientation in a different way, but still without discarding the flexibility
of capability-based protection, even greater improvements should be possible.
For example we have argued elsewhere [lo] that more radical changes to the
432’s procedure-call mechanism could bring it up to a speed that compares
favorably, by most measures, to that of the VAX or MC68010.
7. CONCLUSIONS
The 432 was unique among microprocessors in the degree to which it incorporated
architectural innovations. Perhaps due to the initial barrage of publicity and the
consequent high expectations, the disappointing reality of the 432’s performance
made it the favorite target for whatever point a researcher wanted to make [14,
16, 29, 331. Through a detailed case study, this paper has shown that many of
the RISC criticisms of the CISC design style find apt targets in the Intel 432.
However, we have also argued that, in several cases, published RISC work does
not indicate what the 432 should have done.
 This paper has shown that the 432 loses some 25-35 percent of its potential
throughput due to the poor quality of code emitted by its Ada compiler. Another
5-10 percent is lost to implementation inefficiencies such as the 432’s lack of
instruction stream literals and its instruction stream bit-alignment. These losses
are substantial, and essentially unrelated to instruction set complexity or object
orientation. As such they constitute a stark warning to all computer architects
about the magnitude of losses that can appear in any implementation unless
close control over every aspect of the design is maintained.
 Having established what the 432 should have done differently, we proceeded
to investigate what it could have done had its implementation technology been
incrementally better. We found that a combination of plausible modifications to
the 432, such as wider buses and provision for local data registers, increased
performance by another 35-45 percent.
 This left the 432 executing the benchmark programs used throughout this
paper from one to four times slower than conventional processors (where “one
times slower” means approximately equal in performance). We called this ratio
the inherent cost of the 432’s style of object orientation, but cautioned that other
approaches to object-based architecture are possible.
 There is no doubt that as a commercial venture whose purpose was to earn
profits for its manufacturer, the 432 failed completely. But it is more enlightening
to view it as a research effort that happened to be funded by an IC manufacturer.
The 432 probably tried to do too many new things all at once (while getting a
few old things wrong along the way) to succeed commercially. The market it was
targeted for, high reliability/high availability/large software-systems develop-
ment, may still not be large enough or defined well enough to economically
support the introduction of special systems.

wide interest, but interest has lately been dulled somewhat by a fear that the

I checked every cited claim in the P10 record and wrote the check to `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P10.citations.md`. Most claims hold: 116 rows are found, 8 differ and 2 are not found. Every numeric value the record attributes to a page matches the text at that page. The problems are one cost figure where the paper contradicts itself, one claim the paper never makes, and the inherent-cost ratios: those are quoted correctly, but the paper's figures disagree in ways the record doesn't fully explain.

I read all 44 pages of `research/papers/P10.pdf`, page by page; each page header confirms journal page = PDF page + 295. I checked the bibliographic details against the Crossref record for the DOI, since the scan has none. The file follows the citations template, grouped by the record's sections.

**What doesn't hold:**
1. **Refinement traversal cost (Message mechanism).** The record says the called context traverses the refinement at "148 cycles" and cites p. 307. But p. 307 says "approximately 77 clock cycles". 148 appears on p. 322 (as the cost of a cache miss on a refinement), p. 323 (footnote 7) and p. 326. The record doesn't flag the conflict.
2. **The Cox et al. [6] reference.** Q2 and Message mechanism say the paper defers the Send/port mechanism to Cox et al. [6]. The paper never cites [6] in its body; it appears only in the reference list (p. 338). The link comes from [6]'s title, not from the paper.
3. **"35–45 % of cycles wasted" (p. 330).** The quote is accurate, but the table it summarises (Table XVI, p. 329) gives 2.2 %, 14.9 %, 39.6–44.7 % and 93.7 %. Only the CFA benchmarks fall near 35–45 %. The record repeats the figure in Contribution (2) and cause (g), and its list of the paper's inconsistencies leaves it out.
4. **Inherent-cost ratio.** All four phrasings are quoted correctly at their pages. But the abstract's "one-fourth to one times the speed" (p. 296) means the same as "one to four times slower" (p. 337). The real split is by scope: 1–4x covers all benchmarks (p. 337), while 3–4x and 2–3x are Dhrystone only (p. 336). The record's Notes line presents them as four conflicting values.
5. **Smaller wording problems:**
   - The paper never says the procedure call is "synchronous".
   - It never says George Cox was a designer; that is inferred from his co-authorship of refs [6] and [30].
   - Publicity is given, hedged with "Perhaps", as the reason the 432 drew criticism, not as a cause of its commercial failure (Fate and Adoption factors). The two stated causes are trying too many new things at once and the market.
   - "Rough" appears on p. 336, not p. 309.
   - Ref [5] is cited on pp. 304, 325 and 328, not p. 309.
   - The abstract contains no percentages (Q6).

**Values confirmed:**
- **Speed ratios (p. 309):** "10x / 26x / 2–23x" matches the text. Table IV doesn't reproduce these ratios from a single row (Release 2 Search is 25x the VAX).
- **Table values:** Table VI, XVI and XXII values and the Weicker ranges all match.
- **Single figures:** 982, 850 / 430 / 144, 77 / 148, 31 % and 20.5 % all match.
- **Other inconsistencies:** the two already in the record's Notes are confirmed ("30–40 %" against Table XVI, and the duplicated Sieve value in Table XXI).
- **More inconsistencies, not in the record:** Table VIII gives CFA5's original total as 32,168,445 against 34,916,445 in Table VI. The "baseline total of 60,502" on p. 315 is actually the post-fix figure from Table VIII.

I could not re-check the Internet Archive / ACM DL access history in the Source note.

**Decisions for you:**

1. **Refinement cost (77 vs 148)** in `P10.md`:
   - A (recommended): in Message mechanism, replace "(148 cycles)" with "(about 77 cycles per p. 307; 148 per pp. 322–323, 326)", and add a bullet to "Internal inconsistencies found".
   - B: keep 148 and change that field's pages to "p. 297–298, 306–307, 322–323, 326, 338", with no Notes entry.
   - C: leave it as is.

2. **The Cox [6] claim** in `P10.md`:
   - A (recommended): in Q2 change "(p. 298; deferred to Cox et al. [6], p. 338)" to "(p. 298); the paper cites no source for it in the text, though ref [6] in the list covers it (p. 338)". In Message mechanism change "(refers to Cox et al. [6])" to "(not described; ref [6] in the reference list, p. 338, is the likely source)".
   - B: delete the [6] mentions from Q2 and Message mechanism and keep [6] only under "Related work to snowball".

3. **The 35–45 % figure** in `P10.md`:
   - A (recommended): in Contribution (2) write "35–45 % (the paper's summary, p. 330; Table XVI ranges 2.2–93.7 %, CFA 39.6–44.7 %, p. 329)", and add the mismatch to the Notes inconsistencies and to Q6.
   - B: add it to Notes only.
   - C: leave it as is.

4. **The inherent-cost Notes line:**
   - A (recommended): rewrite it as "1–4x over all benchmarks (p. 337; the abstract's 'one-fourth to one times the speed', p. 296, is the same range) vs Dhrystone-only 3–4x before and 2–3x after the technology allowance (p. 336)".
   - B: keep it as is.

5. **Minor wording fixes** in `P10.md`:
   - A (recommended): apply all of these.
     - Drop "synchronous" from Message mechanism, or mark it "implied by call/return".
     - Change "(George Cox, private communication, i.e. a designer)" to "(George Cox, private communication; co-author of 432 design papers [6], [30])".
     - Remove "high expectations after initial publicity made its performance disappointing" from Fate's reasons and "expectations raised by publicity" from Adoption factors, or tag each "(given as why it drew criticism, p. 337)".
     - Correctness: cite "rough" at p. 336 only.
     - Context: cite [5] at "p. 304, 325, 328, 338".
     - Q6: change "The abstract's speedup and conclusion percentages" to "The conclusions' percentages".
   - B: leave them as they are.

6. **The extra inconsistencies** (Table VIII vs Table VI for CFA5; "baseline total 60,502" on p. 315; the p. 309 ratios vs Table IV):
   - A: add them as three bullets to "Internal inconsistencies found".
   - B (recommended): leave them out. They don't touch any value the record relies on, except the 20.5 % figure, whose denominator is already noted in the check file.

23:- **Clarity:** Clear. There is one "Concern" section per scalability worry, and each ends with a boxed conclusion (pp. 3–8). There is a dedicated caveats section (pp. 8–9). One numeric inconsistency: the abstract says storage is "2% of total cache size for even 512 cores" (p. 1). The summary says 5% with two cache levels or 2% with three (p. 8). The abstract does not say that the 2% figure needs three levels.
30:| Q3 | partly | Almost all evidence is analytical. The only executed artefact is a recall simulation on a synthetic random miss stream (p. 7). There is no silicon, FPGA or real-program run (p. 8). |
33:| Q6 | yes | Each number in the abstract and conclusions appears in the body. 20% traffic: Table 1 (p. 4). √C storage and 2% at 512 cores: Fig. 4 (p. 6). Zero latency for non-shared misses: p. 7. 2–9% non-inclusive overhead: p. 8. |
43:| System | (a) The authors' proof-of-concept protocol: a hierarchy of inclusive caches with embedded tracking bits and explicit eviction notifications. Status: design only, analytical model plus one simulation. Built by the authors, 2011–2012. (b) Its base protocol is "loosely based upon" Intel Core i7 (Nehalem): silicon, deployed commercially. (c) Also discussed: SGI Origin 2000 (silicon, commercial), Sun/Oracle UltraSPARC T2, NVIDIA Fermi, AMD Bulldozer and AMD HT-Assist (silicon). | p. 1, p. 2, pp. 5–6, p. 8 |
44:| Levels with message semantics | Instruction set: no. Cores "communicate via loads and stores to a shared address space". Hardware (cache controllers): yes for coherence actions only. A private-cache miss "issues a coherence request message"; the shared cache forwards, invalidates or sends recall messages; "communication involves only point-to-point messages". Cache hits change state with no message. Microcode, kernel, runtime, language: not stated. Message-based start later extended: not stated. | p. 1, p. 2, p. 3 |

18:- **Context:** Builds on earlier real-world bug studies, mainly of C, C++ and Java (Lu et al. ASPLOS '08 [45], TaxDC [40], Node.js [57]), and on deadlock and race detection work (P9, pp. 5, 12). It sets out to test Go's claim that "explicit message passing is less error-prone" than shared memory (P9, p. 2). It cites earlier static checkers for Go channels (Lange et al. [38, 39], Ng and Yoshida [49]) (P9, p. 12).
27:| Q2 | partly | The channel mechanism is described for the studied programs. It covers naming (the channel value), behaviour when the receiver is busy (unbuffered channels block, buffered channels block only when full) and ordering in `select` (random choice). Message format is not described (P9, p. 3). |
29:| Q4 | partly | The defect comparisons name their baseline. Shared-memory bugs are the baseline in the same applications, and gRPC-C is the baseline for goroutine use (P9, pp. 4, 6). The fix and detector results give no baseline (P9, pp. 8, 11). |
44:| Message mechanism | Channels (`chan`). Unbuffered: send or receive blocks until the other side acts (synchronous). Buffered: send blocks only when the buffer is full. The receiver is named by the channel value. `select` waits on several channel operations and picks at random when more than one is ready. Rules: a nil channel blocks forever; sending to a closed channel, or closing a channel twice, panics at run time. `context`, `Pipe` and the `time` library are other forms of message passing. | p. 3 |
52:| Attributed causes | Not applicable for performance. Related cause, stated by third parties (the authors, not Go's designers): the built-in deadlock detector's limits are "largely due to the design goal of the built-in detector—minimal runtime overhead". This is inherent to detecting deadlocks in the scheduler. No measurement isolates it. | pp. 8–9 |
53:| Fate and reasons | Not applicable: no system is evaluated for fate. Go was the 9th most popular language on GitHub in 2017, with 187K repositories. | p. 3 |
73:| New: channel usage rules | The rules Go enforces on its channels: no use before initialization, no double close, no send on a closed channel, and every send or receive needs a matching partner. Breaking these rules is "one major reason" for concurrency bugs. | pp. 3, 12 |

lines: - **Context:** It answers predictions that on-chip coherence will not scale and will give way to software-managed coherence, scratchpads or message passing without shared memory. It cites DeNovo [5], Intel's 48-core message-passing processor [10] and Cohesion [13] (p. 1, p. 3). It builds on directory protocols [1, 8], the SGI Origin 2000 [14], Intel Core i7 [17], AMD HT-Assist [6] and Linux scalability studies [2, 3] (p. 1, pp. 4–6).

- **Correctness:** Some assumptions are stated: coherence does not change the number of misses, though false sharing and poor synchronization may change it (p. 4). Others are stated too: an inclusive shared cache (p. 2), a single chip (p. 9), and no queuing or contention modelled (p. 8). Some are left implicit: the cost model counts bytes per miss and ignores how invalidation bursts are spread over time, and the energy analysis is inferred from the traffic and storage results, not modelled (pp. 7–8).

- **Contributions:** (1) An amortized argument that traffic per miss does not depend on core count when sharers are tracked exactly (p. 3, Fig. 2b p. 4). (2) Coherence traffic is at most 20% above a cache system without coherence (Table 1, p. 4). (3) With a hierarchy of inclusive caches, storage grows as √C (two levels) or ∛C (three levels) (p. 6, Fig. 4). (4) With explicit eviction notifications, recalls are rare: below 0.1% at a 4× capacity ratio with 8 ways (p. 7, Fig. 5). (5) Latency and energy arguments (pp. 7–8). (6) An extension to non-inclusive caches (p. 8).

-- **Clarity:** Clear. There is one "Concern" section per scalability worry, and each ends with a boxed conclusion (pp. 3–8). There is a dedicated caveats section (pp. 8–9). One numeric inconsistency: the abstract says storage is "2% of total cache size for even 512 cores" (p. 1). The summary says 5% with two cache levels or 2% with three (p. 8). The abstract does not say that the 2% figure needs three levels.

lines: | Attributed causes | (a) "Most programmers think sequentially" and assume small code regions run atomically, causing atomicity violations; (b) programmers assume an order between threads and forget to enforce it, causing order violations; (c) heavy workload raises the chance of hitting the bug-triggering order; (d) locks "cannot guarantee to enforce" happens-before intentions. All stated by the authors (third party to the applications), about defects not performance. The paper frames (a) as how programmers think, (b) as an omission by programmers, and (d) as a limit of locks and basic TM together ("cannot be easily enforced by the basic TM design or locks"); it calls none of them inherent. No measurement isolates any of them | p. 329, p. 333, p. 334, p. 336, p. 338 |
| Fate and reasons | Not applicable: no system | p. 329 |

| Concurrency defects | Population: 4 C/C++ multithreaded applications; about 500 keyword-matched reports screened, 105 bugs kept (74 non-deadlock, 31 deadlock; MySQL 14/9, Apache 13/4, Mozilla 41/16, OpenOffice 6/2). Categories: atomicity violation 51, order violation 24, other 2 of 74 non-deadlock (3 counted in both); deadlock 31, not subdivided; data race deliberately not a category. Manifestation: 101/105 need at most two threads; 49/74 non-deadlock involve one variable, 25/74 more than one; 30/31 deadlocks involve at most two resources; 7/31 deadlocks involve one thread; 97/105 manifest under an order among at most 4 accesses. Fixes: locks used for 20/74 non-deadlock fixes (COND 19, Switch 10, Design 19, Other 6); deadlocks fixed by giving up a resource 19/31. 17 of 57 Mozilla bugs had at least one buggy patch (23 buggy patches: 6 incomplete, 5 new concurrency bugs, 12 new non-concurrency bugs). Impact: 34 crashes, 37 hangs. Split by mechanism: none; no message-passing count; the paper never uses the term "shared memory" for its population. Prevention by construction: basic transactional memory could avoid 41/105, 44 more if long-region, rollback and code-nature concerns are addressed, and cannot help 20/105 because the violated intentions, "such as order intentions", cannot be guaranteed by basic TM; AtomicSet "can help avoid some multiple variable related" bugs (no count) | p. 331–338 |

-| What shapes programs | Language and synchronization primitives: order intentions "may not be easily expressed via synchronization primitives like locks and transactional memories" and "cannot be easily enforced by the basic TM design or locks"; some order bugs can still be fixed with coarser-grained locking or avoided by TM as a side effect; programmers think sequentially; programmers lack diagnosis tools (29 of 57 Mozilla reports mention no tool) and rely on reading code and reproducible test cases. Evidence: qualitative reading of bug reports, patches and discussions, with counts | p. 329, p. 333, p. 336, p. 338 |

lines: ## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and implementation description of a working processor chip (the MDP) and its multicomputer (the J-Machine), with cycle counts but no evaluation section (pp. 1–3, 13–18).

+- **Context:** Message-passing multicomputers (Cosmic Cube, iPSC, N-CUBE, Ametek), shared-address machines (BBN Butterfly, IBM RP3), single-chip nodes (Transputer, MOSAIC, iWARP); the authors' earlier MDP architecture paper [11] (p. 6) and k-ary n-cube network work [10, 12, 14] (pp. 2–3; [13] p. 12).

- **Correctness:** The premise is that sequential-processor mechanisms do not support synchronisation, communication and global naming efficiently, so these "must be implemented largely in software with prohibitive overhead" (p. 2). It is argued, and backed only by one comparison with iPSC message times (p. 2). The cycle counts are given as design facts, not as measurements (pp. 9–11).

- **Contributions:** A single-chip node in which message arrival creates and dispatches a task in hardware, with no receive instruction (p. 1). It adds SEND instructions, hardware message queues, presence tags (FUT/CFUT), name translation (XLATE/ENTER) and three priority register sets (pp. 5–9). The chip is running silicon (p. 16), and Concurrent Smalltalk and Id are implemented on it (pp. 20–23).

- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with worked assembly examples (combining tree, CALL handler, size-of-tree; pp. 5, 10–11, 22). In this preprint most figures are blank and only their captions remain (see Notes).

| Message mechanism | Buffering: a hardware-managed FIFO queue in on-chip RAM, one per priority (P0, P1), circular, located by the QBM/QHL registers. Buffer memory is allocated automatically on the receiver. Network blocking flow control compresses blocked messages into routers. Queue overflow behaviour is not stated. | pp. 2, 9, 13, 15 |

| Message mechanism | Busy receiver: the message waits in the queue until it reaches the head. A P1 message preempts a P0 task (separate register sets). The next message is dispatched 2 cycles after SUSPEND. | pp. 6, 9, 11 |

| Message mechanism | Dispatch: the header opcode is loaded into the IP and A3 is set to the message segment (3 cycles). Remote procedure call messages go to a CALL handler that translates the method ID with XLATE. In CST, COSMOS selects the function from a selector object by the receiver's class. | pp. 9–10, 20–21 |

Related mechanisms: all transports sit behind a common interface (p. 10), the protocol and transport are late-bound (p. 6), and the name service maps a name to a service reference (p. 10). These suggest a transport or service could be swapped without changing the sender or receiver, but the paper neither claims nor measures this. | pp. 6, 10 |

| Operating system functions | *Protection*: each core's CPU driver enforces protection and authorisation (p. 8), and capabilities are modelled on seL4 (p. 10). Coordination is involved: yes, because all cores must keep their capability lists consistent (p. 10). *Scheduling*: the CPU driver time-slices locally and runs dispatchers by upcalls, with user-level thread schedulers (pp. 8–9). Cross-core threads are handled by messages, and CPU drivers can be coordinated for gang scheduling (p. 11). Central component: not stated. *Memory*: virtual memory is managed at user level through capabilities (p. 10). Unmap uses a one-phase commit and retype a two-phase commit between all monitors (p. 11). That is coordination: yes. *Devices*: drivers are user-level processes (p. 8), placed on cores by the system knowledge base (p. 11). Whether the SKB is one instance: not stated. *Naming*: a name service (p. 10); centralisation not stated. *Failure*: none; "the complete system is a failure unit" (p. 17). *Costs of decentralising*: the capability scheme "was a mistake … unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient than scalable per-processor memory managers" (p. 10). Replica consistency adds latency and developer burden (p. 7). Two-phase commit "serializes more messages" than shootdown (p. 14). | pp. 7–11, 14, 17 |

Builds on the Berkeley 432 measurements of Hansen et al. [13] (p. 309), Colwell's CMU thesis [5] and Gehringer and Colwell's procedure-call paper [10] (p. 309, 338).

-- **Correctness:** Assumes that only incremental changes, checked with the 432's silicon architects, are fair (p. 300); that cycle savings measured per category from simulator logs can be combined after adjusting for overlap (p. 333); that cross-machine comparisons with different languages (Ada vs C/Pascal) and technologies are "rough" (p. 309, 336). The remaining 2–3x gap is attributed to object orientation as a residual, not measured directly (p. 336).

Return: about 850 cycles, of which about 430 restore three environments (144 per environment). Passing two integers in a recursive call: 148 cycles. DS-cache miss: 77 cycles (148 for a refinement). Enter-environment: 9 memory operations. Moving memory clearing to dedicated hardware would speed a call by about 31 %. Send (IPC) latency: not reported. lines: ## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Empirical study of real-world concurrency bugs: "the first systematic study on concurrency bugs in real Go programs", 171 bugs from six applications (P9, p. 1).

-- **Context:** Builds on earlier real-world bug studies, mainly of C, C++ and Java (Lu et al. ASPLOS '08 [45], TaxDC [40], Node.js [57]), and on deadlock and race detection work (P9, pp. 5, 12). It sets out to test Go's claim that "explicit message passing is less error-prone" than shared memory (P9, p. 2). It cites earlier static checkers for Go channels (Lange et al. [38, 39], Ng and Yoshida [49]) (P9, p. 12).

+- **Context:** Builds on earlier real-world bug studies, mainly of C, C++ and Java (Lu et al. ASPLOS '08 [45], TaxDC [40], Node.js [57]), and on deadlock and race detection work (P9, pp. 1, 5, 12). It sets out to test Go's claim that "explicit message passing is less error-prone" than shared memory (P9, p. 2). It cites earlier static checkers for Go channels (Lange et al. [38, 39], Ng and Yoshida [49]) (P9, p. 12).

- **Correctness:** The assumptions are mostly sound, but the sampling is under-reported. Bugs were found by searching commit logs for keywords (3211 matching commits), then randomly sampling those commits and studying them by hand (P9, p. 5). The paper does not say how many commits were sampled. It does not say who classified each bug, and it gives no agreement figure between classifiers. Only bugs that were fixed and well documented were kept (P9, p. 6). One claim, that message passing is "even more likely" to cause blocking bugs, divides bug counts by static counts of primitive use (Table 4). It does not measure how often each primitive is exercised at run time (P9, pp. 4, 6).

- **Contributions:** (1) The first empirical study of Go concurrency bugs, in six production applications. (2) Nine observations and eight implications about bug causes, fixes and detection. (3) A taxonomy along two orthogonal dimensions: behaviour (blocking or non-blocking) and cause (shared memory or message passing). Study data is published at github.com/system-pclub/go-concurrency-bugs (P9, p. 2).

- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised. Each section ends with numbered Observations and Implications, and counts are in Tables 5–12 (P9, pp. 5–11). The numbers in the tables match the numbers in the text.
| Q | Answer | Why |
| Q1 | yes | The aim and a three-item contribution list are stated in the introduction (P9, pp. 1–2). |

-| Q2 | partly | The channel mechanism is described for the studied programs. It covers naming (the channel value), behaviour when the receiver is busy (unbuffered channels block, buffered channels block only when full) and ordering in `select` (random choice). Message format is not described (P9, p. 3). |

+| Q2 | partly | The channel mechanism is described for the studied programs. It covers behaviour when the receiver is busy (unbuffered channels block, buffered channels block only when full) and ordering in `select` (random choice). Naming is not described. Message format is not described (P9, p. 3). |
| Q3 | yes | Defects come from the GitHub commit histories and linked bug reports of six real applications (P9, p. 5). |

-| Q4 | partly | The defect comparisons name their baseline. Shared-memory bugs are the baseline in the same applications, and gRPC-C is the baseline for goroutine use (P9, pp. 4, 6). The fix and detector results give no baseline (P9, pp. 8, 11). |

+| Q4 | partly | The defect comparisons name their baseline. Shared-memory bugs are the baseline in the same applications, and gRPC-C is the baseline for goroutine use (P9, pp. 4, 6). The fix results are compared only qualitatively with traditional deadlock fixes and an earlier C/C++ study (P9, pp. 8, 11); the detector results give no baseline (P9, pp. 8, 11). |

| Q5 | partly | The paper gives the programs and why they were chosen (P9, p. 3), and sample sizes and run counts (171 bugs; 41 reproduced; each race test run 100 times) (P9, pp. 5–6, 11). It gives no hardware configuration for the gRPC runs or the detector runs. |

| Q6 | yes | The abstract's 171 bugs are in Table 5 (P9, p. 5). Its "more than half … Go-specific" can be derived from Tables 6 and 9 (P9, pp. 6, 9), but the paper never adds it up. The conclusions' claims are in Tables 6 and 9 (P9, p. 12). |

| Q7 | no | Causes are asserted, not isolated. Examples: "we suspect Go's new programming model" (P9, p. 7); the detector failures are put down to design goals (P9, p. 9); "possible reasons" for the race detector's misses (P9, p. 12); "we suspect" that programmers see channels as safer (P9, p. 11). |

| System | No system is built. The paper studies the Go language (Google, 2009) and six open-source Go applications: Docker, Kubernetes, etcd, CockroachDB, gRPC-Go and BoltDB. Each has 3.3–4.9 years of history and 9K–2297K lines of code, and all are deployed in production. gRPC-C (C/C++, 140K lines) is used as a comparison. | pp. 1, 3, 4 |

| Levels with message semantics | Language: no. Channels are one primitive beside shared-memory primitives; Go "provides frameworks for both shared memory and message passing" and encourages channels. Hardware, instruction set, kernel: not stated. Runtime: goroutines are user-level threads that the runtime maps M-to-N onto kernel threads; whether they communicate by messages is not stated. Started message-based and later added other paths: not stated. | pp. 2–3 |

| Receiving unit and state ownership | The unit is the goroutine, which receives from channels. Its state is not private. Local variables declared before an anonymous function are shared between parent and child goroutines. Shared memory is reachable through Mutex, RWMutex, Cond, atomic, Once and WaitGroup. A reference sent over a channel lets both goroutines reach the same variable (Docker#22985, CockroachDB#6111). | pp. 3, 9 |

-| Message mechanism | Channels (`chan`). Unbuffered: send or receive blocks until the other side acts (synchronous). Buffered: send blocks only when the buffer is full. The receiver is named by the channel value. `select` waits on several channel operations and picks at random when more than one is ready. Rules: a nil channel blocks forever; sending to a closed channel, or closing a channel twice, panics at run time. `context`, `Pipe` and the `time` library are other forms of message passing. | p. 3 |

+| Message mechanism | Channels (`chan`). Unbuffered: send or receive blocks until the other side acts (synchronous). Buffered: send blocks only when the buffer is full. `select` waits on several channel operations and picks at random when more than one is ready. Rules: a nil channel blocks forever; sending to a closed channel, or closing a channel twice, panics at run time. `context` and `Pipe` are other forms of message passing (p. 3); the `time` library uses channels internally (p. 10). | pp. 3, 10 |

| Non-message primitives | At the language and library level: Mutex, RWMutex (in Go, write requests take priority over read requests, unlike `pthread_rwlock_t`), Cond, atomic, Once, WaitGroup, and shared local variables through anonymous functions. The paper gives no reason why Go keeps them; it only says Go "supports traditional shared memory accesses". | pp. 3, 6 |
| Self-definition | Not applicable: a defect study of applications; the paper does not discuss how the language or runtime is implemented. | — |
| Interposition | Not stated. | — |
| Cost of message primitives | Not measured. | — |

| Performance results | No performance result is measured. Table 3 gives goroutine counts and lifetimes, not performance. On three gRPC benchmarks, gRPC-Go creates 2.67–201.46 times as many goroutines as gRPC-C creates threads. The average goroutine lifetime is 63.23–92.73% of total run time, against 100% for gRPC-C threads. "gRPC-C is faster than gRPC-Go" is quoted from [22], not measured. | p. 4 |
| Scaling | Not applicable: no scaling measured. | — |

-| Attributed causes | Not applicable for performance. Related cause, stated by third parties (the authors, not Go's designers): the built-in deadlock detector's limits are "largely due to the design goal of the built-in detector—minimal runtime overhead". This is inherent to detecting deadlocks in the scheduler. No measurement isolates it. | pp. 8–9 |
-| Fate and reasons | Not applicable: no system is evaluated for fate. Go was the 9th most popular language on GitHub in 2017, with 187K repositories. | p. 3 |

+| Attributed causes | Not applicable for performance. Related cause, stated by third parties (the authors, not Go's designers): the built-in deadlock detector's limits are "largely due to the design goal of the built-in detector—minimal runtime overhead". The authors add that a detector in the runtime scheduler finds complex blocking bugs only with great difficulty without losing performance. No measurement isolates it. | pp. 8–9 |
+| Fate and reasons | Not applicable: no system is evaluated for fate. Go was the 9th most popular language on GitHub in 2017; at the time of writing there were 187K Go repositories. | p. 3 |

| Concurrency defects | **Population:** six Go applications; 3211 commits matched keywords, and a random sample of them gave 171 bugs (p. 5). **Categories:** behaviour, either blocking (broader than deadlock: it includes waiting with no circular wait) or non-blocking; cause, either shared memory or message passing (p. 5). **Totals:** 85 blocking, 86 non-blocking; 105 shared memory, 66 message passing (Table 5, p. 5). **Blocking** (Table 6, p. 6): shared memory 36 (Mutex 28, RWMutex 5, Wait 3), about 42%; message passing 49 (Chan 29, Chan with other primitives 16, messaging libraries 4), about 58%. **Non-blocking** (Table 9, p. 9; p. 10): shared memory 69, about 80% (traditional 46, anonymous function 11, WaitGroup 6, library 6); message passing 17, about 20% (channel 16, library 1). Message-order defects: 3 bugs from `select`'s random choice (p. 10). Protocol violations: closing a channel twice, missing send, receive or close (pp. 7, 10). **Fixes:** blocking-bug patches average 6.8 lines, and about 90% adjust synchronization primitives (p. 8). About 69% of non-blocking bugs are fixed by restricting timing (p. 11). Channels also fix shared-memory bugs (Table 11, p. 11). **Detection:** the built-in deadlock detector finds 2 of 21 reproduced blocking bugs (Table 8, p. 8). The race detector finds 10 of 20 non-blocking bugs within 100 runs (Table 12, p. 11). **By construction:** the paper claims no design prevents any of these defects. It tests the belief that message passing is less error-prone and refutes it for blocking bugs (Observation 3, p. 6). It supports the belief for non-blocking bugs "when used correctly" (Implication 6, p. 11). | pp. 5–11 |

| What shapes programs | Language features and libraries shape correctness: anonymous-function goroutines, buffered versus unbuffered channels, `select`'s random choice, the `time`, `context` and `testing` libraries, and Go's RWMutex implementation (pp. 2, 6, 9–10). So does programmers' understanding: "the lack of a clear understanding in new Go features" (p. 9), and channels are only useful if programmers understand them and Go's other synchronization (p. 12). Evidence: manual root-cause analysis of 171 real bugs. | pp. 2, 6, 9–10, 12 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Not applicable: hardware is not discussed. | — |
| New: cause dimension (shared memory vs. message passing) | Bugs are classified by how goroutines communicate: by misprotecting shared memory or by misusing message passing. | pp. 2, 5 |

| New: message passing is less error-prone (common belief, refuted for blocking bugs) | "Contrary to the common belief", message passing causes 58% of blocking bugs, while shared-memory primitives are used more. Message passing causes fewer non-blocking bugs. | pp. 2, 6, 10–12 |

# Protocol change: reading-pilot

Saved as \`sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md\`.

## What changed
- \`extraction-form.md\`:
  - New *Applies to* column (I1–I4 per field); a field outside the paper's criteria is \`n/a (I3)\`, and \`not stated\` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
  - Values in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* are tagged measured / simulated / design figure / analytical / read off.
  - *Reference*: pages are those printed on \`papers/P*.pdf\` (else its PDF page), with the version (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), the publisher's page range and any offset; abstract-only content cites \`abstract\`. Criteria I1–I4.
  - *Paper type*: one or more types, plus "position or analytical argument".
  - *Levels with message semantics*: adds \`partly\` (a message is a primitive at the level but other paths exist, naming the message-only operations), and for kernels and multicomputers separate answers between cores or nodes and within a core.
- \`quality.md\`:
  - Scale adds \`n/a\`, only for a source not read or a question that cannot apply, with the reason.
  - Q3: analytical models count as no.
  - Q4: a hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3, yes if the counts are compared with another named study.
  - Q5: for I3, the sampling procedure replaces the hardware setup.
  - Q9: for I3, yes if no author developed the studied programs.
- \`criteria.md\`, I3: adds "Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term."

## Why
The reading pilot (P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22, P33) showed the form and the checklist did not fit most papers:
- most fields did not apply to bug studies or analytical papers;
- readers cited five different kinds of page numbers;
- the strict yes/no on levels hid the differences the review is about;
- abstract-only and I3 records could only answer "no" to quality questions that could not apply.

Lu et al. (2008) met I3 only by inference, because it speaks of shared variables, not shared memory.

## Papers affected
The pilot records P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22 and P33 were written under the previous form and are not re-read. Their fields are mapped to the new form at synthesis (4a). P5 meets I3 as changed. Every later record uses the new form.
EOF
